title: GBT begins series production of solid-state battery cells - electrive.com
content:
Greater Bay Technology, a Chinese battery developer supported by the GAC Group, has started series production of solid-state battery cells in Guangzhou. Production is taking place on a converted lithium-ion line with an initial capacity of 1 GWh, which can be expanded to up to 4 GWh.
GBT starts series production of solid-state cells in Guangzhou.
Image: Greater Bay Technologies
On 13 October, GBT began series production of all-solid-state battery cells at its plant in Nansha, near Guangzhou. Instead of building a new dedicated facility, the company repurposed an existing lithium-ion production line. The plant currently has a capacity of 1 GWh for solid-state cells. According to the company, if demand increases, the remaining capacity of the 4 GWh plant can also be converted to solid-state cell production.
According to GBT, two of its production cells have met the requirements in tests conducted by the National Power Battery Innovation Center. The company claims to be the first manufacturer whose cells have been verified under the new regulatory framework. The standard is, among other things, meant to provide a clearer distinction between true solid-state batteries and semi-solid or hybrid cells.
The core technological innovation lies in the manufacturing process. Many solid-state battery programmes rely on sulphide electrolytes, which require oxygen-free and extremely dry environments for processing, often necessitating specially designed production facilities.
GBT states that its cells are the first to be tested and certified according to the requirements of the Chinese
Standard GB/T 48093.1-2026
. The standard, “Solid-state battery for electric vehicle – Part 1: Terms and classification,” was published on 28 August 2026 but will not formally enter into force until 1 January 2028.
China has introduced a new standard, GB/T 48093.1-2026.
GBT is taking a different approach. The company’s proprietary organic-inorganic composite electrolyte is first introduced into the cell as a liquid precursor and then solidified inside. This is said to create an adaptable, elastic interface with the electrodes.
Since the electrolyte is formed inside the cell, key production steps such as electrode manufacturing, stacking, formation, and testing can continue on conventional lithium-ion equipment, according to GBT. The main modification was to the electrolyte filling process, where the precursor is injected and cured in a dry, oxygen-free environment.
GBT relies on repurposed lithium-ion production
The Chinese cell manufacturer says the production line can manufacture both conventional lithium-ion cells and solid-state cells, switching between the two technologies as demand requires. GBT aims to reduce capital investment and economic risk during the ramp-up of the new cell technology. The company also produces the solid electrolyte and key raw materials itself and claims to hold more than 50 patents for the technology.
“This is not a new line built from scratch; it is an existing line with a new core,” says GBT founder and CTO Huang Xiangdong, who says the project progressed from A-samples in April to series production in October.
For its technology platform, GBT cites energy densities between 260 and 480 Wh/kg, depending on the cell generation and material configuration. The first generation now in production is based on pouch cells for automotive applications and established electrode materials. Later generations are expected to use lithium-metal anodes, among other innovations. GBT states that samples are already being tested by customers from various industries, with some cells also undergoing testing and validation with automakers.
In terms of safety, GBT refers to tests conducted in accordance with the Chinese
Battery Standard GB 38031-2025
. In an externally conducted nail penetration test on a fully charged cell, neither fire nor explosion occurred. Regarding lifespan, the manufacturer has so far only stated that the cycle stability is comparable to conventional lithium-ion cells.
Alongside the start of production, GBT has announced its first cooperation partners. Hubei Liming Lithium Technology is to integrate the cells into battery systems for vehicles and stationary storage. Additionally, there is a collaboration with an eVTOL aircraft development centre in Shenzhen. Furthermore, GBT states that it is in advanced discussions with several major automakers regarding series applications.
The battery developer, supported by GAC, is entering an environment where battery quality has recently become a major focus for the automotive group itself. There have been increasing reports of
issues with LFP cells from supplier CALB
in the widely used Aion S in China, particularly in high-mileage vehicles. GAC Aion and CALB have responded with extended warranty and service measures. There is no connection to GBT or its solid-state technology.
GBT sees electric vehicles as the primary target market for its solid-state cells. The company also mentions other applications, including eVTOLs, humanoid robots, stationary storage, and special vehicles. In Europe, the battery developer is working with the
commercial vehicle startup Flynt
and offers its technology through cell supplies, technology transfer, and joint ventures.
Whether this approach truly enables a faster and more capital-efficient path to the industrialisation of solid-state batteries will now be demonstrated in series production. The decisive factor will be whether the technology can be manufactured in larger quantities with stable quality, competitive costs, and the announced performance specifications.

title: Trafigura secures access to lithium from EnergyX - electrive.com
content:
Commodity trader Trafigura has signed a binding 10-year offtake agreement with EnergyX for 100,000 tonnes of battery-grade lithium products from its projects in the USA and Chile. A significant portion of the lithium is to be supplied to US battery plants.
EnergyX lithium project in Chile
Image: EnergyX
Through an agreement with EnergyX, Trafigura has once again secured access to battery-grade lithium. This follows a binding offtake agreement signed in March with
Smackover Lithium
for the supply of battery-grade lithium carbonate from the South West Arkansas Project, involving a volume of 80,000 tonnes over ten years.
The agreement with EnergyX is a big deal too. Trafigura has secured 100,000 tonnes of lithium products over ten years, sourced from two projects. This means Trafigura will obtain lithium carbonate from EnergyX’s Black Giant project in Antofagasta, Chile, as well as lithium hydroxide from the Lonestar project in Texas, USA. Lithium carbonate is typically used as a precursor for LFP cathodes, while lithium hydroxide is more commonly used for NMC and NCA cathodes.
Trafigura has committed to purchasing 66 per cent of the offtake volume from the first phase of Black Giant and 30 per cent of the offtake volume from the first phase of Lonestar. A significant portion of these volumes will be used to supply the US battery industry, according to the company.
Lithium offtake deal worth around USD 2 billion
According to EnergyX, the agreement is valued at more than two billion US dollars based on current lithium market prices. What remains unclear is whether Trafigura will pay spot market prices or if the two companies have agreed on a fixed price tier. Both companies have declined to comment on the matter.
“Offtake agreements are among the most important steps in taking a lithium project from development to production,” said Teague Egan, founder and CEO of EnergyX. “A long-term purchase commitment from a counterparty of Trafigura’s scale and credit quality shows that the market wants EnergyX’s product. It also gives lenders and investors the revenue visibility they need before committing capital to commercial construction.”
Strengthening the US battery supply chain
Daniel von Arx, Head of Battery Metals at Trafigura, added: “We are pleased to support EnergyX as it develops its lithium projects in Chile and the US. Long-term offtake is an important step in moving projects into production, and this agreement reflects our ability to help bring strategic critical minerals projects online and build secure, diversified supply chains. Drawing on our logistics network and market expertise, we look forward to supplying these battery-grade lithium products to customers, supporting supply chains for the US automotive and energy storage industries.”

title: Gravita eyes African lead recycling expansion with new Mozambique unit – Batteries International
content: India-based lead battery recycling group Gravita is considering a potential expansion of its operations in Africa by incorporating a new business in Mozambique, Batteries International can reveal. Gravita confirmed on October 8 that the enterprise, Green Maputo Recyclers, had been formed through two existing subsidiary units — Gravita Netherlands and Singapore-registered Gravita Global. Future business opportunities for Green Maputo, formally incorporated on October 2, could include lead recycling in addition to aluminium and rubber, the group said in a filing with the National Stock Exchange of India. The announcement came just days after Gravita confirmed it had formed another company as a springboard to entering the US market. Gravita said it was not giving further details about Green Maputo at this stage as the enterprise was newly incorporated and yet to commence business. However, the move could herald a strategic expansion of operations in the southeast African nation, where the group’s Gravita Mozambique battery recycling business was launched in 2007. That operation is located 15km from Maputo, Mozambique’s capital. Latest available data shows Gravita Mozambique handles used lead batteries, aluminium and plastics, with an overall recycling capacity of 13,400 tonnes. The Gravita group also has plastics recycling operations in Tanzania, Ghana, Senegal and India. In 2023, the group announced the start of commercial production of lead at its battery recycling plant in the West African nation of Togo. title: Second life storage has an information problem, not a chemistry one – Batteries International
content:
Industry Insights, Lead
Written by:
Engr Anis ur Rehman, graduate researcher in Electrical Engineering, Griffith University, Australia.
Read Later
The case for second life batteries has always been easy to make. A pack retires from a vehicle with most of its useful energy still intact. Stationary applications ask far less of a cell than traction does, and the alternative is recycling something that still works. The engineering is sound. The economics should follow.
But, mostly, this hasn’t happened. And the reason isn’t chemistry – it’s paperwork.
Consider what actually arrives at a second life integrator. Packs from several manufacturers, in different formats and chemistries, with different module architectures. Some came out of written-off vehicles, some from fleet replacements, some from warranty returns. What almost none of them bring with them is a credible account of how they were treated. No temperature history. No record of how often they were fast charged, or how long they sat at full charge in a hot car park, or how deeply they were cycled. In many cases the battery management system holds some of this and will not give it up, because the data is proprietary and the vehicle manufacturer has no commercial reason to share it.
Ageing is a path, not a state
So the integrator is handed a population of assets and asked to say what they are worth.
This is where the standard toolkit fails. Every degradation model in the literature is history dependent. Ageing is a path, not a state. Calendar ageing at high state of charge does something different to the cell than aggressive cycling does, and the two leave the pack in different conditions even when they arrive at the same remaining capacity. Two packs measuring 80 per cent today can have very different futures depending on how they got there. If you do not know the path, the models you have are not the models you need.
There is a second problem underneath that one, which is that capacity is not health. Measuring remaining capacity is easy and it is the number everyone quotes, but it misses resistance growth, it misses whether lithium plating has occurred, and above all it misses spread. A pack is a population of cells, and a second life asset is a population of packs. What matters commercially is not the average. It is the distribution, and specifically the bottom tail of it, because the weakest module sets the usable window for the string it sits in. One cell hitting its voltage limit early stops the whole string, whatever the other cells could still deliver.
That spread widens over time. Cells that started close together drift apart, and the drift accelerates as the weaker ones work harder to keep up. In a first life pack, with a single manufacturer, one chemistry and one thermal history, this is manageable. In a second life pack assembled from mixed sources it is the central design problem, and it is the one that quietly destroys revenue three years into a project when a string that was rated for a certain throughput stops delivering it.
This is why financing is hard, and it is worth being precise about why. Lenders and insurers are not frightened of degradation. Degradation is expected and can be priced. What they cannot price is unquantified uncertainty. If you hand an underwriter a single number for state of health with no statement of confidence behind it, they will either assume the worst case or decline to write the policy. Neither outcome gets the project built. What the financial side actually needs is a defensible distribution of remaining useful life, with a stated confidence interval, a monitoring plan that will detect divergence early, and a replacement reserve sized to match. That is an information product, and the industry does not currently make it.
It is solvable by the industry if it decides the prize is worth it
The encouraging part is that quite a lot can be recovered from cheap measurements at the terminals. Internal resistance across a few rates and temperatures says something about degradation mode. Relaxation behaviour after a pulse says more. Features extracted from a slow charge, of the kind familiar to anyone who has worked with differential voltage or incremental capacity analysis, carry information about what has been lost and by what mechanism. Self discharge measured over a rest period picks up the packs that will cause trouble. Balancing energy required during a full charge is a direct read on spread. None of this needs a laboratory, and all of it can be done at goods inwards.
The limitation is not the measurement. It is the labelling. To turn those features into a statement about remaining life you need a reference set of packs whose true history and true subsequent life are both known, and you need enough of them to cover the chemistries and the use patterns coming back. Everybody who has such data regards it as commercially sensitive, so nobody has built the shared reference set that would make the whole sector’s estimates credible. That is a collective action problem, not a technical one, and it is solvable by the industry if it decides the prize is worth it.
There is a design response too, which is to stop fighting the heterogeneity and build for it. Module level power electronics let each unit work to its own limit instead of the weakest. Shorter strings reduce how much capacity one bad module can strand. Grading incoming packs into tiers and matching them within a tier costs handling time and saves years of life. Control that respects the weakest element rather than the average will always beat control that assumes uniformity, because the assumption is simply false in this application.
Regulation will help eventually. Battery passport requirements will give future packs a documented history and much of this argument will fall away for anything built after the rules bite. But the packs arriving now predate them, and so will the packs arriving for most of the next decade. The industry needs an answer for the vehicles already on the road, and that answer has to be inference rather than records.
None of this diminishes the case for second life. It sharpens it. The technology works. What it lacks is a way to certify a mixed population of assets with unknown pasts, to a standard that a lender will accept. Until somebody builds that, second life will keep producing good demonstrations and small projects, and the packs will keep going to recycling because that is the route with a price attached.

title: Whitmer Touts Michigan EV Battery Investment Push
content:
Battery News
Battery Manufacturing
Stationary Batteries
Automotive & Mobility
Speaking at The Battery Show North America in Detroit, the governor says she'll "work with anyone" to keep landing EV investment before her term ends.
October 13, 2026
5 Min Read
Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer addresses attendees of The Battery Show North America on October 13, 2026.
Battery Technology
At a Glance
Whitmer spoke at The Battery Show North America, highlighting Ford, LG Energy Solution and Mitra Chem deals.
Her tenure weathered the EV industry's changing fortunes under vastly different presidential administrations.
Whitmer visited South Korea and Taiwan to pursue new EV manufacturing partnerships before leaving office.
Standing before an international audience of battery executives, engineers, and investors at
The Battery Show North America in Detroit
this morning, Governor Gretchen Whitmer delivered what may be remembered as a capstone address on her signature economic project: transforming Michigan into one of the nation's premier battery manufacturing hubs. With her second term set to conclude in January 2027, the speech read as both a victory lap and a pitch — a governor eager to cement her legacy while still trying to close deals on her way out the door.
Whitmer framed her eight years in office as a response to an industry at an inflection point, pointing to the rise of electric vehicles and driverless technology as forces reshaping an industry Michigan has led "for more than a century." Her message was one of agency: "We had a choice to make: watch the future happen somewhere else, or build it right here in Michigan. And of course, we're choosing to compete." That framing reflects a strategic bet many battery experts endorse — that the US cannot legislate its way to manufacturing competitiveness, but must build expertise by working directly with companies and countries that already have it.
Related:
Battery Breaking-News Headlines
Counting the wins
Whitmer tallied the investments her administration has helped secure, giving top billing to
Ford's battery plant in Marshall
— built on a licensing partnership with China's CATL for LFP technology.
Ford's BlueOval Battery Park. Credit: Ford
She also cited LG Energy Solution's
"historic investment" in Lansing's Delta Township
, as well as LGES’ “
major expansion in Holland
, building on a relationship that goes back for 15 years.” She noted as well Mitra Chem's $370 million investment in Muskegon County — which she said established "the first mass production facility in LFP cathodes in North America," extending Michigan's supply chain ambitions beyond cell assembly into materials. She rounded out the list with
Our Next Energy
, a homegrown company she said proves Michigan-made batteries can power the grid, commercial transportation, and national defense, not just cars.
A Gotion-shaped absence
One name was missing: Gotion. The omission is telling, because the Gotion saga is arguably the most consequential episode in Whitmer's battery strategy — not for what it built, but for what it exposed about the political cost of pursuing the same technology-transfer logic she championed again today.
When Gotion Inc., the US arm of China's Gotion High-Tech, announced its $2.4 billion plant near Big Rapids in 2022, it carried the same rationale as Ford-CATL: foreign expertise deployed on American soil to close a manufacturing knowledge gap. As Celina Mikolajczak, then Chief Battery Technical Officer at Lyten, put it at a 2024 industry panel, "There's a world of difference between writing a recipe or seeing a recipe and going, 'Yeah, I know how to do that,' and actually producing the dish.
Asia has been doing the cooking
" — accumulating decades of hands-on production knowledge American manufacturers still lack.
Related:
As Energy Storage Demand Explodes, The Battery Show North America Delivers Industry's Most Comprehensive Showcase
Battery manufacturing expert Celina Mikolajczak (center) at The Battery Show North America in 2025. Credit: The Battery Show
Instead, the project became a political battleground, fought on starkly different terms by both sides.
Opponents
, led by Representative John Moolenaar, chair of the House select committee on China,
framed Gotion as a national security threat
, working to block federal subsidies for Chinese-affiliated battery firms and amplifying unsubstantiated claims the plant could be used to surveil nearby military installations. A reported $30 million ad campaign branded the plant a "Trojan horse" for the Chinese Communist Party; voters recalled Green Charter Township's entire board over its support in 2023; and PAC-funded ads tying the project to the CCP helped GOP candidate Tom Barrett defeat Democrat Curtis Hertel in Michigan's 7th District in 2024. Some local resistance also reflected more conventional land-use and farmland concerns.
Related:
Toyota's New Michigan Battery Lab Signals Commitment to Flexible EV Strategy Amid Market Uncertainty
Anti-Gotion sign on a pickup truck outside a horse farm where GOP VP candidate J.D. Vance spoke on August 27, 2024. Credit: JeffF Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images
Gotion and its allies
countered that the opposition had little to do with legitimate security review. In a letter to Michigan's economic development agency reported by Reuters, Gotion's attorney blamed "politically motivated" opposition driven by "racist and ethnically charged stereotypes" for the delays that doomed the project. Industry voices pointed to Ford-CATL and GM-LG as proof the technology-transfer model itself wasn't the problem — Volta Energy's James Frith has argued structured licensing deals like Ford's could be "more broadly explored" to address security concerns without blocking knowledge transfer, while Avicenne Energy's Michael Sanders called building battery capability in total isolation "a fool's proposition."
Still dealmaking, still building
Whitmer also highlighted the institutional architecture behind her strategy — the Office of Future Mobility and Electrification, the Michigan Innovation Fund, a restored R&D tax credit, and workforce investments built around "skills across the continuum" rather than traditional degrees alone.
Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer speaks to exhibitors at The Battery Show North America in Detroit on October 13, 2026. Credit: The Battery Show
Perhaps most newsworthy: her disclosure that she led a Michigan delegation to South Korea and Taiwan weeks ago to deepen ties with advanced manufacturing companies. "Whether it's folks from another state or another country, I will go anywhere and work with anyone to bring jobs and grow investments here in Michigan," she said — an implicit defense of the same international-partnership approach that cost her politically with Gotion, delivered with roughly three months left in office.
Context for the legacy
The speech arrives as Whitmer's battery agenda faces real headwinds: Gotion's collapse, a defunded state investment fund,
and tariff-driven uncertainty under the second Trump administration
complicating automaker decisions nationwide.
Against that backdrop, this morning's remarks were an attempt to control her own narrative — leading with the wins, reinforcing the institutional legacy, and reaffirming a commitment to international collaboration that has defined, and complicated, her tenure as she heads toward the exit in January 2027.

title: John Warner Maps Four Trends Transforming The Battery Industry
content:
Industry Outlook
Battery News
Market Analysis
At The Battery Show North America, John Warner assessed the battery industry’s current state and why its future is shifting.
October 13, 2026
3 Min Read
Dr. John Warner delivering the Chairman’s Welcome Address.
Maria Guerra
The Battery Show North America
, during the Chairman's Welcome Address, John Warner offered an industry assessment of the battery sector's current state. What was once viewed largely through the lens of electric vehicles (EVs) is now expanding into a much broader industrial story. Warner organized that story around four major currents shaping the sector today: changing demand, a more complex supply chain, the rise of defense as a driver of adoption, and the continued evolution of next-generation batteries.
The first of those currents is bifurcating demand. Warner directly challenged the narrative that batteries are losing momentum. “If you listen to the news, you’re going to think that EVs are dead and batteries are dead,” he said. “I’ll argue that they’re not dead, but we’re seeing a shift in where the demand is coming from.” While some EV growth has slowed in the US, other applications are accelerating. Warner pointed to grid energy storage, AI data systems, military applications, and drones as areas seeing increased interest and opportunity. This matters because it shows the battery industry is becoming a multi-sector platform technology relevant to infrastructure, computing, transportation, and national defense.
Related:
Peak Energy’s Dr. Lucy Li on Sodium-Ion Battery Innovations
State of the battery industry by John Warner. Courtesy of Maria Guerra.
The second current Warner mentioned is the supply chain. Warner said that battery sourcing used to be a logistics question,” he said. “You used to ask, ‘Where do I get my cathode materials? Who’s going to be my cell supplier?’” That has changed dramatically. But now he said, “It’s a compliance issue. It’s a legal issue, and in some cases a national security issue.” With
FEOC rules,
tariffs, and new Treasury guidance influencing sourcing choices, companies must now navigate regulatory exposure and geopolitical risk alongside cost and availability.
Third, Warner said defense is becoming a new center of gravity for the industry. As defense organizations push further into electrification and
unmanned systems, battery demand
is taking on a different character. Military and defense use cases can influence performance requirements, production priorities, and long-term investment decisions. They also reinforce Warner’s broader point that batteries should no longer be discussed only as clean energy tools. They are increasingly part of the infrastructure of national capability.
The fourth current is the next generation of batteries. Warner was clear that innovation remains the foundation of the sector’s future. “Technology continues to move,” he said. “It’s the basis for everything we do here.” He highlighted several examples: “Solid state continues to move closer and closer to production.
Sodium-ion
is starting to find homes in certain applications… LFP continues to be the breadwinner when you’re talking about low-cost applications.” In other words, multiple chemistries are advancing in parallel, each finding its place based on cost, performance, safety, and application fit.
Related:
Battery Show Keynotes Tackle Supply Chains, AI Impact & Manufacturing Scale from Oct. 12-15
Warner concluded: “Demand from the industry isn’t shrinking; it’s shifting.” The market is evolving, and the battery industry’s future will be shaped by technology, policy, and supply chain resilience.

title: Exploring AI and Resilience with Celonis' Peter Budweiser
content:
Exploring AI and Resilience with Celonis' Peter Budweiser
Prioritise Us
on Google
Supply Chain Digital speaks to Peter Budweiser about self-healing supply chains.
Amid ongoing supply chain disruption and AI integration, Supply Chain Digital speaks to Peter Budweiser, General Manager of Supply Chain at Celonis
In today's environment, supply chains are increasingly complex, facing challenges of modernisation,
fragmentation and AI implementation
Amid this, Supply Chain Digital spoke to Peter Budweiser, General Manager of Supply Chain at Celonis. In this role, he leads the development of innovative supply chain applications, overseeing work on inventory management, procurement and logistics.
Peter is at the forefront of Celonis' digital supply chain transformation, and is a regular visiting scholar at UC Berkeley, where he learns about modern digital technologies.
1. What does self-healing mean in the context of a supply chain, and how is it different from the approach most companies already use?
Most companies still operate purely in a reactive mode. Their data is spread across dozens of different systems, including ERP systems, warehouse management tools and transportation platforms. Then, when disruptions strike, traditional software essentially acts like a smoke detector. It sounds the alarm but leaves it up to your team to put "out the fire” manually by gathering data from various sources, stitching it together in spreadsheets, and patching the problem. Of course, this requires so much time and effort that responses are slow. And many smaller problems end up being ignored entirely.
With a self-healing supply chain, this model basically undergoes a 180-degree change. With a context model like the Celonis Context Model (CCM) as a basis, it creates a
real-time digital twin of your entire operation
across all your systems in use. So when a shipment is delayed, it can go beyond simply flagging the problem to directly analysing the downstream effects on inventory levels, production schedules and customer commitments. Even one step further – the system then simulates corrective actions, forecasts the outcome and automatically reallocates inventory – often before anyone even notices a disruption.
You can compare it to the human body. Your immune system handles everyday aches and minor issues in the background without you having to think about it, and you only intervene when there are major problems. That’s what "self-healing” means here: a system that continuously monitors, acts and learns on its own.
2. How does the Context Model trace the impact of disruption through to specific purchase orders and customer commitments?
When a major disruption like a port strike or a supplier failure happens, the real challenge is in assessing the impact — I call this the “blast radius.” Typically, this is a complete black box. But a context model fundamentally changes this situation by automatically tracking this “blast radius” in real time and showing you the exact impact on your customers.
So, how does the CCM work? At its core, it's a real-time digital twin of your business operations, based on a dynamic knowledge graph. It doesn't store static data; instead, it understands how every element of your business is connected to everything else. And because it captures these connections, you can simulate how a single roadblock will ripple through your entire business.
To make this a bit more tangible, here’s a real-world example. Say one of your
critical suppliers experiences a plant shutdown
. As soon as this news becomes known, the system directly maps it to the relevant supplier in your digital twin. From there, it automatically tracks the supply chain. It identifies open orders, traces them to raw materials, links these materials to production schedules and connects them all the way to active customer orders.
Within seconds, you can see the entire network at risk. You receive an order-specific alert of a disruption, and you can run through alternative scenarios and pick the smartest workaround before your customers feel the impact.
Peter Budweiser, General Manager, Supply Chain at Celonis
3. How does Celonis extract and encode tribal knowledge, and what happens to it during staff changes?
Mapping objects, events and relationships gives you a foundational view of how a company operates, but that alone is not enough. What's missing is the unique operational context that AI agents need to make intelligent decisions tailored to your specific business.
To solve this, the Context Model integrates this rich operational context directly into the system. We're talking your process models, your business objectives, guidelines, roles and key metrics, everything that matters to your business — for example via specialised knowledge repositories.
You can think of these knowledge repositories as a private, company-specific “Wikipedia” designed specifically for AI. A vast amount of critical domain knowledge lives in SOPs, guidelines, contracts, or simply in the minds of experienced employees. Knowledge repositories allow you to capture this tacit expertise and transform generalist AI models into specialists for your specific business operations.
You can extract and integrate this knowledge in the way that best fits your set-up — whether that's by having
agents gather insights directly
Alexander Rinke, Celonis Co-Founder and CEO. Credit: Celonis
4. How does Celonis's approach avoid risk from sudden policy changes?
As our Co-CEO Alex Rinke recently wrote in an open letter, AI holds incredible potential, but it cannot be used in isolation. Basing your entire operational AI strategy on a single provider’s LLM is an enormous risk.
That’s why Celonis serves as an independent, open knowledge layer for businesses. The Context Model translates the complex reality of your business into a structured language that any AI model can understand. Since it is completely system-agnostic, you retain full control over your operational intelligence.
I really want to stress that, because it's so important. Your data and your knowledge stay with you, even when the systems or models change.
You could use OpenAI today, switch to Anthropic tomorrow, or integrate an open-source model next year without losing even a shred of context. Ultimately, you retain complete control over your data, your processes and your long-term AI strategy
5. What does a truly self-healing supply chain look like in five to ten years, and what's the biggest barrier standing between companies and that future?
In five to ten years, a truly self-healing supply chain will operate as a fully composable and autonomous ecosystem in which highly specialised AI agents constantly analyse and optimise workflows in real time.
The biggest hurdle currently holding companies back is what I call the “
AI productivity gap
.” It closely resembles the productivity lag during the electrification of factories in the 1890s. When electricity became more broadly available, factory owners simply swapped out their old steam engines for electric ones, but kept the exact same rigid floor plan and line shafts. Productivity barely improved for another thirty years. Real progress didn’t come until executives completely redesigned the factory floor around the new technology.
Today, I see companies making the exact same mistake with AI by simply plugging copilots and bots into outdated, inefficient processes. You can’t simply integrate
new technologies into old ways of working
. You have to fundamentally redesign the way work is done. The companies that truly build self-healing supply chains will be those that use Process Intelligence to redesign their operations from the ground up for the AI era.

tk accelis: Building a Predictive Supply Chain Control Tower
Prioritise Us
on Google
tk accelis is helping organisations with end-to-end supply chain solutions. Credit: Getty Images
Ilse Henne, CEO of tk accelis, explores how the company is driving end-to-end solutions to help organisations stay resilient amid turbulence
The modern supply chain is complex, requiring visibility and resilience, as well as flexibility and keen insights.
Organisations around the world are beginning to integrate visibility into their operations, understanding it to be crucial to success, but many still lack the ability to
use this visibility to prevent
disruption.
tk accelis is working to support supply chains around the world as they move towards prediction and action.
A new business model
In June 2026, thyssenkrupp Materials Services unveiled its new name – tk accelis. This aligns with its path of becoming an independent company, as part of thyssenkrupp AG’s ACES 2030 strategy program.
Alongside this, is it a representation of moving away from being a
pure materials distributor
and towards a supply chain service provider. The name comes from “accelerate” and “access”, with a purpose of “Moving industries – from source to success”.
The aim is to accelerate the success of its customers’ business operations, aiming to operate over a vast global supplier network, offer customised processing of materials with increased transparency and efficiency, as well as offering supply chain management solutions.
tk accelis is working to form a growing portfolio of data-driven and AI-enhanced digital solutions that help drive resilience, flexibility and transparency.
Since the launch of its new name, tk accelis has been signing agreements and expanding operations,
establishing itself as a global leader
At Capital Markets Day, CEO Ilse Henne said: “Our performance demonstrates that tk accelis is ready for the capital markets. We have shaped the company with the right strategy and the right team.
Ilse Henne, CEO of tk accelis. Credit: thyssenkrupp AG
“Today, we see ourselves exactly where industry needs us and where we can create sustainable value. This is why we serve as a partner of choice for
materials and supply chain solutions
across many advanced industries. Demand for our products and solutions is increasing across all our core markets, particularly in North America.
“As an independent company, we want to make decisions even faster, take targeted investments and grow our higher-margin businesses.”
Key facts
tk accelis operates across more than 400 locations
It has more than 250,000 customers
The company saw sales of €11.4bn (US$12.7bn) in fiscal year 2024/25
tk accelis has operations in more than 30 countries
The addressable market for tk accelis is expected to grow at an annual growth rate of 4%
End-to-end supply chain support
tk accelis aims to help companies transform their supply chains, unlocking a strategic advantage. Its Global Control Tower acts as an intelligent hub, designed to drive end-to-end visibility, control and execution.
The control tower operates across a range of services, working to meet the needs of its clients. Through tk accelis, clients can have access to
support on global sourcing
, inventory management and materials expertise. The tower operates from end-to-end, starting with sourcing queries, taking the client through logistics, modernisation and integration.
Through its supply chain resilience services, tk accelis is offering multi-tier transparency, which then translates to strategic positioning, predictive planning and integration of ESG governance.
“For decades, global supply chains have been optimised for efficiency, availability and cost. Today, companies must navigate another dimension at the same time: geopolitical risk,” Ilse wrote on LinkedIn.
“Tariffs and sanctions can change the economics of a supply chain. Political developments can change sourcing options. And uncertainty itself has become something businesses need to manage. This makes the ability to understand and manage supply chains more important than ever.”
As supply chains become more complex, having an end-to-end solution is critical. It ensures that they are not stalling as soon as they have the information, but can strategically use it to transform their operations.

title: Volkswagen, PowerCo and Gotion Plan Battery JVs
content:
Volkswagen, PowerCo and Gotion Plan Battery JVs
Prioritise Us
on Google
PowerCo has experience operating Gigafactory production facilities in Salzgitter, Germany.
Thomas Schmall, Volkswagen Group technology board member, says China's Gotion will invest in strengthening Europe's battery cells supply chain
Volkswagen and Chinese battery cell supplier Gotion High Tech have announced a deal as part of which the two companies will build battery gigafactories in Spain and Slovakia alongside a cathode production plant in Morocco. The agreement between Volkswagen, its battery-focused subsidiary PowerCo and Gotion High Tech was announced in late September. As part of the agreement, the two companies will invest EUR3.22 billion (US$3.7 bn) in two battery production facilities in Spain and in Slovakia in late September 2026, as well as an LFP (lithium-iron-phosphate) cathode production facility in Morocco. Gotion is investing approximately EUR1.598bn in total.
“I am delighted that we are expanding our long-standing partnership with Gotion into the joint industrial production of LFP batteries to strengthen Europe’s battery industry,” says Thomas Schmall, Member of the Board of Management of Volkswagen Group for Technology and Chairman of the Supervisory Board of PowerCo SE.
“This marks a major breakthrough for both companies and brings us one step closer to the forefront of electric mobility. Volkswagen is the first European automotive manufacturer to cover the entire battery value chain, from development and cathode materials through to production.”
Thomas Schmall, Volkswagen Group Board Member for Technology (Credit: Volkswagen AG)
Localising Volkswagen’s battery supply chain
In March, Volkswagen
announced
that it would be producing Unified Cells at its Salzgitter, Germany gigafactory based on Gotion High-Tech’s technology for the electric vehicles (EVs) that it manufactures under the Volkswagen, ŠKODA and SEAT brands.
However, Volkswagen has been importing a proportion of its Unified Cells from Gotion High-Tech’s production facility in Anhui, China since 2025. One advantage of the deal is that it will allow a greater proportion of the Volkswagen Group’s EV battery requirements to be sourced from gigafactories located within the EU.
One of the major goals of the joint venture with Gotion is to develop the Valencia site into a European production hub for Unified Cells based on LFP technology. Unified Cells tend to be focused towards automotive applications.
“Volkswagen and PowerCo are building Europe’s battery industry,” says Frank Blome
CEO of PowerCo SE.
“The partnership with Gotion is the next milestone on this path: It strengthens the resilience of our value chain, accelerates industrialisation and combines PowerCo’s capabilities with the strengths of a long-standing partner.”
Frank Blome, CEO of PowerCo SE. Credit: LinkedIn
Production Capacities
The production facilities will be established as three separate joint ventures.
The initial industrial production capacity of battery cells at the Valencia gigafactory will be 29.1 GWh, while the Šurany factory will have a smaller 8.4 GWh capacity. The Valencia Gigafactory is currently in the ramp-up phase and will start operations in 2027, a PowerCo representative confirmed to Supply Chain Digital.
The Kenitra (Morocco) production site will have a production capacity for 100,000 tonnes of lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) cathode material per year. Initial production of cathode material has begun at the facility, with the plant operator plans to ramp-up production of LFP cells by the end of the year.
The agreement also covers joint procurement and sales activities in Europe.
Key facts about the Gotion and Volkswagen deal
Valencia, Spain: Unified Cell production with planned annual capacity of 29.1 GWh; PowerCo will hold 51% and Gotion 49%.
Šurany, Slovakia: battery-cell production for electric vehicles and energy-storage systems with planned annual capacity of 8.4 GWh; PowerCo will hold 49% and Gotion 51%.
Kenitra, Morocco: LFP cathode-material production with planned annual cathode production capacity of 100,000 tonnes.
Supply chain: The partnership links cathode materials, cell production, procurement and sales across Europe and North Africa.
Chemistry: LFP means lithium iron phosphate, a battery chemistry used in EVs and stationary energy storage.

title: Tesla Powerwalls supply most of record 745 MW California grid dispatch
content:
Tesla Energy
Tesla Powerwall
Tesla Virtual Power Plant
Fred Lambert
| Oct 14 2026 - 7:46 am PT
Image: Sunrun
Tesla Powerwalls did most of the heavy lifting as California’s home batteries set a new grid record last week. On October 6, more than 85,000 Powerwall owners sent over 600 MW to the grid, the bulk of a combined 745 MW dispatch that Sunrun announced today.
That’s 28% more than the 580 MW record the two companies set less than a month ago. And it’s bigger than most gas peaker plants in the state.
Tesla posted its record first
Tesla Energy put out its own numbers on October 8, two days after the event. The company said 85,000+ Powerwall owners across California dispatched more than 600 MW to help meet peak demand, calling it “a new record for the largest Powerwall VPP event.”
Sunrun followed this morning with a
that has Sunrun “leading” the dispatch. It says “the companies” delivered 669 MW on October 5 and 745 MW on October 6, but it doesn’t break out how much came from Sunrun customers versus Tesla customers.
Put Tesla’s figure against Sunrun’s total and Powerwalls account for roughly 80% of the record. In September, the share was even higher:
517 MW of the 580 MW came from about 110,000 Powerwalls
, and Sunrun owns or operates 55% of those.
So both companies are taking a victory lap for largely the same batteries. Sunrun is the biggest Powerwall channel in the country, which is why the two keep showing up in each other’s press releases.
There’s also an interesting detail in Tesla’s math. Just over 600 MW from about 85,000 homes works out to roughly 7 kW per home, well above the 5 kW continuous output of a Powerwall 2. That points to a fleet increasingly made of Powerwall 3 units, rated at 11.5 kW, and homes with more than one battery.
How the dispatch worked
The events came during an October heat wave, at the request of the California Energy Commission and the state’s utilities. Batteries discharged through multi-hour evening peaks to cut demand and push down real-time power prices.
Sunrun says October 5 was the first event this year where the state’s Demand Side Grid Support (DSGS) and Emergency Load Reduction Program (ELRP) both called dispatches at the same time across every participating investor-owned utility territory. DSGS kicks in once CAISO’s day-ahead price passes $200/MWh.
According to Sunrun, 745 MW is enough to cover every household in San Francisco and San Jose combined during peak hours. The company now has more than 120,000 home batteries enrolled in California grid programs.
The pace is what stands out. The previous residential record, 539 MW, stood from July 29, 2025, until September 9, 2026. It grew 8% in over a year, then 28% in four weeks.
Customers get paid for this, too. Sunrun CEO Mary Powell said “customers are being compensated for helping strengthen grid reliability.”
Next up: San Jose
Sunrun also says a Google-funded distributed power plant with PG&E in the San Jose area plans to enroll nearly 21,000 devices with Tesla and Everyday Electric, the company formerly known as Renew Home. Initial dispatches are expected this month.
It’s the first concrete piece of the
16.8 GW virtual power plant plan for data centers
that Tesla, Sunrun, and Renew Home announced in June. But it’s early: Sunrun notes the Tesla and Everyday Electric part of the project is still under a non-binding letter of intent.
Electrek’s Take
Tesla’s real advantage shows up here: a huge installed base and software that gets 85,000+ homes to respond to the same grid signal at once. Nobody else in residential storage is close.
The credit grab between Tesla and Sunrun is a bit silly. It’s one fleet, mostly Powerwalls, with Sunrun as the biggest owner. Fine. Both deserve it.
What I’d really like to see is energy, not just power. Both companies report MW, and neither gives MWh or exact duration. A 745 MW peak for 20 minutes and 745 MW held for three hours are very different things for the grid. The September event ran a three-hour evening window, which is good. Publishing MWh every time would make the case even stronger.
And this works because California pays for it. DSGS and ELRP put real money in homeowners’ pockets for discharging at the right time. Most states have nothing like it, so these batteries just sit there during peaks.

title: Ford opens preorder invites for the $30,000 Fathom EV pickup
content:
Ford Fathom
Peter Johnson
| Oct 14 2026 - 7:14 am PT
Want to be among the first to own
new EV pickup? You can now sign up for a preorder invite for the upcoming $30,000 Ford Fathom.
Ford Fathom preorder invites go live
Although preorders for the Fathom won’t officially open until early 2027, Ford is now inviting interested buyers to sign up for a preorder invite and become one of the first to own its all-new electric pickup.
The Fathom will start at $28,350 for the standard range battery model, or about half as much as the F-150 Lightning, Ford’s first attempt at an electric pickup. Even with the $1,595 destination fee, it will still start at under $30,000.
As the first model based on its new Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, Ford promises the Fathom will be a step change from its first-generation EVs.
Ford has yet to announce driving range figures, towing capability, and other key specs, but it did reveal a few details about the upcoming EV pickup.
Ford opens Fathom preorder invite list (Source: Ford.com)
For one, Ford previously said the Fathom will offer more passenger room than a Toyota RAV4, and that’s not including the frunk or truck bed. The company also claims it will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.
The interior will feature a “large touchscreen display” and will be the
first to have Apple Maps
directly integrated into the navigation system.
Other standard features include a Digital Key, Ford app remote control, and Apple CarPlay and Android Auto support.
Ford Fathom EV pickup prototype (Source: Jim Farley)
All Ford Fathom models will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free highway driving and will offer bidirectional charging capability.
It will use lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries to cut costs and vehicle weight, while also opening up interior space.
The cobalt-free and nickel-free LFP battery pack serves as the vehicle’s floor. As such, the low center of gravity improves handling and creates a quieter, more spacious interior.
Ford midsize EV pickup spotted testing in Arizona (Source: KindelAuto)
The low center of gravity, instant torque, and “obsessive chassis engineering” will make it fun to drive, Ford promises.
With even more downforce, Ford said the Fathom will have a targeted 0 to 60 mph time as fast as a Mustang EcoBoost.
Ford describes the Fathom as a “midsize, four-door electric pickup,” but the prototypes spotted testing appear to be about the size of a Maverick, which is generally considered a compact truck. Again, we’ll have to wait until closer to launch for final dimensions.
Covered Ford Fathom vehicle (Source: Ford)
We also know Ford’s upcoming EV pickup will have an NACS port after a few test mules were
captured at a Tesla Supercharger
over the summer.
You can sign up for your preorder invite on
Ford’s website here
to receive updates and to be among the first on the list.
Ford will officially open Fathom preorders in early 2027. The first Fathom prototypes are scheduled to roll off the production line at its 3-million-square-foot Louisville Assembly Plant (LAP) in 2027, with deliveries expected to begin later in the year.
CEO Jim Farley admitted at the
2026 Automotive News Congress
a few weeks ago that “It’s going to be a heck of an effort to launch this at scale, at cost, on time.”
A Ford spokesperson
confirmed with
Electrek
, however, that “We’ve said previously, ‘Fathom will launch in 2027’ – and there is no change to that.”
We should learn more about Ford’s upcoming EV pickup soon. Stay tuned for the latest updates.

title: The world record for the longest electric motorcycle ride has just been obliterated
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Zero Motorcycles
Guinness World Record
Micah Toll
| Oct 14 2026 - 1:08 am PT
The world record for the longest journey on an electric motorcycle on a single charge has just been absolutely demolished.
And it was done so by a Zero Motorcycles rider traveling 436.5 km (271.2 miles) before finally running out of juice.
The ride, completed by Belgian rider Jelle Verstaen aboard a Zero DS electric motorcycle, earned a new Guinness World Records title and blew past the previous record of 310.7 km (193 miles) by more than 125 km (78 miles).
And this wasn’t some one-off aerodynamic streamliner built specifically to chase a record. The bike was a production Zero DS equipped with the company’s optional Power Tank, bringing total battery capacity to 19.2 kWh. Verstaen was joined for the ride by two others on Zeros as well, with all three beating the previous record.
The record attempt began high in the French Alps and eventually wound its way down toward the Mediterranean coast, with Verstaen aiming to maintain an average cruising speed of around 52 km/h (32 mph).
That might not sound particularly fast for a motorcycle – and it certainly wasn’t – but speed was very much the enemy here. Aerodynamic drag increases dramatically as speeds rise, making relatively slow riding one of the best ways to stretch an electric motorcycle’s battery.
The result was a ride that lasted deep into the night and through the next morning.
Zero says the team specifically chose nighttime riding to reduce traffic, helping Verstaen maintain a steady, efficient pace. That became especially important as the route transitioned from the Alps toward lower elevations and eventually the Mediterranean.
And while Verstaen ultimately took the crown, he of course wasn’t the only Zero rider out there seeing just how far an electric motorcycle could go.
His riding partners on a Zero SR/S managed 350 km (217 miles) on a charge, while a DSR/X stretched its battery to 384 km (239 miles). Both would make for impressive range figures on their own, but the DS simply kept going.
The final portion of the record ride apparently wasn’t exactly pleasant, either.
Heavy rain arrived for roughly the last 100 km (62 miles), turning what was already an overnight endurance run into an increasingly soggy battle toward the finish.
But Verstaen and the DS continued onward until the bike ultimately covered 436.5 km, surpassing the previous record by more than 40%.
The ride
was tracked using GPS and independently witnessed as part of the Guinness World Records verification process.
For an electric motorcycle carrying less than 20 kWh of battery, traveling 271 miles on a charge is an impressive demonstration of just how efficient two-wheeled EVs can become when ridden carefully.
Electrek’s Take
This is quite a feat, and I love seeing electric motorcycles used for
all kinds of challenges
. There’s still a surprisingly persistent belief that electric motorcycles are inherently short-range machines, and traveling over 270 miles on less than 20 kWh of battery is a pretty good way to demonstrate just how much energy a motorcycle actually needs to move a person down the road.
But there are also some fairly large asterisks here.
For one thing, the route started high in the French Alps and worked its way toward the Mediterranean, meaning the riders enjoyed a significant net decrease in elevation. It wasn’t exactly 271 miles of coasting downhill, of course, and there were plenty of climbs and other terrain along the way, but gravity was nevertheless lending a helping hand over the course of the trip.
The bigger factor, though, was speed.
A target of around 52 km/h (32 mph) is incredibly efficient for an electric motorcycle, but it’s not representative of how most people actually ride motorcycles on the open road. At typical highway speeds, aerodynamic drag would chew through that battery much more quickly.
In fact, that low target speed may also help explain why so much of the attempt took place overnight. Maintaining around 32 mph on roads where daytime traffic is moving considerably faster could range from annoying to downright dangerous. Doing it in the middle of the night with much lighter traffic makes considerably more sense.
So no, this doesn’t mean you should expect to hop on a Zero DS and ride 271 miles at 70 mph without stopping.
But that’s not really the point of a record attempt, either.
Records are about finding the limits of what a machine can do under carefully optimized conditions, and Zero just demonstrated that a production electric motorcycle carrying less energy than many plug-in hybrid cars can travel more than 270 miles through the real world on a single charge.
That’s a heck of an achievement – even if you probably don’t want to replicate the pace on your next road trip.

title: Europe's second energy crisis largely skipped the solar hours - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In the 2026 crisis window, night-time day-ahead prices in Spain, Germany and Greece rose by €36 ($40.0) to €51/MWh against the same dates in 2025, while midday prices moved by between −€4 and +€14/MWh. Solar earned 43% to 50% of the baseload price over the first 227 days, against 85% to 91% after the 2022 shock, and the widening gap between noon and night is where the case for storage now sits.
14 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Europe has now lived through two energy crises in four years, and on the surface the second looks like a smaller copy of the first. In Spain, Germany and Greece, day-ahead prices rose in both, and in each case the shock followed a war that began in late February. Underneath, the two crises played out very differently across the day. In the months after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the cheapest hour of the average day still cost €149 ($165.6)/MWh in Spain, €193/MWh in Germany and €252/MWh in Greece. Between March and September 2026, front-month TTF averaged roughly €54/MWh, about half as much again as in the same months of 2025, which puts the fuel cost of a gas plant running at 55% efficiency near €97/MWh before carbon. Yet averaged over the 2026 window, the cheapest hour of the day fell to between €16/MWh and €25/MWh in all three markets, far below what any gas plant needed to run, while night prices rose by €36 to €51/MWh against the same dates in 2025.
That difference is consistent with the much larger solar fleet that sits between the two shocks. Average output in the peak solar hour doubled in Spain and Greece between the 2022 and 2026 windows and rose by half in Germany, and prices in the hours that output covers moved far less with fuel prices than they did four years ago. This analysis asks what that larger fleet means for energy security: how much of the day now stays clear of crisis prices, why that stops at sunset, and how far battery storage could carry it into the evening and night. To answer it, the comparison uses two event windows of identical length. The first runs for 227 days from the invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022 to 8 October 2022, and the second for 227 days from the start of the war with Iran on 28 February 2026 to 12 October. Both open in late February, so day N of each crisis falls in nearly the same week of the year, and each contains 21,788 quarter-hour price intervals. The same calendar dates in 2025 serve as a reference without an energy crisis.
Midday output doubled in Spain and Greece
Far more solar was running when the second shock arrived. Solar output reported to ENTSO-E over the 227-day window rose from 23.8 TWh in 2022 to 49.4 TWh in 2026 in Spain, from 48.5 TWh to 74.7 TWh in Germany and from 4.7 TWh to 10.0 TWh in Greece. In the average hour of peak output, Spanish solar delivered 21.2 GW against 10.8 GW in 2022, German solar 39.8 GW against 26.5 GW and Greek solar 5.2 GW against 2.7 GW.
Figure 1. Average solar output by local hour over the first 227 days of each crisis and the same dates in 2025. Author’s aggregation from ENTSO-E data.
That output arrives in a narrow band. In the 2026 window, 66% of Spanish solar energy and 75% of German and Greek solar energy was produced between 10:00 and 17:00. On a full-year basis, ENTSO-E solar output rose from 31.1 TWh in 2022 to 52.4 TWh in 2025 in Spain, from 55.7 TWh to 73.8 TWh in Germany and from 6.3 TWh to 11.5 TWh in Greece.
Where the shock landed
In the 2022 window, prices were high in every hour. Front-month TTF averaged roughly €155/MWh between March and September 2022, and even the cheapest hour of the average day stayed at €149/MWh or more in all three markets. In the 2026 window the same markets produced a deep midday trough, and the average day stayed below €50/MWh from 10:00 to 18:00 in Spain, from 10:00 to 17:00 in Greece and from 11:00 to 16:00 in Germany.
Figure 2. Average day-ahead price by local hour, first 227 days of each crisis and the same dates in 2025. Author’s aggregation from ENTSO-E data.
Set against 2025, Spanish prices between 10:00 and 17:00 averaged €22/MWh, about €5 above the same hours a year earlier, while evening prices between 19:00 and 23:00 were €44/MWh higher and night prices between midnight and 06:00 about €50/MWh higher. The seven midday hours make up 29% of the day but contributed 4% of the rise in Spain’s baseload price and 13% in Germany. In Greece the midday block was €4/MWh cheaper than a year earlier, while night prices rose by €46/MWh.
Figure 3. Change in average day-ahead price by local hour, 2026 crisis window minus the same dates in 2025. Author’s aggregation from ENTSO-E data.
Gas prices are consistent with this shape. Monthly TTF closes rose from about €31/MWh in February 2026 to about €84/MWh by 12 October, and even the lowest price from March onwards, around €38/MWh in April, implies a fuel cost of roughly €70/MWh for a gas plant. The cheapest hours of the average day, at €16 to €25/MWh, and the 10:00 to 17:00 averages of €22 to €45/MWh sit well below that cost, so these hours show little sign of the fuel shock. The increase appeared instead in the hours solar cannot reach, where night and evening averages of €116 to €178/MWh sit above the €97/MWh average fuel cost of a gas plant. The ENTSO-E data do not name the price-setting plant in each interval, so this reading rests on price levels and timing.
Negative prices show how far the midday has moved. The 2022 window had none in Spain or Greece and 32 hours in Germany. The 2026 window had 547 hours in Spain, 459 in Germany and 476 in Greece, and between 19% and 23% of solar output in each market was produced while prices were below zero.
Solar’s revenue fell on two counts
Capture prices in the 2026 window are 74% lower than in 2022 in Spain, 76% lower in Germany and 83% lower in Greece, and capture rates are between 36 and 48 percentage points lower. Both the level and the shape of prices changed. Splitting the fall in the capture price between the two on a logarithmic basis, the lower baseload accounts for 55% of the decline in Spain, 62% in Germany and 57% in Greece, and the weaker relative value of the solar profile accounts for the rest.
Figure 4. Solar capture price and capture rate over the matched 227-day windows and the 2025 reference. Author’s aggregation from ENTSO-E data.
The 2025 reference shows that most of the relative decline was already in place before the new crisis. Over the same dates last year, solar’s capture rate was already 52% in Spain, 47% in Germany and 52% in Greece. Against that reference, the 2026 window was 5.6 points lower in Spain and 9.4 points lower in Greece, and 2.7 points higher in Germany. On a full-year basis the decline is steady: Spain’s capture rate fell from 90% in 2022 to 55% in 2025, Germany’s from 94% to 51% and Greece’s from 94% to 58%.
Another way to read the result is to ask how much of each euro added to the baseload price reached solar. Between the 2025 reference and the 2026 window, Spanish solar captured 37 cents of each extra euro and German solar 57 cents. Greek solar captured almost nothing over the full window: its capture price from March to June fell from €49/MWh to €33/MWh, in months with 285 negative-price hours against 12 a year earlier, which offset its summer gains. Monthly baseload prices stayed more than 10% above their 2025 levels in every month from May in Germany, July in Spain and August in Greece, while gas climbed from a monthly average of about €46/MWh in June to about €74/MWh in September. From July to 12 October, the costliest stretch of the window, solar captured 41 cents of each extra euro in Spain, 45 in Germany and 32 in Greece. Germany is the exception in the matched comparison. Its capture rate rose slightly against 2025 even though solar output in the window grew by 18%, and its negative-price hours fell from 548 to 459.
Is the second crisis simply milder?
In September, Spain’s day-ahead market averaged €143/MWh, slightly above the €141/MWh of September 2022, yet Spanish solar earned €66/MWh against €116/MWh four years earlier, and its capture rate fell from 82% to 46%. The obvious objection is that the second crisis is simply milder, and it is fair as far as it goes: TTF averaged roughly €54/MWh between March and September 2026 against roughly €155/MWh in the same months of 2022, baseload prices in the three markets are less than half their 2022 levels, and a smaller fuel shock leaves a smaller premium to spread across the day. The September comparison, however, holds the baseload almost constant and still shows solar earning 43% less than four years ago. With the baseload almost equal, the difference shows up in the shape of the day.
Figure 5. Spain, monthly baseload and solar capture price, January 2022 to 12 October 2026. Author’s aggregation from ENTSO-E data.
Moving noon into the night
The same shape that cuts solar’s capture rate creates the trade for storage. On the average day of the 2026 window, a battery charging in Spain’s two cheapest consecutive hours would have paid about €16/MWh and one discharging in the two dearest would have sold at about €147/MWh, a spread of €131/MWh against €88/MWh over the same dates in 2025. In Germany the spread widened from €123/MWh to €161/MWh, while in Greece, where evening prices were already high in 2025, it moved from €150/MWh to €157/MWh.
Figure 6. Spread between the two dearest and the two cheapest consecutive hours of the average day, by window. Illustrative, before losses. Author’s aggregation from ENTSO-E data.
The volume waiting to be moved is large. Across the three markets, solar output produced while prices were negative in the 2026 window averaged about 128 GWh a day. Every megawatt-hour shifted from those hours into the evening would work on both sides of the problem: it would add demand in hours when prices are below zero, which would support the capture price, and it would add supply in the night and evening hours where the 2026 price rise was concentrated. The spreads above come from averaged profiles rather than a dispatch model, so they leave out round-trip losses and day-to-day variation, and each new battery narrows the spread the next one earns.
What it means
For the energy trilemma, the data point the same way. In the hours solar covers, prices stayed far below the rest of the day through this gas shock, which serves decarbonisation and part of affordability. Extending that to the whole day, and reducing exposure to the next gas shock, would mean carrying part of that midday energy into the evening and the night, the hours where prices tracked the gas shock, and solar paired with storage is a direct way to do it. Contracts and support schemes that value the profile a plant delivers rather than its raw output, and grid connections shared between solar and batteries, could push investment that way.
Four years ago, solar hedged its owner against a crisis that reached every hour of the day. In 2026 the hours the fleet covers stayed largely insulated from the gas shock, a protection the baseload average hides because it blends noon with midnight. The next step is to carry that protection past sunset.

title: Modi Energy launches zero-upfront solar-plus-storage offer in Denmark - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Emaldo-backed Modi Energy says it will install, own, and operate rooftop solar and home batteries at no upfront cost to Danish households, funding a guaranteed 20% bill reduction through energy optimization and participation in power and flexibility markets.
Brian Publicover
14 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
Copenhagen-based Modi Energy has opened registrations in Denmark for a new energy-as-a-service offer. The company installs and owns solar and battery systems on customers’ homes and guarantees bills 20% below the market price of the electricity they use, defined as the spot price without markup plus tariffs, taxes, and VAT.
Modi Energy said the saving appears as a separate line on each monthly statement and lasts as long as the customer keeps both the hardware and Modi as electricity supplier. Electricity contracts carry a six-month binding period and the hardware agreement 12 months, after which both roll over. Removal fees apply during the first five years, and contracts can be transferred to a new homeowner free of charge.
Each home gets 15 kW to 24 kW of solar, typically 24 kW, and 30 kWh to 40 kWh of battery storage.
Modi Emergy plans to trade the batteries in Denmark’s frequency containment and frequency restoration reserve markets as well as day-ahead and intraday markets, alongside optimizing household consumption. The company said spreading revenue across these markets protects the guarantee as reserve prices fall.
Emaldo has itself reported growing competition and declining capacity revenues in Danish reserve markets this year, as battery deployment accelerates. Denmark registered
191 MW of new battery capacity
in the 12 months to the end of June.
The company has 50 units in field tests in Danish homes, and its first commercial installations are planned before the end of 2026. Modi runs on the platform of Emaldo, which says it manages more than 10,000 systems in the Nordics and
partnered with Twig in August
to widen its access to Nordic energy trading.
Modi Energy is led by Steffen Bjerregaard, who co-founded Emaldo and serves as its CEO for Europe. Financing comes from Modi’s owners and Emaldo, along with other financial instruments. The company said it has closed its latest financing round but did not disclose the amount.
Households are a small but fast-growing part of Denmark’s storage market. Residential battery installations rose from 546 to 1,403 over the 12 months to June, though they account for only 12.1 MW of capacity, against 112.4 MW at utility-scale plants. Denmark offers no subsidies for battery deployment, leaving market signals and price volatility as the main drivers,
according to board members
of the Danish solar association Dansk Solcelleforening.

The magenta-colored CdTe PV modules
A research team from Sweden and Italy has investigated the performance of semitransparent, magenta-colored cadmium telluride (CdTe) thin-film PV panels designed to transmit wavelengths favorable for broccoli growth in an agrivoltaic system.
“Most existing agrivoltaic systems use conventional crystalline-silicon solar panels, which are opaque and therefore primarily manage how much sunlight reaches the crops. Our approach also considers the quality, or spectrum, of that light,” corresponding author Silvia Ma Lu told
pv magazine
. “The magenta-colored panels were specifically customized to transmit more blue and red light, corresponding to major absorption regions of plant chlorophyll pigments.”
Ma Lu said the research represents one of the largest published open-field experiments to date involving semitransparent, colored solar panels in agrivoltaics. “Our system explores the emerging concept of wavelength-selective agrivoltaics. The broader goal is to investigate whether sunlight can be used more efficiently by allocating different portions of the solar spectrum to crop growth and electricity generation,” she explained.
The researchers conducted a field experiment at Kärrbo Prästgård in central Sweden during the 2024 growing season, comparing broccoli grown in an open-field control plot with broccoli cultivated beneath two CdTe PV systems. The systems had nominal transparency levels of 50% and 70%, corresponding to average photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) transmittance values of 13.2% and 19.2%, respectively. Each PV system consisted of 21 panels supplied by Chinese manufacturer Advanced Solar Power, installed at a minimum height of 1.5 m and a tilt angle of 6 degrees.
Each plot contained 44 Marathon broccoli plants, transplanted on July 2 and protected by white insect nets. The researchers monitored light availability, air temperature, relative humidity, soil moisture, and soil temperature. They sampled six plants per treatment on Sept. 19, followed by six additional plants from each PV treatment on Oct. 14.
The team measured plant dimensions, fresh and dry biomass, broccoli head nutrient composition, and leaf photosynthetic responses. It also estimated electricity generation using the System Advisor Model (SAM).
At maturity, broccoli grown beneath the 50% and 70% transparency systems had average fresh head weights of 173.7 g and 168.5 g, respectively, compared with 187.6 g in the open-field control. The differences were not statistically significant. “One of the most interesting findings was how similarly the broccoli performed under the two systems despite their different transparency levels. We observed no meaningful differences in crop growth or nutrient composition between the two panel configurations at harvest,” Ma Lu said.
Broccoli grown beneath both PV systems reached maturity 104 days after transplanting, compared with 79 days for the open-field control, representing a 25-day delay.
“The delay in crop maturity compared with the full-sun reference was less surprising because both systems substantially reduced the amount of light reaching the plants,” explained the researcher. “Nevertheless, the similar performance between the two agrivoltaic treatments suggests that the broccoli responded to the conditions beneath both panel types in broadly similar ways despite differences in light availability.”
The comparable crop performance led the researchers to favor the 50% transparency configuration, which had a higher PV cell density and greater electricity generation potential. Radiation use efficiency, measured as aboveground dry biomass produced per unit of photosynthetically active radiation received, was 4.5 times higher under the 50% transparency system and 2.8 times higher under the 70% system than in the open-field control.
The researchers estimated that the approximately 1.1 kW prototype of the 50% transparency configuration could generate 447.6 kWh during the cultivation period. A theoretical hectare-scale calculation yielded a land equivalent ratio (LER) of 1.18.
“We have already started investigating how semi-transparent magenta panels, as well as panels that selectively transmit individual colors, such as red and blue, affect plant growth and physiological processes under more controlled experimental conditions,” concluded Ma Lu. “These experiments are designed to minimize light entering from outside the panels, allowing us to distinguish better the effects of different transmitted light spectra while keeping other environmental conditions as similar as possible.”
The findings are presented in
Evaluating land productivity with semi-transparent colored CdTe thin-film PV and broccoli cultivation in agrivoltaic systems
, published in
Cell Reports Physical Science
. Researchers from Sweden’s
Mälardalen University
, Italy’s
National Research Council
, and the
Catholic University of the Sacred Heart
contributed to the study.

title: Panasonic unveils R454C air-to-water heat pumps for residential use - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The new series comprises four models with heating capacities of 3 kW, 5 kW, 7 kW and 9 kW. The units feature a refrigerant-split configuration, with the indoor and outdoor units connected by refrigerant piping.
Emiliano Bellini
14 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Heat pumps
Residential
The Aquarea High-Performance N Series
Japan-based
Panasonic
has introduced the Aquarea High-Performance N Series, a new range of air-to-water heat pumps designed for residential heating and domestic hot water production.
The systems use R454C refrigerant, which has a global warming potential (GWP) of 148. “Built around the next-generation R454C refrigerant, the new range gives installers a compact and adaptable solution suited to a wide variety of residential projects, from detached houses to multi-family apartment buildings,” the company said in a statement.
The new series comprises four models with heating capacities of 3 kW, 5 kW, 7 kW and 9 kW. The units feature a refrigerant-split configuration, with the indoor and outdoor units connected by refrigerant piping. Panasonic said the systems support piping lengths of up to 50 m and elevation differences of up to 30 m, allowing installation in different residential building configurations.
The range includes a compact all-in-one indoor unit measuring 1,575 mm in height, with a footprint of 599 mm × 602 mm. The manufacturer said the reduced dimensions are intended to simplify installation in properties with limited indoor space.
The heat pumps are designed to operate at outdoor temperatures as low as -25 C, according to Panasonic. The 5 kW model reportedly has an outdoor sound power level of 58 dB(A).
The systems also feature integrated connectivity for remote operation and maintenance through Panasonic’s cloud-based control platforms.
According to the manufacturer, the heat pumps achieve energy efficiency ratings of up to A+++ at a water flow temperature of 35 C and A++ at 55 C. Domestic hot water efficiency is rated up to A+.
The company has not yet disclosed detailed model-specific coefficient of performance (COP) or seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) values, refrigerant charge quantities, or pricing information.
Panasonic said the new heat pumps will be manufactured entirely in Europe. The company previously indicated that the N Series is scheduled to enter the European market in April 2027.
