title: Unico launches 330 kW bidirectional inverter - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Unico GTI supports solar generation, energy storage or emerging high-power loads in a compact, rack-mounted unit, made in the USA.
Anne Fischer
14 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Inverters
The Grid Tie Inverter
Unico, a U.S. specialist in advanced power conversion technologies, launched its new 330 kW bidirectional Grid-Tie Inverter (GTI). The compact, scalable power conversion platform supports solar generation, energy storage or high-power loads, such as data centers.
The inverter was developed in 2025 when Unico signed an agreement to supply Eos Energy Enterprises with DC-to-DC converters, and thus launched a new product line of ultra compact power conversion products for energy storage solutions.
Unico reports that the GTI, its first inverter, operates at 98.5% efficiency and boasts a power density of 7 2W per cubic inch. The same platform can address a range of system configurations: AC voltages from 380 to 900 VAC are supported and it features a programmable DC voltage range from 600 to 1500 VDC.
The GTI supports parallel operation in groups of ten or more to deliver system power levels exceeding 3.3 MW, the company reports.
“With the explosion of data centers, increase in alternative power generation, and expansion of battery storage across industries, bidirectional capability at 1,500 VDC is increasingly required but remains underserved at the C&I scale by U.S.-manufactured products,” said Mike Canada, Unico CEO.
Unico was launched in 1967 in Wisconsin, originally focusing on testing, oil & gas applications and industrial automation systems. Today the company develops and manufactures power conversion products for data centers, microgrids, electrical systems, and energy storage in its 10 GW manufacturing facility in Franksville, Wisconsin
The Unico GTI is launching at The Battery Show 2026, which runs from October 12 to 15 in Detroit.

title: Study reveals up to 15% gap between expected and actual bifacial gains in utility-scale PV - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in Spain have found that the effective bifaciality of solar modules in utility-scale PV plants can be up to 15% lower than their nominal rating. Based on two years of operational data from a 50 MWp solar plant in Spain, with findings validated across four additional installations in Spain and the United Kingdom, the study highlights the influence of irradiance, temperature, mounting geometry and operating conditions on rear-side power generation.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
14 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Utility-scale
A research team from the
Universitat Politècnica de València
and Spanish engineering company Grupotec has investigated the gap between nominal module bifaciality and actual performance under operating conditions in utility-scale PV plants.
The study
The bifacial gain gap: Nominal and regulatory vs. effective performance across five utility-scale PV sites
was published in
Renewable Energy
The researchers analyzed two years of operational data from a 50 MW bifacial PV plant equipped with single-axis trackers in Spain. They subsequently validated their findings using data from four additional solar installations in Spain and the United Kingdom.
Their analysis revealed significant differences between nominal module bifaciality and effective bifacial performance at plant level, with mounting configurations, irradiance, temperature and operating conditions all influencing the contribution of rear-side irradiance to power generation.
Effective bifaciality
At the reference plant, the modules have a nominal bifaciality factor of 0.70. However, the researchers calculated an average effective bifaciality of 0.610 on a time-weighted basis and 0.599 on an irradiance-weighted basis, representing a reduction of approximately 13% to 15% from the nominal value.
The discrepancy was particularly pronounced at medium and high irradiance levels, which account for a substantial share of annual electricity generation. At irradiance levels above 600 W/m², effective bifaciality dropped below 0.60, falling to approximately 0.55 to 0.57 at irradiance levels exceeding 1,000 W/m².
The researchers used 15-minute supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) records collected in 2024 and 2025, including meteorological measurements and string-level electrical data.
Rear-side irradiance was measured using albedometers equipped with pyranometers, while module temperatures were recorded using PT100 sensors installed on the rear surface of the modules. The dataset was filtered to remove nighttime measurements, anomalous readings and sensor failures, while retaining fluctuations associated with variable cloud cover.
During the middle of the day, available rear-side irradiance at the Spanish plant amounted to approximately 20% to 25% of average front-side irradiance. Although substantially lower than front-side irradiance, this additional contribution had a measurable effect on string electrical operating conditions and module temperatures.
Higher rear-side gains
The researchers calculated a time-weighted average bifacial power gain (BPG) of 0.495 at the reference plant, with a median of 0.511 and a 90th-percentile value of 0.804. Their analysis identified an inverse relationship between BPG and effective bifaciality.
In the second quarter, BPG reached its quarterly maximum of 0.579, while effective bifaciality declined to 0.590. In the first quarter, BPG fell to 0.352, while effective bifaciality increased to 0.641.
According to the researchers, higher irradiance levels in spring and summer increase the absolute contribution of rear-side irradiance to power generation. However, the associated rise in module temperature reduces the efficiency with which that additional irradiance is converted into electricity.
The effect was also reflected in the modules’ electrical characteristics. As rear-side irradiance increased, string current rose from approximately 3.9 A to 8.2 A, representing an increase of up to 110%. Meanwhile, string voltage declined from around 1,275 V to approximately 1,165 V, a reduction of 8% to 9%. Module temperatures increased by as much as 3.5 C, resulting in an estimated BPG reduction of 0.013.
Mounting geometry
To assess the broader applicability of their findings, the scientists compared results from five utility-scale PV installations featuring the same module technology – bifacial monocrystalline silicon half-cell modules – but different mounting configurations and climatic conditions.
The installations comprised three Spanish plants equipped with single-axis trackers and two fixed-tilt PV plants in the United Kingdom. Across the five sites, irradiance-weighted effective bifaciality ranged from 0.464 to 0.722, equivalent to approximately 66% to 103% of the nominal bifaciality factor of 0.70. Median BPG values ranged from 0.229 to 0.535.
The researchers observed a common relationship between effective bifaciality and irradiance across all installations. Effective bifaciality initially increased with irradiance, reaching a peak at approximately 400 W/m² to 500 W/m², before declining at higher irradiance levels. However, the shape of this relationship varied according to the mounting configuration. Single-row trackers exhibited the most pronounced response, followed by dual-row trackers, while fixed-tilt systems displayed a flatter relationship.
The findings suggest that mounting geometry and the rear-side view factor play important roles in determining effective bifacial performance, alongside ground albedo, row spacing, shading, soiling and electrical losses.
Regulatory bifacial factor
The study also examined the relationship between measured bifacial performance and the bifacial factor of 1.15 established under Spain’s Royal Decree 997/2025. The researchers argued that the regulatory factor should be interpreted as an administrative capacity-conversion coefficient rather than an indication of the power gain that can be expected during actual plant operation.
At the 50 MW reference installation, none of the observed BPG values approached 1.15. The mean BPG was 0.495, while the 90th-percentile value reached 0.804.
The authors also cautioned that BPG should not be interpreted directly as the energy yield gain relative to an equivalent monofacial PV plant. Instead, they described it as a metric for characterizing the bifacial contribution under actual operating conditions.
Implications for PV system design
The researchers said their findings have implications for energy yield modeling, DC-side system design and PV performance assessment. In particular, relying on a single nominal bifaciality factor could lead to an overestimation of rear-side contributions under the irradiance conditions responsible for a substantial proportion of annual electricity generation.
They recommended incorporating the irradiance and temperature dependence of effective bifaciality into PV performance models, rather than assuming a constant nominal value across all operating conditions.
The researchers also proposed using field-data-based performance metrics to enable more meaningful comparisons between PV installations with different mounting configurations and climatic conditions.
Their findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between nominal module specifications, regulatory conversion factors and the actual contribution of rear-side irradiance to electricity generation in utility-scale bifacial PV systems.

title: Mercedes-Benz launches bidirectional charging in Germany - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Mercedes-Benz has launched a bidirectional charging service in Germany, allowing EV owners to earn payments by supplying power to the grid. The offering initially targets households without rooftop PV systems, with plans to expand to more vehicle models and markets.
Ralph Diermann
14 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
Like BMW, Ford, Audi, and other automakers,
Mercedes-Benz
is now offering bidirectional charging to electric vehicle (EV) customers in Germany. The company uses vehicle batteries to participate in the electricity market through vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology. In return, customers receive a payment of €0.1175 ($0.13) for every hour their vehicle remains connected to the wallbox. Mercedes-Benz is collaborating on the initiative with Munich-based e-mobility service provider The Mobility House.
The package, called MB.Charge Home Pro Intelligent, includes the ChargeLine BiDi, an 11 kW bidirectional DC wallbox. The unit was developed by The Mobility House in partnership with Munich-based charging technology specialist EcoG and Chinese manufacturer Zhejiang EV-Tech. It uses nonproprietary technology designed to ensure a high level of interoperability.
The wallbox costs €2,990. The first 500 customers will receive a €1,000 discount, available until the end of March 2027, as well as a €250 voucher for public charging through MB.Charge Public.
Initially, the offer is available only to households without rooftop PV systems. Households with PV installations could otherwise lose their feed-in tariff payments under Germany’s Renewable Energy Act (EEG), as it has not yet been possible to clearly distinguish whether EV batteries are charged with solar power or grid electricity. However, this is expected to change following the German Federal Network Agency’s MiSpeL decision. Grid operators have until the end of September 2027 to implement the new rules.
Expansion to other countries planned
The bidirectional charging offer initially covers the all-electric Mercedes-Benz GLC and the new C-Class. The automaker plans to extend the feature to additional models, including the VLE, GLA, EQS, CLA, CLA Shooting Brake, and GLB. Depending on the model, bidirectional charging will be activated via an over-the-air update following its market launch. Mercedes-Benz also plans to introduce its V2G offering in other countries.
“For us, bidirectional charging is the next logical step in electric mobility,” said Jörg Bartels, head of powertrain systems at Mercedes-Benz AG. “We are transforming the vehicle from a mere consumer into an active component of the energy system. In doing so, we combine innovative vehicle technology with the more efficient use of renewable energy, creating sustainable added value—for our customers and for the energy infrastructure alike.”

title: Oswal Pumps to set up 1.2 GW TOPCon solar cell factory in India - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Oswal Pumps plans to invest $48 million in a TOPCon solar cell manufacturing facility in Karnal, in the Indian state of Haryana. Commercial production is expected to begin by April 2028, with the entire output earmarked for captive solar module manufacturing.
Uma Gupta
14 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
solar cells
Indian solar pump, module and electric motor manufacturer Oswal Pumps Ltd. has announced plans to establish a 1.2 GW solar cell manufacturing facility based on tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) technology, as part of its efforts to expand backward integration.
The company’s board of directors has approved the proposed facility, which will be developed through its wholly owned subsidiary, Oswal Solar Energy Pvt. Ltd. (OSEPL).
Oswal Pumps expects the facility to begin commercial production by April 2028.
The company said the entire output will be used by OSEPL’s in-house solar module production lines, securing a steady supply of domestically manufactured cells under India’s domestic content requirement (DCR) rules while reducing exposure to spot-market price volatility and supplier pricing.
The investment will also extend OSEPL’s operations from module assembly to cell manufacturing, potentially improving its cost structure, competitiveness in government-backed programs and long-term profitability.
The project is expected to cost approximately INR 4.56 billion ($48.1 million), of which INR 2.96 billion will be financed through debt. The remaining INR 1.60 billion will come from unutilized proceeds of the company’s initial public offering (IPO), originally allocated to an aluminum frame facility and the remaining planned capacities of a 300 MW ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) encapsulant facility and a 500 MW solar module facility.
The company plans to deploy the IPO proceeds toward the solar cell project by fiscal 2028.
Once operational, the 1.2 GW facility is expected to meet approximately 75% of OSEPL’s solar cell requirements, with the remainder sourced from external suppliers. It will be located in in Karnal, in the Indian state of Haryana.
The company currently operates 570 MW of solar module manufacturing capacity, with an additional 1 GW under construction.
“Bringing cell manufacturing in-house gives us greater control over quality, cost and timelines,” said Vivek Gupta, chairman and managing director of Oswal Pumps. “With ALMM List-II now in force, demand for domestically manufactured cells is set to rise sharply. We see this as the right opportunity to invest. Choosing TOPCon technology ensures we are building for the future, with higher efficiency and better long-term performance for our customers.”

title: Heliup offers lightweight rooftop PV modules with waterproofing membrane - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
French lightweight solar panel manufacturer Heliup has partnered with Holcim’s Elevate brand to launch Solar Light TPO, a rooftop PV system that combines lightweight solar modules with a waterproofing membrane. The solution is designed for roofs with limited load-bearing capacity.
François Puthod
14 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Residential
French lightweight PV module manufacturer
has partnered with Elevate, a Holcim Group brand specializing in waterproofing and insulation, to launch Solar Light TPO, an offer combining Heliup’s lightweight Stykon PV modules with Holcim’s UltraPly TPO waterproofing membrane, available in thicknesses ranging from 1.5 mm to 2 mm.
Solar Light TPO weighs 7 kg/m², compared with 15 kg/m² to 20 kg/m² for conventional systems, including the waterproofing membrane. It uses a mounting method that requires no roof penetrations, additional rails, or ballast.
“This makes it possible to install PV systems on flat roofs that were previously difficult to equip, particularly on commercial, industrial and logistics buildings, as well as public facilities,” Jean-Luc Roudaut, director of new photovoltaic market development at Holcim, told
pv magazine France
Suitable for new buildings and roof renovations
The system can also accommodate different roof designs, including pitched roofs, sawtooth roofs with slopes of up to 100%, and curved surfaces. It is suitable for both new construction and roof waterproofing renovations.
The UltraPly TPO membrane is available in three thicknesses: 1.5 mm, 1.8 mm and 2 mm. The thickest option is particularly suitable for roofs requiring regular maintenance and servicing.
“Our profiles are highly complementary, allowing us to leverage multiple routes to market based on specific needs: a network of waterproofing contractors and project managers on Holcim’s side, and project owners, solar industry players and developers on Heliup’s side,” said Roudaut.
PV installation possible up to two years after waterproofing
Solar Light TPO has obtained an
Enquête de Technique Nouvelle
(ETN), a French technical assessment for innovative construction systems, and a Broof (t3) fire classification.
The system also meets French regulatory requirements for buildings open to the public (ERP) and facilities classified for environmental protection (ICPE).
“The advantage of the ETN is that it allows photovoltaic panels to be installed up to two years after the membrane is laid,” said Julien Gaume, technical director at Heliup. “This offers the flexibility to renovate the roof first and then add solar capacity later to comply with regulatory obligations.”
In March, Heliup raised €16 million ($17.9 million) to accelerate large-scale deployment of its lightweight PV technology.
Heliup said the funds will strengthen its commercial teams, expand production capacity at its French industrial site, prepare replicable industrial units, and continue technology development.
The company, based in Le Bourget-du-Lac in France’s Savoie region, operates a 4,000 m² factory in Le Cheylas, Isère, which has been operational since January 2025. The facility can produce up to 100 MW per year, which is equivalent to about 500,000 m² of panels.
Heliup launched a 10 MW pilot production line in 2023 under the France 2030 program and previously raised €10 million. In 2025, it expanded to industrial-scale production with support from the European Union’s Innovation Fund through the Solar HEliup Energy for Flat roofTop (SHEEFT) project.

title: US DOE partners with ABS to advance nuclear tech for commercial ships
content: The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) and the American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) have signed an agreement to explore the use of advanced nuclear technology in commercial maritime applications, including nuclear-powered vessels and floating power plants.Announced on October 13, the memorandum of understanding (MOU) establishes a framework for feasibility studies, technical research, and coordination between government agencies and industry. The effort will also examine the ports, shipyards, and industrial infrastructure needed to build and support nuclear-powered maritime systems.The agreement brings together the DOE’s Office of Nuclear Energy and ABS, a maritime classification society that develops technical standards for ships and offshore facilities. The partners aim to assess how advanced nuclear technology could be applied safely to commercial operations at sea.Exploring nuclear power at seaThe agreement identifies floating nuclear power solutions and nuclear transportation corridors as key areas for concept and feasibility studies. It also includes support for developing a U.S. shipbuilding sector capable of building and operating nuclear-powered assets.Floating nuclear power plants could provide electricity from marine-based platforms, while nuclear-powered vessels would use onboard reactors for propulsion. However, the MOU does not specify particular reactor designs, vessel projects, locations, or construction timelines. is focuses on assessing the feasibility of these applications rather than committing to specific projects.The work will consider technical, regulatory, economic, and policy questions associated with establishing a maritime nuclear sector. These assessments are intended to help determine what would be required to move potential applications beyond the conceptual stage.Coordinating research and industry developmentUnder the agreement, ABS will co-manage the Maritime Nuclear Applications Group (MNAG), a research hub and resource center focused on maritime nuclear technology. The organization will also provide technical, regulatory, economic, and policy support for concept and feasibility studies.ABS will coordinate related work through the U.S. Maritime Administration’s U.S. Center for Maritime Innovation, for which it serves as Secretariat. The partnership is also aims to foster coordination among relevant federal agencies as the government works to develop a viable domestic maritime nuclear sector.“Advanced nuclear technology is moving from concept to application, and the maritime industry needs to be ready for it,” said John McDonald, ABS chairman and CEO.He said the agreement provides a framework for expanding work already underway with the DOE and industry partners to make nuclear energy a practical option for commercial maritime applications.DOE Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy Ted Garrish said the partnership would help explore how decades of experience with nuclear technology could be applied to maritime operations and support American innovation in the sector.Building on existing nuclear maritime workABS has already worked to establish the technical and regulatory foundations for maritime nuclear applications. The organization says it has published comprehensive classification rules for floating nuclear power plants and awarded approvals in principle for several nuclear projects.An approval in principle is an early-stage assessment of a proposed design. It does not, by itself, indicate that a project has received final authorization or is ready for construction. The new MOU extends this work through a formal partnership with the DOE, bringing research, feasibility studies, and government coordination under a shared framework.The agreement does not announce a specific nuclear-powered ship, floating power plant, or construction program. Instead, it establishes a process for examining the technologies and industrial capabilities that could support commercial nuclear applications at sea.

title: China proposes new submarine tank that could operate underwater
content: Chinese researchers have proposed four types of modular combat equipment designed to switch configurations for missions across land, water, air, and electromagnetic battlefields. One proposed configuration could operate underwater at depths of up to 164 feet for two hours, although the reported tests have yet to verify this capability.The designs are intended for the evolution of armored warfare between 2030 and 2050. Scientists from Inner Mongolia First Machinery Group, which works on China’s tanks and armored vehicles, and the Beijing Institute of Technology are leading the project.The researchers said prototype development and field tests had advanced the concept towards engineering application and “combat-oriented validation.”Four equipment types target different combat environmentsAs reported by South China Morning Post, the proposed system centers on four types of equipment intended to support operations across different battlefield environments. Rather than relying entirely on fixed vehicle hardware, the designs use interchangeable physical modules to adapt to changing mission requirements.The approach is intended to help armored units respond to threats that develop too quickly for conventional platforms. According to the researchers, traditional vehicles can take more than 45 seconds to switch from reconnaissance to striking a target.The paper also estimates that conventional vehicles’ ability to intercept multiple targets could fall from 89 percent to 38.6 percent during a 10-second drone attack.Modular connections aim to shorten response timesThe researchers aim to reduce the observe-orient-decide-act (OODA) decision cycle to nine seconds, a fivefold improvement over current performance.Tests recorded an average module-connection time of 8.7 seconds and a 98.3 percent success rate across 1,000 trials. The trials covered temperatures from minus 4 to 122 degrees Fahrenheit, strong electromagnetic interference, and muddy terrain.The system is also designed to keep fluctuations in the power supplied to high-energy payloads within plus or minus 3 percent.Underwater configuration of submarine tank targets amphibious operationsOne of the detailed configurations is a dedicated water module (submarine tank) designed to operate at depths of up to 164 feet for two hours. Switching between operating environments could take as little as 12 minutes.The proposed capability could allow a vehicle to approach a shoreline underwater before changing to its land configuration. The researchers also envision drone-assisted obstacle clearance, projecting that the system could clear 30 obstacles per minute and cut landing-operation time by 60 percent.However, the reported tests did not establish underwater performance of the proposed submarine tank, and the paper provided no underwater speed or range figures.Land performance and cost savings remain projectionsThe land-based core module is designed to reach at least 43 mph on roads and 25 mph off-road. Its proposed hybrid power system would provide a minimum range of 373 miles.The researchers estimate that the concept could improve performance across five key areas compared with existing modular armored vehicles, including Germany’s Boxer. They also project a reduction of around 40 percent in whole-life costs.These figures remain projections. Further testing will be needed to establish whether the four equipment types can deliver their proposed capabilities in operational conditions.The study was published in the peer-reviewed journal Acta Armamentarii.

title: Tesla batteries boost Texas energy storage site to 300 MW capacity
content: Nightpeak Energy has brought a second battery storage project near Houston into commercial operation, doubling its Bocanova site’s capacity to 300 megawatts as data centers and other large electricity users drive demand growth in Texas.The 150 MW Bocanova 2 project in Brazoria County began commercial operation on September 17. Nightpeak announced the milestone and successful financial close on October 13, adding two-hour battery storage to support flexibility on the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) grid.Equipped with Tesla’s Megapack 2 XL systems, the project expands Nightpeak’s storage development in Southeast Texas. It follows Bocanova 1, the site’s first 150 MW phase, which entered commercial operation in August 2025.Tesla batteries expand Bocanova’s capacityThe second phase brings another 150 MW of battery capacity to the site, matching the power capacity of the original development. Its two-hour duration describes how long the new batteries can discharge at their rated output.That combination gives Bocanova 2 a storage capacity of 300 megawatt-hours. The distinction matters: megawatts measure the power the project can deliver, while megawatt-hours measure the amount of energy it can store.Nightpeak positioned the expansion as a flexible resource for a power market experiencing rapid demand growth. Battery storage can absorb electricity and release it later, helping operators respond to changing grid conditions.The company identified data centers and other large loads as drivers of that growth. These users are increasing the need for infrastructure and resources that can respond quickly.Large loads reshape power planning“We’re seeing large loads come to the grid at a pace and scale that is fundamentally changing how the power sector plans for new demand,” said Paris Hays, co-founder and CEO/CDO at Nightpeak Energy.“Texas is at the forefront of that growth, and meeting it will require significant new infrastructure as well as resources that can respond quickly as conditions change,” he added. “With 300 MW now operating at Bocanova, we’re putting that kind of flexibility to work in one of the most dynamic power markets in the country. We’re grateful to the City of Alvin, Brazoria County, and the local community for their support in bringing Bocanova to life,” Hays said. The expansion is part of a two-phase development, with the first entering operation roughly a year before the second.Banks back storage expansionBocanova 2 operates under a long-term offtake agreement with an investment-grade counterparty. Nightpeak did not identify that counterparty or disclose the agreement’s financial terms in its announcement.MUFG Bank provided a tax equity bridge loan and a construction-to-term loan for the project. U.S. Bank supplied traditional tax equity.Founded in 2022, Nightpeak said it has developed and acquired a portfolio exceeding one gigawatt of operating and de-risked capacity. That portfolio spans gas-fired generation, battery storage and powered land development.The company also continues to advance an additional pipeline of flexible generation and large-load projects. Bocanova’s expanded operating capacity adds to that portfolio as Nightpeak develops assets intended to meet growing electricity and AI demand.

title: New coating cuts platinum use by 88% for hydrogen production systems
content: Researchers at Austria’s TU Wien have found that a much thinner platinum coating could protect components used in hydrogen production. It can potentially reduce the amount of the precious metal needed for these protective layers by around 88%.The experiments examined platinum-coated titanium bipolar plates used in proton exchange membrane (PEM) water electrolysis. Under the conditions studied, a coating just 24 nanometers thick remained largely intact and retained good electrical conductivity after electrochemical stress.The findings point to a possible way to reduce equipment costs. However, the researchers cautioned that the optimal thickness depends on factors including how the coating is manufactured and how uniformly it covers the surface.Why hydrogen equipment needs platinumWater electrolysis uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. At one electrode, the process produces oxygen, positively charged hydrogen ions (protons), and electrons. The protons pass through a membrane to the second electrode, where they combine with electrons to form hydrogen. Keeping the equipment operational in this environment is more complicated than the basic reaction suggests.“Electrolysis creates a chemical environment that is damaging to many metallic components. Metal can dissolve, while oxide layers can form at the same time and impede the flow of electric current,” explained Helmut Riedl-Tragenreif from the Institute of Materials Science and Technology at TU Wien.“If the system is to remain operational for a long time, the different components have to be carefully matched to one another. Bipolar plates play a particularly important role here, accounting for up to 30% of total system costs,” he added.These plates support the equipment mechanically, conduct electricity, and help transport water and gases. Titanium resists corrosion well, but an oxide layer forms on its surface and obstructs electrical current.A thin platinum coating addresses that problem by conducting electricity while protecting the titanium underneath.A thinner coating survives the testsThe TU Wien team systematically investigated how thick that protective layer needs to be. A 24-nanometer coating proved sufficient under the conditions tested, while an eight-nanometer layer showed clear problems.Compared with a 200-nanometer coating of the kind currently used in industry, the successful thinner layer represents a potential reduction of around 88% in platinum consumption for the protective coating.The researchers also examined whether the coatings remained resistant after electrochemical stress, rather than assessing only their initial performance.“We analyzed the coatings before and after electrochemical stress using high-resolution methods. One particularly important question is whether microscopic defects develop in the coating,” said Riedl-Tragenreif. Small defects can accelerate damageA defect in the platinum layer can expose the titanium below to attack. The titanium oxidizes, and small oxygen bubbles may form at the interface, creating mechanical stresses that further damage the coating.As larger sections detach, more titanium becomes exposed, allowing the damage to accelerate.The eight-nanometer coating showed clear indications of this process. After electrochemical stress, researchers observed larger defects and found that significantly more titanium and platinum ions had entered the electrolyte.The 24-nanometer coating remained largely intact, maintained good conductivity, and kept metal ion release at a very low level under the studied conditions.

title: High-tech X-rays reveal how nuclear fuel rods stand the test of time
content: Researchers at Switzerland’s Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) used a new X-ray imaging technique to examine corrosion inside nuclear fuel rod cladding in 3D, detecting pores as small as 80 nanometers.The study investigated whether the protective layers surrounding fuel rods remain effective after years of exposure to cooling water and radiation.Working with samples from cladding tubes that had operated in a nuclear power station, the team used PSI’s Swiss Light Source to map internal structure. The tubes remained leak-tight after service, and the measurements showed that protective oxide layers continued to perform their function.The findings help assess fuel rod safety and establish whether conventional laboratory corrosion tests accurately represent material exposed to reactor conditions. The supplied announcement did not specify when the experiments took place.Tiny samples reduce radiation exposureFuel rod cladding must remain sealed throughout reactor operation, despite conditions that can cause corrosion. Researchers therefore need to understand how quickly corrosion layers form and how porous they become.The cladding tubes typically contain more than 98 percent zirconium, with small amounts of other metals added to improve their properties. It encloses stacked uranium dioxide fuel pellets, forming the fuel rods used in nuclear reactors.The study brought together three PSI research centers covering nuclear engineering, photon science, and neutron and muon sciences.At the institute’s Hot Laboratory, staff used precision saws inside shielded hot cells to cut wafer-thin sections from spent fuel rod cladding. And then used a focused ion beam to shape the material into cylinders.The samples came from the zirconium oxide layer formed on the cladding surface during operation.“In the end, our tiny zirconium oxide cylinder had a diameter of just 20 micrometres – making it barely visible to the naked eye. A human hair is three to four times as thick,” said first author Okan Yetik.Their size kept radiation emissions low enough for examination outside specially shielded hot cells.X-ray scans reveal protective layersThe team examined the cylinders using ptychographic X-ray computed tomography, or PXCT, developed at PSI’s Swiss Light Source. An X-ray beam scans the sample point by point from different angles, generating high-resolution three-dimensional images of its internal structure.“We were even able to identify pores as small as eighty nanometres,” said co-author Andreas Menzel.The measurements also showed that the oxide layers retained their protective function after prolonged use.“The measurements taken at the SLS showed that the protective oxide layers on the cladding tubes remain intact and continue to fulfill their purpose even after years of use,” said PSI researcher Liliana Duarte.Laboratory tests reflect reactor conditionsResearchers compared the used material with non-irradiated cladding samples exposed to high pressure, high temperatures, and water inside an autoclave.The density of the reactor-used samples was practically identical to that of the autoclaved material, supporting the value of standard corrosion tests.This means researchers do not always need spent cladding for investigations. The findings can also help operators refine reactor water chemistry, and manufacturers tailor alloys and heat treatments.The technique opens possibilities for similarly detailed examinations of components for small modular reactors and nuclear fusion reactors.The researchers published their findings in the Advanced Engineering Materials journal.

title: New system helps humanoid robots squeeze through tight, messy spaces
content: Galbot introduced PASSAGE, a research framework that helps humanoid robots navigate cluttered environments by adapting their movements to obstacles.The system enables robots to choose different ways of passing through tight spaces, including stepping over objects, ducking under barriers, and turning sideways to fit through narrow gaps. The framework combines environmental perception, motion planning, and whole-body control to help humanoid robots navigate complex surroundings while maintaining balance and reaching their destinations.Recently, Galbot’s humanoid robot completed over 100 rallies in a live autonomous tennis match, tracking balls, adjusting positions, and returning varied shots. Humanoids navigate obstaclesThe new research framework lets humanoid robots navigate cluttered environments by adapting their whole-body movements to obstacles. The system lets robots choose suitable movements, such as stepping over objects, ducking under overhead barriers, or turning sideways to pass through narrow gaps.The framework addresses a key challenge in robotics: coordinating a robot’s movements with its understanding of the space around it. Humanoid robots must account for more than whether their feet can pass through an opening. Their heads, shoulders, arms, and torsos must also clear surrounding objects. A robot may have an unobstructed path for its legs but still collide with a low ceiling or a narrow doorway.Perceiving the environment, understanding spatial constraints, and coordinating whole-body motion are essential for humanoid robots to integrate into human society—and remain major challenges in robotics. To address this, the Galbot team introduces PASSAGE, a framework that… pic.twitter.com/oYXC7GLvgo— Galbot (@GalbotRobotics) October 13, 2026PASSAGE combines environmental perception, motion planning, and whole-body control to address this problem. According to the project page, its system uses a planner to generate short movement sequences and a controller to execute them while responding to surrounding geometry.The framework integrates movement selection and execution into a single planner-controller approach. Rather than relying on separate policies for different obstacle types, it can combine movements to negotiate varied spatial constraints.The research team collected 100 hours of human motion data across 1,500 virtual scenes. Operators demonstrated obstacle traversal using virtual reality and inertial motion capture, providing examples of how people adjust their bodies to move through restricted spaces.The system uses this data to connect human movements with the environmental conditions in which they occur. During robot operation, LiDAR supplies information about the surrounding environment, helping the framework account for obstacles and available clearance.According to the project documentation, PASSAGE runs on an Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin computer and does not require prebuilt maps or offboard computation. This setup allows the system to process environmental information and coordinate movements on the robot itself.Trials reveal challengesThe research paper reports a 98.67 percent success rate across 750 simulated trials in 150 previously unseen scenes. This figure measures whether the robot reached its destination, rather than whether it avoided every obstacle.When success required completing the task without touching obstacles, the reported rate fell to 70.3 percent. The difference highlights the challenge of coordinating a humanoid’s entire body through confined spaces.The team also tested PASSAGE on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot across 50 previously unseen physical layouts. The researchers reported that the robot completed all 50 trials without falling or requiring safety intervention. It traversed 45 of the layouts without contacting obstacles. These results come from a limited research evaluation and do not establish reliability across all real-world environments.PASSAGE focuses on a capability humanoid robots may need to work in furnished rooms, factories, and other spaces designed for people. Adapting posture to available clearance could help robots navigate environments where fixed walking patterns are insufficient.However, the published results also show that reaching a destination and moving through it without contact remain different challenges. The project page lists the framework’s code as coming soon, leaving its broader adoption and performance in additional settings to be evaluated.

title: Scientists discover 11,742 deep-sea viruses with 99% new to science
content: A new study has uncovered vast, previously unknown viral diversity in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCFZ), a Pacific deep-sea region rich in polymetallic nodules.The CCFZ is the world’s largest deep-sea mineral exploration region. In fact, researchers have never seen 99 percent of the viruses discovered there before.China-based researchers analyzed seabed sediment samples and identified 11,742 distinct viruses, over 99 percent (11,662) of which were entirely new to science and unique to this heavy-metal-rich, nutrient-scarce environment. Environmental disruption from potential commercial mining could disrupt these viral communities. “Protein-sharing network and phylogenetic analyses showed extensive benthic viral diversity, with over 99 percent of viral clusters not represented in current reference databases,” the team from Chongqing University wrote in the study paper. Massive novel diversityResting up to 6,000 meters (19,700 feet) deep in the Pacific Ocean between Mexico and Hawaii, the Clarion-Clipperton Zone is strewn with millions of potato-sized metallic rocks.Deep-sea mining companies are targeting this vast reserves of metal-rich nodules to power the electric vehicle market. However, scientists are only beginning to understand this ecosystem, which also hosts myriad kinds of organisms. Several previous studies have already pointed out that the prospective industrial operations risk disrupting this complex, pitch-black deep-sea ecosystem. The new study analyzed over 60 sediment samples collected deep within the CCFZ by the China Ocean Mineral Resources R&D Association. Genetic comparisons revealed that deep-sea viral communities in the region are almost entirely unique, with just 4 percent of their protein clusters matching global databases.These viruses infect diverse deep-sea prokaryotes that drive vital cycles of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur, and metals. Viruses influence host survival and regulate local metabolic processes through auxiliary metabolic genes and targeted infections. In addition, viral gene exchange helps microbes adapt to metal toxicity. All these benefits show that the viruses play a vital role in maintaining the nodule field ecosystem.Pre-mining baselineThese deep-sea viruses pose little to no threat to human health.These deep-sea viruses pose almost no threat to human health. Most belong to Caudoviricetes, a class of syringe-like tailed phages that exclusively attack bacteria. These tiny architects of the deep sea actively regulate microbial populations.Despite the deep ocean floor being a nutrient-poor environment laden with toxic heavy metals, complex viral communities actively sustain the ecosystem. These viruses act as nutrient recyclers by breaking down organic matter to release nitrogen and phosphorus. They also function as metabolic directors and stress managers. For instance, some encode genes that boost bacterial survival and facilitate genetic exchange, helping microbes adapt to extreme toxicity.If industrial mining machines churn up the seafloor, these delicate biological networks could collapse. Heavy sediment plumes might wipe out host bacteria, halting essential nutrient cycles that sustain the broader ocean.The International Seabed Authority has granted 17 exploration licenses in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, with five held by China, whose researchers conducted this viral survey. Rising global demand to extract battery metals like cobalt, nickel, and manganese makes mining increasingly likely. Scientists insist that mapping these invisible viral networks remains essential before any commercial dredging begins.The findings provide a pre-mining benchmark of deep-sea microbial and viral ecosystems to guide future environmental impact assessments.The study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

title: Oxygen-based technique controls 2D chip crystal growth with 99% success
content: Researchers in South Korea have developed a semiconductor manufacturing technique that controls where individual crystals form with more than 99% success across 400 patterned growth regions, potentially helping manufacturers build vertically stacked computing chips.The technique allows researchers to grow a single crystal of molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂), a semiconductor only a few atomic layers thick, at a predetermined position instead of allowing multiple crystals to form randomly.A team led by the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), working with UNIST, Hanyang University and TDS Innovation, developed the method using oxygen released from an oxide barrier to control where crystal growth begins.The researchers say the approach could address a major obstacle in manufacturing stacked chips, where semiconductor layers must be formed precisely on top of existing circuits without introducing defects that affect performance.Oxygen controls crystal formationConventional semiconductor growth methods can define the general area where a thin film forms, but controlling the exact starting point of each crystal remains difficult.When several crystals grow independently and meet, they create grain boundaries. These boundaries disrupt the regular arrangement of atoms and can interfere with the movement of electrons through the semiconductor.The researchers developed a process called etching-flux-mediated single-centered nucleation (EF-SCN). Nucleation is the initial stage of crystal formation, when atoms begin arranging themselves into an ordered structure.The process uses an oxide barrier, such as hafnium oxide (HfO₂), surrounding the designated growth region. Oxygen released from the barrier acts as an etching agent, suppressing unwanted crystal formation.The oxygen’s effect is strongest near the edges of the patterned region and gradually weakens toward the center.This creates conditions that favor crystal formation at a single central point. Once growth begins there, the process also suppresses additional crystals from forming nearby.Using this method, the researchers successfully grew individual MoS₂ crystals at designated central positions in more than 99% of 400 patterns.The team also demonstrated selective metal deposition using structures combining molybdenum disulfide and molybdenum diselenide (MoSe₂).In these structures, a thin ruthenium metal film formed selectively on the MoSe₂ regions, demonstrating another way to control material placement during semiconductor fabrication.Stacked chips move closerTwo-dimensional semiconductors are being investigated for future chips because they retain semiconductor properties despite being only a few atomic layers thick.Their small thickness could allow manufacturers to stack computing and memory components vertically, reducing the distance data travels between them.Moving data within a chip consumes energy and contributes to processing delays. Placing components closer together could reduce those costs, particularly in systems handling large computational workloads.However, producing such chips requires precise control over semiconductor growth on surfaces containing previously fabricated circuits.The KAIST technique offers a possible way to grow high-quality 2D materials directly at designated locations, avoiding the need to manufacture them separately and transfer them onto a chip.The researchers examined the mechanism through growth experiments and simulations, but they have not demonstrated a complete stacked processor or measured improvements in computing speed or energy consumption.The findings establish control over crystal nucleation rather than commercial chip performance. Further development would be needed to determine whether the method can be integrated into semiconductor manufacturing at scale.The study was published October 8 in Nature.

title: Microfluidic chip stores memories in flowing water using tiny fibers
content: Yale researchers have found a way to make flowing fluids remember what happened before, using tiny flexible fibers that change shape under pressure. The discovery could help engineers develop soft robots that process information without conventional electronic controllers.The idea turns a familiar engineering problem on its head. Most fluid systems respond to the conditions they encounter, but the Yale design can retain traces of earlier flows. Its physical components effectively store information, allowing past events to influence how the system behaves next.Fibers that rememberInside a microfluidic chip, researchers placed flexible fibers within a network of narrow channels. Each channel measures roughly half the width of a human hair in depth.As fluid moves through the channels, pressure pushes individual fibers between two stable configurations. Each position changes the path available to the fluid, creating a physical record of the system’s previous state.Engineers could represent the two configurations as binary digits, or zeros and ones. Unlike conventional computer memory, the arrangement does not need electronic components to switch between states.Abhineet Rajput, the study’s lead author and a graduate student in Professor Amir Pahlavan’s lab, explained the distinction. “While conventional microfluidics relies on active elements, this system uses microfibers to passively store information,” Rajput said.The fibers can also influence one another. Their interactions allow individual changes to shape the behavior of the wider network, producing a more complex form of physical memory.Brain made of fluidThe research could open another route to controlling soft robots. Such machines often need to bend, squeeze through tight spaces, or operate in environments that challenge conventional hardware.A fluidic controller could use pressure and flow rates to carry signals. Channels would connect different parts of the system, while the flexible fibers would regulate fluid movement and retain information.Pahlavan sees particular value in environments where electronics face limitations. “We could design a fully fluidic controller that can be integrated into a soft robot and effectively act as its brain,” said Pahlavan, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Yale.Electromagnetic interference can disrupt electronic systems in certain operating environments. A controller built around fluid movement could offer an alternative, although researchers still need to demonstrate how reliably it can direct a robot through practical tasks.Can the system learn?Memory is only part of the researchers’ ambition. The next question is whether engineers can train fluidic networks to produce specific responses.Training could change how a network reacts to incoming flows, giving it a way to adapt its behavior. Achieving that would extend the system beyond retaining past information toward physical learning.The same principle could interest biologists studying organisms that navigate their surroundings without a brain. Slime molds, for example, can find efficient routes through mazes. Researchers also want to understand how fungi and plant roots respond to environmental changes.Fluidic networks could offer a physical model for investigating how interactions and accumulated experience shape behavior. Whether the technology can eventually learn useful tasks remains an open question.The findings appear in the journal Physical Review X.

title: Glowing prototype leads to a new 3D monolithic trap for quantum labs
content: Simulating complex quantum systems can overwhelm even powerful supercomputers. Researchers at Rice University have developed a three-dimensional ion trap that could make these systems easier to study in the laboratory.The device works with heavy ions such as ytterbium, addressing a limitation that restricted earlier monolithic designs. Researchers from Duke University and Translume Inc. collaborated on the project.Combining the best trap designsQuantum simulators recreate difficult-to-model systems under controlled laboratory conditions. In trapped-ion experiments, electric fields hold charged atoms in place while lasers control their interactions. Scientists then measure the ions to understand the system they represent.Traditional blade-style traps deliver strong performance but require manual assembly, making consistent reproduction difficult. Microfabricated chip traps offer greater precision and easier scaling, but often struggle to match their performance.Rice physicist Guido Pagano and his colleagues wanted to combine these advantages in a compact, three-dimensional design. Earlier monolithic traps worked with lighter ions, such as calcium, but heavier species presented additional engineering challenges.Three generations of redesignThe team started with a block of fused silica glass. Lasers and chemical processing created channels for the ions and trenches for the electrodes. Researchers then installed the electrodes and coated the structure with sputtered gold.The trenches helped isolate the electrodes, preventing short circuits during manufacturing. They also reduced the risk of electrical breakdown under high voltages inside a vacuum.The first prototype exposed a major problem. When researchers applied the required radio-frequency voltage, the trap developed thermal and electrical issues. It even began glowing visibly as it heated up.A second version fixed the main flaws but introduced unwanted axial micromotion and high ion-heating rates. Both problems threatened the precise control required for reliable quantum experiments.The third generation addressed these issues with improved heat dissipation and reduced ion movement. The researchers also used plasma-based surface treatment to lower ion-heating rates.Pagano’s laboratory and collaborators at Duke tested the finished traps individually. Their measurements agreed with previous computer simulations, confirming that the devices performed as intended.Expanding quantum research accessThe new design could make trapped-ion experiments easier to reproduce in academic laboratories. Its compatibility with ytterbium also expands the range of ions researchers can use in monolithic three-dimensional traps.Abhishek Menon, the study’s corresponding author and a graduate student, said solving the engineering challenges associated with heavier ions could also simplify trapping lighter species.The technology could help researchers investigate complex processes, including charge transfer during photosynthesis. Instead of attempting to model an entire quantum system directly, scientists can use controlled experiments to understand its underlying behavior.Roman Zhuravel, a study co-author and assistant research professor in Pagano’s laboratory, said the trap could help scientists break difficult quantum problems into manageable experiments.The design offers laboratories another tool for studying systems that conventional computers struggle to simulate. Its engineering approach could also inform future ion traps for a wider range of quantum technologies.The study is published in the journal Physical Review Applied.

title: Honda's Avatar Robot mirrors human movements to work remotely
content: Honda has demonstrated a robotic hand designed to tackle tasks requiring human-like precision and strength. The demonstration took place at CEATEC 2026 in Japan, showcasing technology that could let people perform physical work remotely.The Japanese automaker’s Honda Avatar Robot combines a multi-fingered hand with an assistance system that helps users control its movements. Honda envisions applications ranging from equipment maintenance and medical support to disaster response and space operations.The demonstration highlights a persistent challenge in robotics. Machines can increasingly navigate complex environments, but manipulating everyday objects reliably remains difficult.Hand built for precisionHonda’s human-scale robotic hand features 16 actuated joints, with each joint reaching continuous speeds of up to 180 degrees per second. That movement allows the mechanism to perform delicate operations while retaining the strength needed for demanding physical tasks.遠隔地にいながら自身の分身として活動することを目指すロボティクス技術「Hondaアバターロボット」を実演🤖#CEATEC2026 pic.twitter.com/oVgeMP9yIW— Honda 本田技研工業 (@HondaJP) October 13, 2026Each fingertip can apply up to 50 newtons of force continuously. Six-axis force sensors measure forces and torques at the fingertips, helping the system interpret physical interactions.The hand also incorporates 288 tactile-sensor channels distributed across its fingers and palm. These sensors provide detailed contact information, helping operators handle objects with greater control.Honda has tested the mechanism through more than 450,000 durability cycles. Those tests included 24,000 cycles involving the lifting of a 11-pound weight.The engineering challenge extends beyond producing a convincing grip. A useful robotic hand must maintain control through repeated movements, withstand physical stress, and handle objects with different shapes and resistance.Honda says its design can tackle jobs ranging from threading a needle to tightening screws. It can also handle scissors and lift heavier objects, giving the system a broad range of potential uses.Working from a distanceHonda’s avatar concept aims to let people interact with physical environments from distant locations. An operator could manipulate equipment through the robotic system without being physically present at the job site.人と同等の器用さ・力強さを備えた多指ハンドの動作にも注目ください👀#CEATEC2026 pic.twitter.com/TBaZmxlo0r— Honda 本田技研工業 (@HondaJP) October 13, 2026The approach could prove useful when specialists need to reach remote facilities or respond to urgent situations. For example, a medical expert could provide remote assistance without traveling to the location.Industrial maintenance offers another potential application. Technicians could operate tools in inaccessible areas, reducing the need to send personnel into hazardous environments.Disaster response and space exploration present similar challenges. Robotic hands could let operators handle objects in locations that pose serious risks or practical barriers to human access.Honda’s broader vision centers on giving people greater freedom over where they work. Its avatar technology aims to let users perform physical tasks without the constraints of travel and location.The manipulation challengeHumanoid robotics has made substantial progress in locomotion. Modern machines can walk, run, and perform increasingly complex movements, but those capabilities do not automatically translate into useful work.Manipulation introduces a different set of demands. Robots must control contact forces, adjust their grip, and respond to unpredictable objects.Honda’s combination of joint actuation, tactile sensing, and force measurement addresses several of those requirements. However, real-world usefulness will depend on how consistently the system performs outside controlled demonstrations.

title: OpenAI says its models helped expose employee's hidden recorder
content: OpenAI said Tuesday that the FBI arrested one of its employees after the company used its own models to investigate a hidden recording device discovered inside one of its offices.The ChatGPT maker said its models helped investigators understand the device, trace its origins and identify an employee suspected of planting it several days earlier. The company subsequently terminated the employee and referred the case to federal authorities.The FBI investigation remains ongoing. OpenAI has not disclosed the employee’s identity, the office where the device was found or the type of recording equipment involved.The company also did not explain which models it used or how they helped establish the device’s origins. It remains unclear whether the models analyzed images, technical components, records or other evidence.Models trace hidden deviceIn a statement posted on X, OpenAI said it discovered a sophisticated recording device concealed in one of its offices and used its models to investigate the incident.“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier,” the company said.OpenAI said it then contacted the FBI, whose agents and prosecutors moved to make an arrest. The company said it would continue cooperating with the investigation.The company has not released technical details showing how the models reached their findings or how investigators verified the results. Consequently, the announcement does not establish how much of the investigation was conducted using automated analysis rather than conventional security methods.OpenAI also said it had found no indication that the employee improperly accessed or removed its model weights, source code or customer information.Model weights are the numerical parameters that determine how a trained model processes information and produces outputs. They are among the technical assets that companies developing advanced models seek to protect.The company’s statement does not establish what information, if any, the recording device captured before it was discovered.Security concerns extend furtherOpenAI described the incident as an example of using its own technology to investigate potential security threats.Its security program is designed to address risks involving employees, cybercriminals and nation-state actors, the company said. The incident also comes amid separate security-related developments involving OpenAI.On Friday, the company said it had dismissed three researchers following an investigation into alleged violations of policies governing sensitive information.The researchers, Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, had published a letter describing their dismissals and raising concerns that the company’s actions could create uncertainty among employees and discourage researchers from speaking openly about safety issues.The two incidents involve different circumstances, and OpenAI has not indicated that they are connected.Earlier this year, a Texas man was charged in connection with an alleged Molotov cocktail attack at the home of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and an attempt to set fire to the company’s headquarters.

title: Google model cuts quantum costs 100x, tackles fusion equations
content: Google has unveiled Gemini 4 Argon, a new model that it says reduced the resource requirements of a quantum computing operation by more than 100 times, while helping researchers develop new mathematical solutions for nuclear fusion and improve real-world robot performance.In one demonstration, Argon generated a quantum algorithm component with more than 100 times lower spacetime cost than a previously published method. The company said the implementation was formally verified using Lean, a system for checking mathematical proofs.The model also helped researchers identify new solutions to a decades-old mathematical problem related to stellarator fusion reactors. In separate robotics tests, training data generated through Argon’s simulations increased a robot’s real-world task success rate from 56% to 75%.Google announced the developments on October 13 as part of the Gemini 4 Argon launch. In another test, the model worked unattended for 11 hours on Google’s existing software codebase, producing changes that reduced session preparation overhead by about 40% and sped up package imports by 21%.Quantum computing gets leanerQuantum computers require carefully designed operations to perform calculations while limiting errors and hardware demands. Some algorithms depend on smaller mathematical components, known as subroutines, that can consume substantial computing resources.Gemini 4 Argon is here.It’s available globally today for developers and enterprises in the paid tier of the Gemini API and the Gemini platform, for Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, and Ultra and Pro subscribers in the Gemini app and Search.Hope you all enjoy it! pic.twitter.com/2jyAgqoylU— Sundar Pichai (@sundarpichai) October 13, 2026Google said Argon optimized an arcsin subroutine used in quantum simulation algorithms. Compared with a published quantum CORDIC implementation, the new version reduced spacetime cost by more than 100 times.Spacetime cost measures the computing resources needed to carry out an operation, accounting for both hardware requirements and execution time. The improvement applies to the specific subroutine tested, rather than quantum computing systems as a whole.Argon also optimized an internal version of AlphaQubit, Google’s machine-learning-based quantum error correction decoder. By converting it into a single hardware-optimized kernel, the model nearly doubled inference throughput, according to Google.The model’s software engineering capabilities were tested on Google’s open-source Agent Development Kit, a framework used to build and deploy autonomous agents.During an 11-hour overnight run, Argon examined a codebase containing approximately 205,000 lines of code across nearly 800 files. It proposed six optimizations, two of which were accepted after human review and merged into the project.The changes reduced in-memory session preparation overhead by about 40% during long sessions and improved package import speed by 21%.In an independent benchmark, a 158-turn agent run fell from 65.6 seconds to 56.1 seconds. However, the time from starting a new process to its first model request remained essentially unchanged.Fusion equations meet roboticsIn nuclear fusion research, Google worked with University of Maryland professor Matt Landreman to identify a broader class of counterexamples to Grad’s conjecture, a mathematical hypothesis dating to 1967.Earlier counterexamples had already challenged the conjecture. The newly identified solutions could provide reference cases for testing simulation software used to design stellarators, which use complex magnetic fields to confine hot plasma.Separately, Argon demonstrated its ability to generate training environments for physical robots.Starting with a single photograph of a tabletop, the model built a physics-based simulation and generated more than 4,500 training episodes for robotic manipulation tasks.Gemini 4 Argon taught a robot to play cornhole just by watching a video.It mapped the physics, coded its own simulation, and taught @Apptronik's Apollo humanoid to sink 7 throws in a row. pic.twitter.com/JIyoKnVc4q— Google DeepMind (@GoogleDeepMind) October 13, 2026Google reported that the resulting training data increased real-world robot success rates from 56% to 75%, while reducing task completion time from 35 to 24 seconds.In another demonstration, Argon helped a Boston Dynamics Spot robot practice opening a foot-pedal trash bin in simulation before attempting the task with physical objects.Beyond robotics, researchers at Gamow Labs used Argon to examine de-identified genetic data from newborns with rare developmental lung disorders. Google said the model identified a chromosomal rearrangement that conventional software had missed for years.The results span scientific research, software engineering and physical robot control. However, the reported improvements remain specific to the experiments described, and broader performance across these fields has not yet been established.

title: US lab designs magnet stands for world's first electron-ion collider
content: A redesigned storage system for superconducting magnets at the U.S. Department of Energy’s Brookhaven National Laboratory is expected to save about $420,000 while increasing storage capacity for equipment needed in a future particle accelerator.The four-level structure can hold up to 45,000 pounds of magnets in a limited space. It was developed by Robert Desjardins, a fourth-year mechanical engineering technology student at Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT), during a 10-week summer internship.The design will help Brookhaven store approximately 80 magnets being removed from its Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). The equipment is intended for reuse in the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC), a next-generation accelerator expected to begin operating in the mid-2030s.Each superconducting magnet measures about 20 feet long and weighs more than 10,000 pounds. The new stands increase storage capacity from three magnets to four per structure without requiring additional floor space.Four levels increase capacityThe original storage stands were designed in the 1990s to accommodate three magnets. Brookhaven needed a taller structure capable of holding an additional magnet while meeting load-bearing and safety requirements.Desjardins redesigned the stands using computer-aided engineering models, reviewed existing blueprints, and worked with manufacturers to assess the proposed structure.“The original stands were designed in the 1990s, and at the time they could hold only three of the magnets. They wanted to up the capacity to four,” Desjardins said.The redesign also required extensive simulations to evaluate structural strength, load tolerance, and seismic performance. These checks were intended to determine whether the stands could safely support the heavy equipment, including under earthquake-related forces.Desjardins worked with Brookhaven mechanical engineer Jonathon Greene, an RIT alumnus who supervised the project. According to Greene, the revised design reduced costs while increasing the height of the storage system.“Rob costed down the original design while increasing the height. We saved about $420,000 by doing so,” Greene said in a Brookhaven article.The reported savings relate to the storage-stand redesign. The supplied information does not specify how the savings were calculated or provide independent verification of the figure.Preparing for future collisionsBrookhaven’s RHIC has operated for more than 26 years, allowing scientists to study matter under extreme conditions. Some of its superconducting magnets will be retained for the new Electron-Ion Collider rather than discarded.The EIC is being developed to investigate the internal structure of protons and atomic nuclei. It will collide electrons with ions, allowing researchers to examine how quarks and gluons behave inside matter.Preserving existing magnets is part of the laboratory’s preparation for the transition between the two facilities. The redesigned stands will provide storage space for the equipment before it is reused.During development, Desjardins presented design updates to Brookhaven engineers and scientists and addressed questions about material selection, safety reviews, and simulation results.A prototype of the four-tier stand has also been documented by Brookhaven. However, the supplied material does not establish that all required stands have been manufactured or that the full inventory of approximately 80 magnets has been transferred into storage.The project demonstrates how a relatively straightforward structural redesign can increase storage density and reduce infrastructure costs while supporting the construction of a major scientific facility.

title: Apple HomeView puts Siri and smart-home controls on one screen
content: Apple has unveiled a new artificial-intelligence-enabled device called Apple ‘HomeView’ equipped with a 7-inch Liquid Retina display that combines entertainment, communication, and smart-home controls of a household in one gadget.The company made the announcement on October 13, stating the preorders begin today. However, customers could get hold of the product only after a month’s time, it added.AI-powered personalized responsesPowered by Apple Intelligence and the latest version of Siri AI, the company’s AI tools let users can get more personalized responses to their queries and have more natural conversations with the assistant. Besides profound conversation, HomeView, when paired with a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, can use personal context from apps such as Messages and Calendar to garner more relevant responses.In a press statement, the corporation said that the new version of Siri installed in the latest product has expansive world knowledge, powering richer music discovery alongside a greater speaker system.Though designed to be used by everyone in the household, the new system can cater personalized content to six users, which is the upper limit for the facial recognition feature.“Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user,” said Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing.Beyond the personalized attention, the new gadget also comes handy as an intercom, helping to communicate with people in the other rooms of the house, much like an Intercom channel.Smarter home controlsElaborating on the range of functions of the smart device, he added that HomeView keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home.The touchscreen also provides a more direct way to access these functions without relying entirely on voice commands. This could make HomeView useful for quick household tasks, such as checking who is at the door through a compatible camera or adjusting room settings while passing by. Its combination of a display and smart-home controls brings several everyday functions together in a single device.According to the company, it allows users to control compatible smart-home devices using voice commands or its touchscreen to adjust lights and thermostats, lock doors, close blinds, and even view camera feeds. Security remains paramount for the company, even in the latest addition to their range of products that offers a personal experience to the users.“..Drawing on personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone’s information private and secure,” said Joswiak.Apple claimed that the device comes in two designs — tabletop and wall-mounted- and can fit in any space. It can be placed centrally on a tabletop or tucked comfortably in the corner of a side table or nightstand, while sharing family photo albums and music can be easily enjoyed by everyone in a household, including guests. The wall-mounted version can take up space in the entryway or hallway, offering entertainment to passersby.With a stainless steel body, Apple’s latest smart gadget comes in different hues ranging from silver, starlight, rose pink, to space gray — each finished with a matching cable.
