title: Counter-drone interceptor shifts from hover to cruise without pilot
content: Powerus Corporation has revealed a counter-drone interceptor that switches from vertical hovering to forward flight without pilot input. The US defense technology company introduced Guardian-3 at the Association of the United States Army’s 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C.The aircraft marks the third generation of Powerus’ Guardian interceptor family. Its defining feature is a flight system designed to manage the transition from takeoff to cruise after an operator authorizes launch.Powerus showcased the interceptor at booth 8341 during the October 12–14 exhibition. However, the company has yet to disclose its specifications, production timeline, or availability.Hover to cruiseGuardian-3 takes off vertically before hovering like a quadcopter. It then automatically pitches forward into nose-first cruise flight without requiring pilot input.The transition gives the interceptor two distinct flight modes. Vertical takeoff supports launch from confined spaces, while forward flight allows the aircraft to pursue its intended interception profile.Powerus has not explained the propulsion architecture behind this transition. It also has not disclosed the aircraft’s speed, range, endurance, or maximum operating altitude. The level of autonomy is a key distinction from Guardian-2. That predecessor introduced semi-autonomous operation, whereas Guardian-3 aims to automate more of the flight sequence.An operator still authorizes launch. After that approval, the aircraft manages its transition into cruise without continuous manual control.GPS and thermal controlGuardian-3 places its GPS receiver on the camera gimbal. Powerus says this arrangement keeps the antenna pointed skyward as the aircraft changes orientation during its transition to forward flight.The design addresses a specific navigation challenge. An aircraft pitching forward changes the orientation of its onboard equipment, potentially affecting how a fixed antenna faces the sky.Mounting the receiver on a gimbal helps maintain its intended orientation during that maneuver. Powerus has not released navigation accuracy figures or explained how the system handles GPS interference.Thermal management presents another engineering challenge. Guardian-3 uses ducted cooling for its electronic speed controllers (ESCs), which regulate electrical power supplied to the motors. Powerus says the arrangement maintains airflow during hovering and sustained full-throttle operation. Those conditions place different demands on the cooling system as the aircraft moves between flight modes.The company has not provided temperature measurements, power consumption figures or details about the cooling ducts. Further specifications would help establish how the system performs under demanding operating conditions.Automation moves forwardPowerus describes Guardian-3 as the next step in reducing operator workload across its interceptor family. CEO Andrew Fox unveiled the system at AUSA, where defense companies present technologies to Army personnel and industry partners.Co-founder and President Brett Velicovich said each Guardian generation has transferred more tasks away from the operator. Guardian-3 extends that approach through automated flight transitions. However, autonomous flight does not establish autonomous target engagement. Powerus has not detailed Guardian-3’s target acquisition, tracking, or interception logic.Its operational capabilities therefore remain difficult to assess. Speed, range, guidance performance, and testing results will help determine how effectively the interceptor can engage aerial threats.

title: Rugged US-made electric truck battery packs 113 kWh of energy capacity
content: A company in the US has recently introduced a rugged 800-volt (V) battery with a 113-kilowatt-hour (kWh) capacity, that can charge from 10 to 80 percent in less than 42 minutes.The battery, known as Aventor, was designed by American Battery Solutions (ABS), a Michigan-headquartered firm that specializes in lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries for commercial and industrial vehicles. ABS unveiled the battery at the unit on October 13, at The Battery Show North America in Detroit.Made for electric trucks, industrial machinery, and other heavy-duty equipment, the battery delivers up to 358 kilowatts (kW) (about 480 hp) of peak power. It can also charge up to 80 percent in 42 minutes or less.Subhash Dhar, ABS founder and CEO, discussed the battery’s potential. “Aventor represents years of work across ABS and an exciting step forward in what we can offer our heavy-duty OEM customers,” Dhar elaborated. Two different versionsThe Aventor battery operates at 800 volts (V). It can store up to 300 watt-hours of energy per liter (Wh/L) and 200 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg). ABS developed two versions to meet the different needs of commercial and industrial vehicles.The first, called the Chassis-Integrated Pack, is designed to fit between a vehicle’s frame rails or in other limited spaces, like roof-mounted installations. The second version, on the other hand, or the Hyper-Rugged Cube Pack, features a reinforced enclosure that can withstand higher levels of vibration, shock, and heavy use.An Aventor chassis-integrated battery pack.Credit: American Battery SolutionsAccording to ABS, the latter can also be installed in different positions. This gives vehicle manufacturers more flexibility when designing EVs. Both versions rely on the same basic technology. This means that producers can use them in different vehicles and equipment.What’s more, the pack also features a wireless battery management system that monitors voltage and temperature at individual cell groups. It includes onboard data storage, cybersecurity protection, and over-the-air software updates.“Safety, reliability and intelligence are central to the design,” said Jeffrey Donaldson, ABS’s SVP of engineering. Additional safety features include gas detection, electrical isolation monitoring, as well as technology designed to prevent battery failures from spreading between cells.A decade of battery lifeThe battery lasts up to 10 years, even under heavy-duty use and harsh conditions. It has IP67 and IP69K protection rating, meaning that it is sealed against dust and can withstand temporary immersion in water and high-pressure water jets.Simultaneously, its fast charging capability could cut downtime for both vehicles and equipment that operate for extended periods. “The result is a highly capable platform that gives customers more energy, more uptime, more value and an excellent foundation from which they can scale electrification across their portfolios,” Dhar stated.An Aventor hyper-rugged cube battery pack.Credit: American Battery SolutionsThe company intends to deliver the first customer samples in 2027. Commercial production is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2028. The initial production capacity is set to reach 6,000 battery packs annually, equivalent to approximately 0.7 gigawatt-hours (GWh).“We set out to develop a battery platform that leads on energy density without any compromises in the safety, durability or performance these applications demand,” Dhar concluded in a press release.

title: New charging system delivers 800 kWh in 18 minutes for electric mining trucks
content: The biggest hurdle facing zero-emission heavy industry hasn’t been building electric haulers. It has been keeping them powered without idling away precious operational hours.To address this, heavy equipment manufacturer LGMG has introduced new technology to phase out diesel and keep fleet operations running smoothly.China-based LGMG showcased a fully integrated clean-energy system in live operating conditions during its inaugural Global Mining Customer Service Festival in Ordos, Inner Mongolia. Over 500 industry leaders watched electric haulers charge up in minutes rather than hours. The integrated system combines renewable solar generation, battery storage, and megawatt-class charging to power electric fleets. Overall, the star was a battery-electric mining truck that surged from 20% to 90% charge in just 23 minutes.23-minute rechargingMining operations depend on strict, continuous schedules to remain profitable. When haul trucks sit idle waiting to recharge, every minute of lost production directly erodes operating margins. Therefore, minimizing equipment downtime is essential for keep the fleet running smoothly and protect profitability.LGMG overcame charging issues by developing a 3C fast-charging system paired with a specialized thermal management setup that operates from -30°C to 50°C. Under test conditions, the technology charges batteries from 20% to 90% in 23 minutes, delivering peak power output of roughly 3.6 MW. Under extreme conditions, the system supplies nearly 800 kWh in 18 minutes to keep fleet downtime to a minimum.Industry participants observed a live demonstration of LGMG’s electric mining trucks operating alongside intelligent fleet dispatch, solar generation, energy storage, and ultra-fast charging infrastructure. The showcase proved that all system components can work together under real-world mine conditions.Cutting emissions A centralized energy management platform manages power distribution, coordinates charging schedules, and optimizes fleet dispatching. Working together, these components maximize equipment utilization and keep mine production running efficiently.Remote mines frequently suffer from weak grid connections, forcing operations to use diesel generators and defeating the purpose of electrification. LGMG resolves this challenge with an integrated solar-storage-charging-transportation system. On-site solar panels capture renewable energy during daylight, while high-capacity batteries store excess power for later use. Intelligent dispatch software coordinates charging schedules with fleet demands to keep equipment operating without interruption and without relying on the grid.“The demonstration illustrated LGMG’s approach to mining electrification, extending beyond individual machines to encompass supporting energy infrastructure,” the press release stated. Mining companies are facing growing pressure to cut emissions. As a result, off-grid megawatt charging offers a viable blueprint for cleaner heavy industry.Transitioning from conventional diesel haulers to battery-electric trucks offers economic and environmental benefits. Surface mining operations can lower fuel and energy costs by 40% to 60% depending on electricity rates and solar availability. And downhill loaded trips also generate energy through regenerative braking, which extends operating range and minimizes wear on physical brakes.Leading equipment manufacturers, including Caterpillar, Komatsu, Liebherr, and SANY, are accelerating efforts to deploy zero-emission haul fleets across the industry. Transitioning to electric transport allows remote mines to avoid spending millions of dollars on high-voltage grid extensions. LGMG is expanding its electric fleet to handle overburden removal, coal mining, high-altitude operations, and extreme environments.

title: Wind turbine waste could replace steel rebar, cut emissions by 90%
content: Wind turbines spend decades generating clean electricity, but their blades pose a difficult waste problem once they stop turning. Built from fiberglass that is expensive to break down, these components can end up in landfills even though much of the rest of a turbine is recyclable.Concrete and cement production offer a way to put that waste back to work. Recycling companies have found methods to recycle around 85% of a blade, recovering materials that can replace cement ingredients, provide kiln fuel, or reinforce concrete. As existing wind farms age, these approaches could help address blade disposal while reducing emissions from another carbon-intensive industry.Why turbine blades are difficult to recycleA wind turbine typically has a service life of around 20–30 years. However, its blades do not always remain in operation for that entire period. Damage can force an earlier replacement, while technological advances can encourage operators to swap older equipment for newer designs.Much of a retired turbine can be recycled, with old equipment also providing recoverable metals. The blades present a different challenge because their fiberglass construction makes processing difficult and costly.That cost helps explain why discarded blades end up in landfills. Their ability to generate clean energy does not make their eventual disposal straightforward.Recycling them for construction gives the recovered material another purpose. Rather than treating the entire blade as waste, processors can break it down and recover ingredients and fibers useful in cement and concrete production.The distinction between those two products matters. Cement is an ingredient used to make concrete, so recycled blade material can enter the construction process in different ways depending on how it is processed.How blades become cement ingredients and concrete reinforcementOne useful material recovered from turbine blades is silica. It can substitute for sand and clay used in cement production, reducing the need for those raw materials.Blade recycling can also supply fibers for concrete. A study published in 2024 concluded that fibers recovered from wind turbine blades can strengthen the material, giving discarded components a role beyond supplying cement ingredients.Another approach uses cut-up blade sections as an alternative to steel reinforcement. Rebar, the steel rods placed inside concrete, helps improve its durability. Replacing it with blade pieces offers a separate route for reusing material that would otherwise be difficult to dispose of.These applications address different parts of construction. Recovered silica contributes to cement manufacture, while fibers and blade sections serve as reinforcement in concrete.They also show why there is no single route for turning a retired blade into building material. Its next use depends on which materials are recovered and whether they become ingredients, reinforcement, or fuel.Where the emissions savings come fromConcrete is the world’s most widely used material and accounts for around 7% of global carbon dioxide emissions. Much of its footprint comes from cement manufacture, which involves heating limestone in a kiln.That process releases carbon dioxide from two sources: the fuel burned to heat the kiln and the limestone itself.Parts of discarded turbine blades can replace coal as kiln fuel. The supplied source reports an approximately 27% reduction in concrete production emissions through this approach.Using blade pieces instead of rebar can reduce emissions associated with the reinforcement stage by around 90%. That figure applies to that stage, rather than the entire concrete production process.As more wind equipment reaches retirement, expanding recycling capacity could keep additional blades out of landfills. Their reuse also creates opportunities to reduce demand for conventional construction inputs, extending the useful life of materials originally built to produce clean electricity.

title: New method to unlock 100,000 tons of lithium for EV batteries, storage
content: The US is set to have access to about 110,000 US tons (100,000 metric tons) of battery-grade lithium over the next decade following a new agreement to produce the critical mineral using advanced lithium extraction technology.The GET-Lit direct lithium extraction (DLE) and refining technology was developed by Energy Exploration Technologies (EnergyX). The Texas-based firm specializes in lithium extraction and critical mineral production.On Monday, October 12, EnergyX announced that it signed a binding, 10-year, take-or-pay agreement with Singaporean global commodity trader Trafigura to supply lithium from two major projects in Texas and Chile. The supply will support electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and other industries that depend on battery materials.The company said commercial production is scheduled to start in 2028. “Offtake agreements are among the most important steps in taking a lithium project from development to production,” Teague Egan, EnergyX founder and CEO, disclosed. A new extraction methodThe US produces about 6,600 US tons (6,000 metric tons) of lithium annually. This accounts for less than one percent of the global production. Moreover, it relies on net imports for more than 50 percent of the lithium it consumes. To address this, EnergyX came up with the GET-Lit direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology. Backed by more than 150 patents, the approach extracts lithium from mineral-rich brines and refines it into materials suitable for batteries. The novel process works by separating lithium directly from liquid brines. EnergyX’s Project Black Giant lithium extraction facility in Chile.Credit: EnergyXEnergyX has already tested the method in labs, pilot facilities, and demonstration plants in the US and Chile. In April 2026, it commissioned its Project Lonestar lithium production plant in Texas, which is the largest DLE lithium production plant in the country.At the same time, the company is also working on another major lithium project in Chile called Black Giant. It has a planned annual production capacity of around 57,871 US tons (52,500 metric tons). The two projects will produce different lithium products. Black Giant will supply lithium carbonate, while Project Lonestar will produce lithium hydroxide. Both materials are essential for rechargeable batteries used in EVs and energy storage systems.Commercial operationsUnder the agreement, Trafigura will buy 110,000 US tons (100,000 metric tons) of battery-grade lithium products over the next decade. The deal covers 66 percent of the planned first-phase output from Project Black Giant, as well as 30 percent from Project Lonestar.Meanwhile, EnergyX is also talking to other potential buyers to secure customers for 80 percent of its planned production. At current lithium prices of about USD 18,100 per US ton (roughly USD 20,000 per metric ton), the deal could generate over USD 2 billion in revenue over its lifetime.“A long-term purchase commitment from a counterparty of Trafigura’s scale and credit quality shows that the market wants EnergyX’s product,” Egan stressed in a press release. “It also gives lenders and investors the revenue visibility they need before committing capital to commercial construction.”Battery-grade lithium hydroxide monohydrate made with EnergyX’s proprietary GET-Lit technology.Credit: EnergyXEnergyX has also secured financial support for its expansion plans. This includes a USD 225 million investment from energy company Eni for Project Black Giant and a USD 690 million letter of intent from the US Export-Import Bank for potential debt financing.“We are pleased to support EnergyX as it develops its lithium projects in Chile and the US,” Daniel von Arx, Trafigura’s head of battery metals, stated. He added that long-term deals are important for starting production and securing reliable supplies of critical minerals.

title: They Almost Vanished. Now 183,000 Giant Tortoises Rule This Remote Paradise
content:
The Aldabra Giant Tortoise. Credit: FotoNatura
Once pushed to the brink, giant tortoises on a Seychelles atoll now outnumber the country’s people, with a new survey estimating nearly 183,000 animals.
Aldabra Atoll, home to the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population, supports an estimated 180,000 animals, according to research led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter. The highest estimate yet for the Aldabra giant tortoise (
Aldabrachelys gigantea
) reflects both a remarkable conservation recovery and a better way of counting animals that are difficult to see.
A Recovery From The Brink
The team’s best estimate was almost 183,000 adult and subadult tortoises, more than the entire human population of the Seychelles. Their numbers appeared relatively stable during the study period.
That abundance would have been difficult to imagine in the 19th century, when heavy exploitation reduced Aldabra’s tortoises to fewer than 1,000. Their recovery has been supported by decades of protection, including the atoll’s designation as a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.
Giant tortoises grazing in large numbers on Aldabra Atoll. Credit: Dennis Hanse
Today, Aldabra and the Galapagos are the two remaining strongholds of native wild giant tortoises, with far fewer animals in the Galapagos. The new findings strengthen Aldabra’s reputation as one of the Indian Ocean’s outstanding conservation successes.
“The monitoring data in this study were collected by SIF staff living and working on the atoll, year after year. More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra,” said Dr. Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF.
Counting The Tortoises Nobody Saw
The larger total comes with an important qualification: it does not mean the population has nearly doubled since 1999. A tortoise can be present without being visible, and earlier surveys did not adequately account for animals concealed in scrub or shade. Those estimates probably missed a substantial number.
To address that problem, the researchers used Bayesian hierarchical distance sampling. This statistical method accounts for animals that observers failed to detect and for differences in visibility across habitats. It produces an estimate of the population, rather than simply a tally of sightings.
“Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring program is one of the longest-running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said study co-author Dr. Nancy Bunbury.
“By modeling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”
Where Giant Tortoises Gather
The animals were most concentrated in Aldabra’s grasslands, known as “tortoise turf.” The next highest densities occurred on open exposed surfaces and in open mixed scrub.
Dense scrub, mangroves, and Pemphis vegetation made tortoises harder to detect. Correcting for those differences helps researchers distinguish places with fewer animals from places where animals are simply harder to spot.
Together, the findings describe a population that has recovered dramatically from historical exploitation and now appears healthy and stable. They also establish a more dependable starting point for measuring future changes, something direct comparisons with older estimates cannot provide.
Climate and Predators Still Pose Threats
Despite their recovery, Aldabra’s tortoises face growing environmental pressures. Droughts are projected to become longer and more frequent, reducing food and shade, while rising seas threaten the atoll’s low-lying habitats.
Feral goats, which devastated Aldabra’s vegetation, were eradicated in 2012. But feral cats and black rats remain and prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The researchers say planned efforts to eliminate these mammals could allow more young tortoises to survive, support further population growth, and help the species withstand climate pressures.
“These results are great news for the tortoises and a testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr. Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter in Cornwall who helped develop the statistical framework used to analyze the monitoring data.
“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline, not an endpoint. Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought, and invasive species.”
Reference: “Inferring the Abundance of an Island Megaherbivore From Semi-Structured Distance Sampling” by Lara B. Hillyard, Nancy Bunbury, Christopher N. Kaiser-Bunbury, Dave Hodgson, Luke A’Bear, Cheryl L. Sanchez, Christopher W. Jones, April Burt, Frauke Fleischer-Dogley and Dave W. Hudson, 4 September 2026,
Ecology and Evolution

title: One of the World’s Rarest Animals Is Facing a Devastating Problem: It Can’t Find a Mate
content:
The Sumatran rhino is the world’s smallest and hairiest rhinoceros species—and one of the rarest mammals on Earth. Credit: Shutterstock
One of the world’s rarest rhinos faces a devastating problem: finding another of its kind before it is too late.
Small, hairy, and cheekily charismatic.
Those words sprung to mind when I first met a Sumatran rhinoceros (
Dicerorhinus sumatrensis
) after traversing the maze of wooden slatted paths at the conservation center in the dense, humid forests of Malaysian Borneo.
It was 1998, and I was an eager student volunteer at the center. At that time,
300 Sumatran rhinos
were thought to exist globally.
Rhinos On The Brink Of Extinction
I saw this female rhino as
a symbol
of conservation hope. But today, according to the International Rhino Foundation’s 2026
State of the Rhino
less than 50
Sumatran rhinos remain. All are found in Indonesia. The
Javan rhino
Rhinoceros sondaicus
) is just as rare.
While these figures rely on estimates, the trajectory is alarming.
So what is driving this decline? And how can we protect the few Sumatran and Javan rhinos that are left?
Familiar Icons, Overlooked Species
In modern culture, rhinos
represent strength
, power, and security. We use them as sports mascots and feature them in everything from
car logos
safety equipment
Their ubiquity in popular culture may lead us to underestimate the urgency of their plight. Species used as marketing emblems are often considered
more common
than they truly are.
There are
five surviving
species of rhinos. I have had the privilege of getting to know all but one while working as a wildlife veterinarian in zoos, sanctuaries, and the wild.
Africa is home to white and black rhinos, whose populations have
fluctuated greatly
throughout history. The water-loving greater
one-horned rhino
lives in India and Nepal and has seen a
steady recovery
Two Rare Rhinos, Different Survival Threats
Compared to their African and Indian relatives, Sumatran and Javan rhinos typically fly under the radar. However, their
critically endangered
status signals these animals are in urgent need of assistance.
According to the latest
State of the Rhino
report, the future of the elusive
Javan rhino
and the small, hairy
Sumatran rhino
is now especially precarious. Distribution is a major reason why.
There are roughly 50 surviving Javan rhinos. All live in a single protected area,
Ujung Kulon National Park,
on the island of Java. Due to nearby converging tectonic plates, it is vulnerable to earthquakes and
tsunamis
natural disaster
could well exterminate the Javan rhino population.
Bringing Isolated Rhinos Together
In contrast, the several dozen remaining Sumatran rhinos
are scattered
into many subpopulations, across two islands. This means the chance of a wild individual rhino encountering another of their kind is remote or even impossible. With no prospect of finding a compatible mate, isolated survivors are destined to be the end of their
genetic line
To protect this fragmented population, the International Rhino Foundation established the
Sumatran Rhino Sanctuary
in 1996. It is located in
Way Kambas National Park
on the island of Sumatra.
The sanctuary is currently home to ten
intensively managed
, semi-captive Sumatran rhinos. The resident animals live in large, natural rainforest habitats. They are provided with nutrition, security, and regular veterinary care.
Increasing rhino numbers through natural or
assisted breeding
requires patience. Females give birth to a single calf after about
16 months
of pregnancy. It may be several years before they have another.
Infertility
is a recognized problem in
some rhinos
New Calves Offer Hope for Recovery
The sanctuary has had some hard-won successes. Five Sumatran rhino calves were born there between 2012 and 2023, in part due to close reproductive
management and monitoring
. Excitingly, authorities have just announced two new pregnancies.
Camera-trap footage
has also confirmed the births of up to five Javan rhino calves in Ujung Kulon in recent years. These precious births go some way towards recovery of these two species.
Poaching is a persistent threat to all rhino species. Worryingly,
global demand
for rhino horn is increasing, especially in China and Vietnam. Besides its long-standing use in traditional medicine,
rhino horn
now plays a role in demonstrating wealth and status, particularly in business circles. Poachers killed as many as 26 Javan rhinos between 2019 and 2023 alone.
Protecting Rhinos Takes More Than Stopping Poachers
Anti-poaching strategies include
behavior change campaigns
, which focus on promoting social and cultural unacceptability of horn use and purchase. Governments may also rely on intelligence-led
law enforcement
and disruption to large crime syndicates to stop poachers. While poaching convictions and court sentences are increasing, including
in Indonesia
, this is not enough to keep the world’s rhinos safe.
Proactive measures, such as protecting and restoring habitat suitable for each species, are vital to the recovery of rhino populations. This is particularly true as humans
increasingly encroach
on wild places.
Translocation
—capturing and then releasing animals in a new place—is one possible way of protecting the world’s rhinos.
Recent research
examined whether this strategy could be used to re-establish populations of Sumatran and Javan rhinos across their former range throughout Southeast Asia. Conservation authorities can learn from past translocations of African rhinos, which show finding
suitable habitat
, anti-poaching protection, and careful planning are crucial to the success of these efforts.
A Future Built On Local Support
More broadly, effective rhino conservation relies on having an army of supporters. Local communities should tangibly benefit from living alongside rhinos, for example through job creation and by sharing in the proceeds of ecotourism. Even from afar, people can help by supporting conservation organizations and avoiding the purchase of products that contribute to tropical deforestation.
Sustainable funding and political commitment
are crucial
to protecting the few Indonesian rhinos that remain. It’s my wish that younger generations, including my future students, have the privilege of meeting a small, hairy rhinoceros for themselves.

title: A Quantum Breakthrough Inside a Diamond Could Help Solve One of Einstein’s Greatest Mysteries
content:
Real-color photo of the lower half of the experimental setup. The diamond with nitrogen-vacancy centers is suspended via a graphite rod above a magnet. When the diamond is illuminated with a green laser, the spin state within the diamond shifts, pushing it down towards the magnet. The diamond glows red due to electrons in the nitrogen-vacancy centers being excited to a higher energy state by the laser. Credit: Cassondra George (OIST)
Electrons inside a diamond have given a floating, centimeter-sized device a quantum nudge, opening a new path toward testing how quantum physics and gravity fit together.
Researchers at the
Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)
have used electron spin inside a diamond to drive the motion of a centimeter-scale (roughly 0.4-inch-scale) levitating device. Published in
Science Advances
, the experiment offers a new way to explore quantum effects in objects massive enough to matter in future investigations of gravity.
Quantum mechanics already makes lasers, MRI scanners, semiconductors, and quantum computers possible. But testing its stranger predictions in larger objects is difficult because heat, vibration, and other environmental disturbances can overwhelm delicate quantum behavior.
A Quantum Push on a Larger Scale
“There have been many efforts to test whether quantum mechanics holds for anything larger than a few tens of nanometers, so far without success. Now, we have observed a classical mechanical response to a quantum force on an object that is eight to nine orders of magnitude more massive than the current state-of-the-art spin-mechanical experiments,” said Professor Jason Twamley of OIST’s Quantum Machines Unit.
A graphical representation of the observed movements. a) When the laser is off, the diamond slab has a small magnetic moment (blue arrow) induced by the latent spin state inside the nitrogen-vacancy centers of the diamond. b) When the green laser is on, the spin state is polarized, causing the magnetic moment to fluctuate weakly, pushing the diamond down towards the magnetic field (red arrows). The amount of movement is labeled as displacement (Δz). Credit: Nayak et al., 2026
The device is roughly 100 million to a billion times more massive than the objects used in the spin-mechanical experiments Twamley describes.
The team’s long-term goal is to test whether gravity follows quantum rules by placing a sufficiently massive object in a superposition of different locations. So far, positional superposition has only been demonstrated in microscopic systems, whose gravitational effects are extremely weak.
“To test the quantum nature of gravity, we ultimately need to put objects with large enough masses into quantum superposition. And these objects need to be levitated in a vacuum to minimize the influence of environmental noise,” said first author Anshuman Nayak, a PhD student in the unit.
Starting Big Instead Of Scaling Up
Many researchers approach the problem by levitating tiny objects and attempting to increase their size. The OIST team is working from the other direction, using magnetic levitation to support a larger device before developing finer quantum control.
“The typical approach has been to start with extremely small, levitated objects and gradually increase their mass until the effects of gravity become relevant. But levitating macroscale objects using conventional techniques, such as optical traps, has proven extremely challenging. That’s why we’re in the opposite camp — going from large to small. Just as diamagnetic levitation can lift maglev trains, it can also be used to levitate centimeter-wide objects holding diamonds, where the effect of gravity can be extremely strong, but quantum effects have not been observed,” Nayak said.
The apparatus combined components the group had previously developed. A
diamagnetically levitated graphite plate
held a small mirror and supported a diamond through a carbon rod. The rod passed through magnetic shielding, with the diamond hanging above a magnet.
The diamond contained billions of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers, defects that hold unpaired electrons. Their quantum property called spin allows these centers to act as tiny magnets whose behavior the researchers can control.
Laser Pulses Turn Spin Into Motion
Green laser pulses prepared the NV centers in a selected spin state. This altered the diamond’s magnetic response, generating a small downward force that moved the suspended device.
A separate laser reflected off the mirror on the graphite plate into an interferometer. This instrument measured changes in position with picometer precision, a scale corresponding to trillionths of a meter.
The setup used to detect movement driven by quantum spin. A diamond sample containing nitrogen-vacancy defects in its atomic structure (inset) is suspended above a magnet by a carbon fiber rod, which runs up through magnetic shielding to prevent interference, then through another magnet assembly to a levitating graphite plate, slotted to minimize movement caused by the magnetic array. A mirror on top of the graphite plate reflects a laser beam from an interferometer, which measures distance changes with picometer precision. Credit: Nayak et al., 2026 & Pavel Puchenkov (OIST)
“NV diamonds are well understood and easy to control. That, and the fact that NV centers have some of the longest known coherence times, allowing them to maintain quantum superposition at room temperature much longer than other systems, makes them particularly attractive for generating macroscopic superposition of the motion or object in future research,” said co-author Daehee Kim, a PhD student in the unit.
Diamond’s durable quantum states could give researchers a way to control motion at much larger scales. The next challenge is to extend that control from producing ordinary motion to preparing genuinely quantum states of the device’s motion.
Toward Quantum Gravity And Sharper Sensors
Einstein wrestled with the foundations of quantum mechanics late in his life, and its relationship with gravity remains unresolved. Questions about gravity’s quantum nature, information in black holes, dark matter, and dark energy continue to expose gaps in our understanding of the universe.
Exploring those gaps requires experiments that can put theoretical predictions to the test. The new apparatus could help researchers develop such tests while also paving the way for exceptionally precise sensors to search for dark matter, gravitational waves, and other elusive phenomena.
“We’ve shown a large classical response from a small quantum effect. It’s no longer a question of whether such technology is possible, but of how we can refine experimental conditions to achieve quantum superposition within the regime of Einstein’s general relativity. And on the way, we’re developing a new class of extremely precise sensors. We’re pushing the bar from nanometers to centimeters. All we need is another order of magnitude, and we can finally observe Schrödinger’s cat in real life,” Twamley said.
Reference: “Spin force from a nitrogen-vacancy ensemble drives a 100-mg levitated resonator” by Anshuman Nayak, Daehee Kim, Shilu Tian and Jason Twamley, 7 October 2026,
Science Advances
DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh0566
This study was funded by Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Graduate University, Japan Science and Technology Agency.

title: Mars’s Strangest Cloud Just Got Even Stranger
content:
Image of the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud from the European Space Agency’s Mars Express spacecraft, taken on June 24, 2024. Credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin
Modeling suggests Mars’s Arsia Mons cloud may form ice without dust, pointing to a process never before observed in a planetary atmosphere.
A white cloud grows downwind of Mars’s Arsia Mons volcano each morning during spring and summer in the planet’s southern hemisphere. Rising beside a volcano 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) tall, this wisp of water ice can stretch up to 1,800 kilometers (about 1,120 miles), nearly twice the length of the UK, before quickly evaporating. The cycle
repeats every morning for several months
during the Martian dusty season.
Attempts to reproduce how the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC) forms had failed to match spacecraft images. Now, a study combining observations from the European Space Agency’s Mars Express with an advanced meteorological model suggests that the cloud may depend on an ice-forming process never before seen in a planetary atmosphere.
Cloud ice may form without dust
The AMEC is an orographic cloud, a type also found on Earth that forms as winds flow past the uneven terrain of a mountain or volcano. In the simulations, Arsia Mons triggers a powerful wave that lifts moist parcels of air several kilometers in just a few minutes. As the air rises, its temperature drops by 30 degrees in just 10 minutes, sending relative humidity soaring. Mars’s thin atmosphere and the volcano’s towering height combine to create the exceptional conditions the model needs.
Image of the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud from the European Space Agency’s Mars Express spacecraft. Credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin (acknowledgment: J. Cowart)
Clouds usually form when moist air cools and water vapor condenses into liquid droplets or ice crystals. Typically, the vapor gathers on tiny particles already floating in the atmosphere, such as salt, pollen, soot, or dust. This process is called heterogeneous nucleation, and dust is thought to provide those starting points for clouds on Mars.
“For the AMEC, it seems that cloud formation takes place without needing any of this ‘stuff’,” says Jorge Hernández-Bernal of LMD/CNRS/Sorbonne Université in Paris, France, lead author of the new study. “Water vapor turns directly into icy cloud particles without any middle step. It’s akin to droplets of condensation appearing in the middle of a room, rather than on a window. We call this
homogeneous nucleation
, and we’ve never seen it before in a planetary atmosphere. It’s wholly unexpected.”
Homogeneous nucleation requires extreme relative humidity levels, more than 100,000 times those usually experienced in everyday life on Earth. Scientists had proposed that it might occur in the upper atmospheres of Earth and Venus, but it has not been spotted there. “We’ve not seen these conditions on Mars before, but our finding now strongly suggests that the planet’s humidity can indeed reach these extreme levels,” says Hernández-Bernal.
Mars Express catches the morning cloud
The observations used to build the model come from a spacecraft that has followed the cloud for years. Mars Express
first revealed the AMEC in 2018
, and repeated observations have allowed researchers to investigate its evolution and
changing behavior
. For the new study, the team used data from three cameras aboard the orbiter: the Visual Monitoring Camera, High-Resolution Stereo Camera, and OMEGA.
Mars Express can capture large stretches of the Martian surface at high resolution. Alongside ESA’s ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, it is also one of the few spacecraft orbiting Mars that can observe during the morning hours when the cloud is present.
Image of Mars from the Visual Monitoring Camera (VMC) onboard the European Space Agency’s Mars Express spacecraft, taken on 10 October 2018. Credit: ESA/GCP/UPV/EHU Bilbao
“Mars Express can also track how the cloud is changing on timescales of mere hours, which gives us an unrivaled view of short-lived phenomena on the planet,” says ESA Mars Express Project Scientist Colin Wilson. “Overall, this finding is a true accomplishment for the mission and its scientists: Mars Express discovered the AMEC, has followed up and monitored it for years, and is now helping reveal the secrets of its formation.”
Exotic physics helps recreate Mars’s cloud
Reproducing those observations required the researchers to expand the physics included in their simulations. “To create the AMEC in our modeling, we found that we needed to include some exotic physics… physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature. It certainly hasn’t been seen in action before,” says Hernández-Bernal. “Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped.”
Some features of the modeled cloud still do not exactly match the observations, although Hernández-Bernal says “the result is remarkable.” He adds: “We don’t have nearly as much information about Mars’s atmosphere as we do about Earth’s, so reproducing the AMEC to this degree is a big success for the model.”
The findings suggest that processes considered unlikely may deserve attention when scientists investigate atmospheres elsewhere, including those of exoplanets. “While clouds on Earth and Mars seem to be governed by the same ‘rules’, understanding this exotic Martian cloud required exotic physics—and this may be true elsewhere in the cosmos,” says Wilson.
Reference: “Homogeneous ice nucleation from water vapour suggested by elongated clouds on Mars” by J. Hernández-Bernal, A. Määttänen, A. Spiga and F. Forget, 7 October 2026,

title: A Star Exploded 850 Years Ago. Somehow, It’s Still Alive
content:
Pa 30, the likely remnant of the historical supernova witnessed in the year 1181, now captured in unprecedented detail by NOIRLab’s Gemini North telescope. This image, obtained with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS), shows that the remnant’s unmistakable firework-shaped ejecta take on a cascading knot-like structure. Credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA; Acknowledgment: PI: T. Cunningham (Center for Astrophysics — Harvard & Smithsonian); Image Processing: J. Miller & M. Rodriguez (International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)
With roughly ten times as many gas filaments now resolved, the supernova remnant Pa 30 could guide searches for other stellar explosions that left surviving stars.
A star survived the explosion that left behind Pa 30, a dandelion-shaped cloud of debris. The sharpest images yet show that the apparently smooth streaks around this “zombie star” are tight chains of gas knots resembling pearls on a string.
A citizen scientist first identified Pa 30 in 2013. Astronomers later connected it to a supernova witnessed in 1181, nearly 850 years ago, and independently documented in Japanese, Chinese, and Arabic historical sources. That association linked Pa 30 to one of just five supernovae recorded before the telescope era whose remnants had long remained unidentified.
An international team captured the images using NOIRLab’s Gemini North telescope. The work was co-led by Tim Cunningham from the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian and Ilaria Caiazzo, assistant professor at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA), and the findings were published in
The Astrophysical Journal
Gemini North’s laser shines through airglow. The Gemini North telescope’s laser guide star beams up into the atmosphere. The laser guide star is used to measure turbulence in the Earth’s atmosphere so the telescope can correct for it and achieve clear images of the night sky. Credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/M. Rodriguez (International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab)
Ten times as many gas filaments
At about 7,500 light-years from Earth, Pa 30 is relatively close on the scale of the universe. For comparison, the center of the Milky Way lies about 26,000 light-years away.
“We can see this much detail because of Pa 30’s proximity to Earth,” says Caiazzo. “This proximity makes Pa 30 uniquely valuable for study.”
Gemini North’s capabilities and its location on Mauna Kea in Hawaii helped the researchers obtain their detailed view. The telescope stands more than 4,200 meters, or roughly 13,800 feet, above sea level at one of the world’s leading astronomical observing sites. It forms one half of the
International Gemini Observatory
, alongside its twin, Gemini South, in Chile. Gemini North is partly funded by the
U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF)
and operated by NSF NOIRLab.
Ilaria Caiazzo, assistant professor at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA). Caiazzo co-led the study with Tim Cunningham from the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, now assistant professor at the University of Warwick. Credit: ISTA
The researchers analyzed emission lines, specific wavelengths of light released by gas, from ionized sulfur (S II) in the red part of the visible spectrum. They also examined emission from doubly ionized oxygen (O III), displayed in blue-green tones. The sulfur observations revealed roughly ten times as many filamentary features as previous images could resolve.
“The planetary region of our solar system could fit in each knot about ten times with room to spare,” says Caiazzo, referring to the region extending out to Neptune’s orbit, the solar system’s outermost planet. “The knots are quite strikingly uniform. We are excited to try to model them.”
Little sideways recoil for the surviving star
The star inside this intricate cloud survived a Type Iax supernova, a rare kind of incomplete stellar explosion. Pa 30 is the only known remnant of its kind in the Milky Way. Astronomers have identified a few similar objects in other galaxies, but Pa 30 is the only one in which telescopes can see the surviving stellar remnant at the core. Researchers have proposed that it formed when two white dwarfs collided. These extremely dense, Earth-sized stellar remnants have exhausted their fuel and shed their outer layers.
The new observations placed the surviving star almost perfectly at the nebula’s center. In many supernovae, an asymmetric explosion gives a surviving star a kick that sends it away from the explosion site. The team investigated that possibility by constraining the star’s transverse speed, meaning how fast it moves across the sky.
“Explosions conserve momentum. If the explosion itself was perfectly symmetric, the ejecta should also be symmetric, and the surviving star should not receive a substantial kick,” says Caiazzo. “We were able to measure a precise upper limit of the remnant star’s transverse kick speed, showing that it was surprisingly small. We practically don’t see the star moving away at all.”
More Type Iax remnants may await discovery
Despite the rarity of Type Iax supernovae, the team does not consider the identification of such a remnant unexpected.
“Reliable historical records of stellar explosions extend back only about a thousand years. For all we know, there might well be similar remnants still lurking in the dark in our own galaxy,” Cunningham says. “Today, we are lucky to study an intriguing object we know was observed by astronomers who made three independent historical records of the event centuries before the invention of the telescope.”
“We will likely identify more similar objects as new telescopes continue to inspect the depths of our night sky,” adds Cunningham, who is now an assistant professor at the University of Warwick in the United Kingdom.
Questions about Pa 30 remain, including how to explain its remarkably uniform knots. The observations also provide a detailed example against which astronomers can compare potential remnants in large surveys.
“Astronomy has entered the big data era,” says Cunningham. “Our findings will help us screen through the enormous datasets.”
Caiazzo adds, “In general, the farther into space we look, the more difficult it is to detect faint signals and interpret them. While we can see Type Iax supernovae in distant galaxies as point sources of light, resolving the remnants of such explosions is only possible in our own galaxy and in very few nearby ones. Eventually, we plan to use Pa 30’s distinctive properties to search the Milky Way and nearby galaxies for similar objects.”
Reference: “Detection of Knots in the Type Iax Supernova Remnant Pa 30” by Tim Cunningham, Ilaria Caiazzo, John C. Raymond and Scott J. Kenyon, 6 October 2026,
The Astrophysical Journal
DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/ae9cb2
This project was supported by NASA through the NASA Hubble Fellowship grant HST-HF2-51527.001-A awarded by the Space Telescope Science Institute, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, Inc., for NASA, under contract NAS5-26555.

title: Unstable Blood Pressure Linked to Higher Risk of Death and Stroke
content:
Fluctuating blood pressure may carry clinical information beyond a single reading. Credit: Shutterstock
People with type 2 diabetes and highly variable systolic blood pressure had nearly triple the death risk of those with normal blood sugar and steadier readings in an observational study.
At a blood pressure check, the cuff around your arm captures a moment in the pressure inside your arteries. Readings that rise and fall across later visits could hold clues to the risk of stroke or death, yet those fluctuations are not routinely considered when assessing health.
Dr. Fariba Ahmadizar and her colleagues in the Netherlands compared readings from 57,611 UK Biobank participants and found that people whose blood pressure varied more between research visits had a higher risk of dying during follow-up. Some measures of that variability were also associated with strokes, suggesting that the movement between readings deserves closer investigation.
“Our findings suggest that changes in blood pressure over time may provide information beyond the average blood pressure readings in routine care,” says Ahmadizar, of the Department of General Practice at Amsterdam University Medical Centre.
Participants returned for at least one blood pressure measurement after their initial assessment, allowing the researchers to compare readings while accounting for the time between visits. Their average age was 55.4 years, and 52% were women. Follow-up began at the first visit when enough measurements were available to calculate variability and lasted a median of 5.1 years. During that period, 1,460 participants died, 571 had a stroke, and 319 developed dementia.
Higher death risk with diabetes and pressure swings
Comparing those outcomes with blood sugar status brought a particularly striking association into view. Participants with type 2 diabetes and highly variable systolic blood pressure, the upper number in a reading, were 2.8 times as likely to die during follow-up as those with normal blood sugar and low variability.
Participants with prediabetes and high systolic variability also had a higher risk of death, by 62%, compared with the same reference group. Prediabetes means blood sugar has risen above normal without reaching the threshold for diabetes. At the start of the study, 5,397 participants had prediabetes, 1,470 had type 2 diabetes, and 50,744 had normal blood sugar.
People in these comparisons differed in both blood sugar status and blood pressure variability, so the additional risk cannot be attributed to fluctuating readings alone. To express the findings as absolute risks, the researchers also estimated the likelihood of death over 10 years. That estimate was approximately 1.0% for participants with normal blood sugar and low systolic variability, compared with approximately 2.9% for those with type 2 diabetes and high variability. These were longer-term estimates, rather than death rates observed over a full decade of follow-up.
Death risk beyond average blood pressure
Each heartbeat pushes blood through the arteries, producing the systolic pressure recorded as the upper number. Between beats, the heart relaxes, and the lower number records diastolic pressure. The researchers examined changes in both, along with mean arterial pressure, the average pressure across a heartbeat, and pulse pressure, the difference between the upper and lower readings.
Greater swings in all four measures were associated with a higher risk of death from any cause. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for average blood pressure, blood sugar status, and other factors. For systolic variability, each increase of one standard deviation was associated with an 11% higher risk of death. For diastolic variability, the corresponding increase was 8%.
Those percentages describe differences in variability across the study population, rather than the consequences of a particular jump on a blood pressure monitor. A standard deviation reflects how widely participants differed in their variability, so the findings cannot be translated directly into a specific rise or fall in millimeters of mercury, or mmHg.
Tracking strokes revealed associations with two of the measures: diastolic pressure and mean arterial pressure. Each standard-deviation increase in their variability was associated with a 12% and 10% higher stroke risk, respectively. The researchers found no statistically significant associations between blood pressure variability and dementia.
Can steadier blood pressure save lives?
Researchers presented the findings at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes. Ahmadizar cautions that the observational study cannot establish that blood pressure fluctuations caused the deaths or strokes. The results suggest that variability might help identify patients whose risk would otherwise be overlooked, but that potential still needs to be tested.
A patient returning to have a cuff wrapped around their arm might eventually benefit from closer attention to the changes between readings. Whether doctors can turn that information into better outcomes remains unresolved.
Ahmadizar says, “However, more research is needed before blood pressure variability can be recommended for routine clinical use. Questions that need answering include whether it is possible to reduce these fluctuations – and if doing so reduces the risk of stroke or death.”

title: Alzheimer’s Breakthrough: Scientists Protect Brain Cells Without Removing Toxic Tau
content:
A surprising connection between immune cells and neurodegeneration may open a new path toward treating Alzheimer’s. Credit: Stock
Mice kept more brain tissue and performed better on a memory test after researchers blocked an immune attack, without removing the tau tangles linked to Alzheimer’s.
Scientists at
Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis
have identified a potential way to protect the brain from damage associated with tau buildup. In mice with Alzheimer’s-like changes, an antibody reduced the entry of immune cells called T cells into the brain. Treated animals retained roughly 40% more tissue in regions involved in memory than untreated mice, despite having similar amounts of tau.
The findings, published Sept. 28 in
, point to a treatment strategy focused on the brain’s response to tau rather than the protein deposits themselves. Growing evidence suggests that this immune response contributes substantially to the cell death that gradually erodes memory and independence.
When The Immune Response Damages The Brain
Tauopathies are neurodegenerative diseases in which tau protein accumulates in twisted clumps. Alzheimer’s belongs to this group, but it also involves another protein, amyloid. In primary tauopathies, tau builds up without amyloid deposits.
Two Alzheimer’s drugs, lecanemab and donanemab, target amyloid plaques that develop between brain cells early in the disease. Amyloid disrupts cellular communication and promotes the formation of tau tangles inside neurons. Although these drugs can slow decline, they have not been shown to prevent brain cell death and do not treat primary tauopathies.
“In tauopathies, including Alzheimer’s disease, there’s no treatment right now that actually decreases neurodegeneration,” said David M. Holtzman, MD, the study’s senior author and the Barbara Burton and Reuben M. Morriss III Distinguished Professor in WashU Medicine’s Department of Neurology. “If we can show that we’re really decreasing brain cell death, it’s certainly worth trying to pursue that pathway to prevent the most devastating consequences of these diseases.”
Holtzman’s laboratory previously identified T cells as a possible contributor to that damage. Its
2023 study in
showed that T cells entered the brains of mice with tau buildup, gathered especially in areas containing the most tau, and caused neurodegeneration. A
related study published earlier in September in
Nature Neuroscience
found that these cells receive their instructions in lymph nodes outside the brain.
Blocking the Route Into the Brain
Those earlier findings left a crucial part of the process unexplained: how activated T cells reached the brain. Immune cells navigate by following chemical signals called chemokines. The researchers focused on CXCL10, a signal they had found at elevated levels in their mouse model and that other groups had linked to Alzheimer’s disease.
Activated T cells detect CXCL10 through a receptor on their surface called CXCR3. Together, the signal and receptor provide a route the cells can follow. Blocking that route offered a way to test whether keeping T cells out could protect brain tissue.
The new study included co-senior author Jason Ulrich, PhD, a professor of neurology at WashU Medicine, and first author Joshua T. Emmerson, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher in Holtzman’s laboratory. In mice with tau accumulation, removing either CXCL10 or the CXCR3 receptor on T cells prevented the cells from infiltrating the brain, even when the researchers deliberately triggered inflammation.
Brain Protection Without Removing Tau
The team then tested an antibody that blocks CXCR3. Young mice with existing tau buildup, but without substantial brain cell loss, received injections every five days for three and a half months.
At the end of treatment, mice given the antibody had about half as many T cells in their brains as untreated animals. They also retained more tissue in memory-related regions, showed fewer signs of nerve cell damage, and performed better on a memory test.
Yet their tau tangles looked much the same. That combination suggests that, in these mice, reducing the immune response could limit damage even while the underlying protein deposits remained.
The antibody also reached the brain’s boundary without entering the brain tissue itself. This raises the possibility of treating a damaging process from outside the brain, avoiding the need to deliver the therapy across the blood-brain barrier.
The results remain an animal finding. More research is needed before the approach can be tested in people, including whether it can safely protect the human brain. The study also leaves open whether treatment would help after substantial neurodegeneration has already occurred.
A New Role for T Cell Therapies
Holtzman suggested that existing drugs targeting T cells could be evaluated as possible Alzheimer’s treatments. Some are already used for multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune disorders, in which the immune system attacks healthy tissue.
“Tauopathies aren’t thought of as autoimmune disorders, so they haven’t been treated the same way, but this study shows for the first time in an animal model that these diseases respond to a specific T-cell therapy,” said Holtzman, who also directs WashU Medicine’s Hope Center for Neurological Disorders and Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center.
“For this therapeutic approach, if it is safe, you wouldn’t have to design the drug to get into the brain—which is a big deal since most molecules don’t cross the blood-brain barrier well—and you don’t have to get rid of the tau to get this therapeutic effect.”
Reference: “Peripheral CXCR3 blockade mitigates T cell infiltration and neurodegeneration in a mouse model of tauopathy” by Joshua T. Emmerson, Hao Hu, Vivek Savani, Peter Lin, Mina Rohde, Prabal Sharma, Wade Self, Yongyi Li, Jonathan Nulman, Megan E. Bosch, Zhe Liu, Javier Remolina Serrano, Xin Bao, Carla M. Yuede, Mehdi Jorfi, Rudolph E. Tanzi, Jason D. Ulrich and David M. Holtzman, 28 September 2026,
DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.08.030
This study was supported by a BrightFocus Postdoctoral Fellowship, National Institutes of Health/National Institute on Aging grants R01AG082328 and R01AG085374, the GHR Foundation, the Carol and Gene Ludwig Initiative in Neuroimmunology Research, a gift from Ronald Schaich, a gift from John Ludwig, a gift from Cindy and Evan Goldberg, and the Freedom Together Foundation.

title: A Hidden Sugar in Red Meat Linked to a 63% Higher Risk of Diabetes
content:
A large French study has uncovered an intriguing difference in how a dietary molecule is associated with diabetes risk depending on its food source. Credit: Shutterstock
A sugar in red meat that the human body recognizes as foreign may help explain the food’s link to type 2 diabetes.
Preliminary findings from a French study of nearly 90,000 adults linked higher intake of a meat-derived sugar called N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc) with a greater risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2D). Participants with the highest intake had a 63% higher risk than those with the lowest intake, although the observational research cannot establish that the sugar caused the disease.
The findings were presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD). Researchers are investigating whether an immune response to Neu5Gc could help explain why red meat consumption has been associated with diabetes.
“Our findings support chronic inflammation as a specific mechanism linking red meat consumption with T2D, partly beyond the amount of red meat a person eats and partly independent of body fat,” said lead author Dr. Leopold Fezeu of Université Sorbonne Paris Nord in Bobigny, France.
Why the Body Recognizes This Sugar as Foreign
Most mammals naturally produce Neu5Gc, but an ancient mutation in the CMAH gene left humans unable to make it. We nevertheless encounter it in food, particularly beef and lamb, with smaller amounts in dairy products.
After consumption, Neu5Gc can enter human tissues. Its presence creates an unusual situation: a foreign molecule becomes incorporated into the body’s own cells. Scientists describe it as a xeno-autoantigen, against which the immune system produces antibodies.
The resulting persistent immune activity (xenosialitis) has previously been linked to cardiovascular disease and cancer. The researchers wanted to explore whether a similar process might contribute to diabetes, a question that had not previously been examined in a large prospective study.
Tracking Diet and Diabetes Over Time
The analysis drew on 89,953 participants in NutriNet-Santé, a long-term French study of diet, lifestyle, and health. Their average age was 42, 79% were women, and none had diabetes or cancer at enrollment. During a median follow-up of 7.2 years, 966 developed T2D.
Participants completed three 24-hour dietary records. Researchers used a validated database of measured Neu5Gc concentrations in foods to estimate how much each person consumed and whether it came from meat or dairy.
The meat analysis included beef, lamb, pork, rabbit, goat, and game. Processed meat products (such as bacon, sausages, and cured meats) were recorded as a separate food group, and dairy products were analyzed separately.
Men and women were each divided into five equally sized groups (quintiles) according to meat-derived Neu5Gc intake. The researchers then compared diabetes risk across these groups, using the lowest-intake group as the reference.
Higher Intake Was Linked to Higher Risk
The highest-intake group had a 63% higher diabetes risk, while the second-highest group had a 41% higher risk (men and women combined). These are relative increases compared with the lowest-intake group, not the percentages of participants who developed diabetes.
The association remained after accounting for age, sex, physical activity, diet quality, smoking, and underlying health conditions. It appeared in both men and women, with no statistically detectable difference between them, and was consistent regardless of total energy intake.
The groups also differed substantially in meat consumption. In the highest-intake group, men ate a median of 97 grams (3.4 ounces) of red meat daily and women 73 grams (2.6 ounces). Including processed meat brought those amounts to 136 grams (4.8 ounces) and 96 grams (3.4 ounces), respectively. In the lowest-intake group, the corresponding totals were just 21 grams (0.74 ounces) for men and 9 grams (0.32 ounces) for women.
The risk rose particularly sharply at higher Neu5Gc intakes. Researchers suggested that this could reflect a threshold at which its accumulation in tissues provokes a stronger immune response, but the study did not identify or establish such a threshold.
Separating the Sugar From the Meat
“Although we do not know exactly what levels of Neu5Gc trigger an immune response, our data suggest that higher intakes of meat-derived Neu5Gc are associated with a progressively higher risk of T2D,” Fezeu said.
Accounting for body mass index (BMI) weakened the association, but it remained statistically significant. The researchers estimated that obesity explained approximately 13% of the association and proposed that inflammation affecting insulin-producing cells and insulin-sensitive tissues might help explain the rest. Those mechanisms still require investigation.
However, when researchers also adjusted for total red meat consumption, the association weakened and was no longer statistically significant. Although it continued to point toward higher risk, this result makes it difficult to separate Neu5Gc’s possible contribution from that of other substances in meat.
Dairy-derived Neu5Gc showed no association with diabetes. The researchers considered this consistent with the lower concentrations in cow’s milk compared with beef and lamb, and with smaller serving sizes typically consumed. Across all food sources combined, the highest Neu5Gc intake was associated with a 37% higher diabetes risk, largely driven by meat.
What Researchers Want To Test Next
“Together, these findings suggest that the association between Neu5Gc and T2D may depend on its dietary source, with meat-derived Neu5Gc showing a stronger association with T2D risk than total dietary Neu5Gc,” Fezeu said. “There may be differences between sources, or other components of red meat may contribute.”
He added, “Given how common red meat is in Western diets, the strong association between meat-derived Neu5Gc and T2D risk is an important finding. Future research should explore whether reducing exposure to meat-derived Neu5Gc, for example by favoring poultry or plant-based proteins over beef and lamb, which have the highest Neu5Gc content, could help prevent T2D. Studies directly measuring anti-Neu5Gc antibodies in large cohorts would also help to directly test the xenosialitis mechanism in humans.”
The team plans to investigate Neu5Gc alongside other red meat components, including heme iron (a form of dietary iron). Measuring antibodies against Neu5Gc would also provide a more direct test of the proposed immune mechanism than dietary estimates alone.
Preliminary Findings Leave Important Questions
The results have not yet been validated, and the estimates could change when the analysis is finalized. The study identifies an association but cannot determine what caused the higher diabetes risk or establish that reducing Neu5Gc intake would prevent the disease.
Although researchers adjusted for several major risk factors, unmeasured lifestyle and social differences could still have influenced the findings. Food records can also misrepresent actual intake, and the analysis did not track dietary changes during follow-up.

title: Wolves Were Supposed To Save Yellowstone. Scientists Say the Real Story Is Very Different
content:
Since their reintroduction to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, wolves have become a celebrated example of how restoring predators can revive damaged ecosystems. But decades of ecological research suggest their influence on the park’s wildlife and vegetation is far more complex than the popular narrative suggests. Credit: Shutterstock
Yellowstone’s wolves helped reduce elk numbers, but tree recovery remained limited, challenging the popular story that their return restored the park’s ecosystem.
You might be among the 46 million people who’ve seen
showing how wolves changed Yellowstone, or you may have heard some other version of this story. Yellowstone, which covers nearly 3,500 square miles of the western United States, was the world’s first national park. Its pioneering reintroduction of wolves, which began in 1995, set a worldwide precedent for conservation.
The first half of the story is well established. Wolves were eradicated from Yellowstone in the 1920s. With the wolves gone, populations of elk (a large species of deer) overgrew. Elk overgrazed the park’s riverbanks, turning groves of willow and aspen and beaver ponds into bare grasslands.
This process was swiftly reversed, or so the story goes, when wolves were reintroduced. Not only did wolves kill elk, keeping their numbers in check, but they also scared them away from the valleys, giving trees a chance to regrow.
A range of beneficial effects followed: beavers moved back and rebuilt their dams, and the regrown shrubs attracted more bears, who further helped keep elk in check.
It’s a neat and captivating story, widely cited as evidence that wolves can restore ecosystems and reforest the land. Unfortunately, reality is much more complicated.
Wolves did not, by and large, restore Yellowstone. Understanding the science behind this fact can teach us a lot about how ecosystems work. Even more interestingly, reflecting on why so many people are keen to believe this story can tell us a lot about ourselves, and our relationship with nature.
Why wolves did not save Yellowstone
The story originated with
scientific studies
in the early 2000s, built on a theory known as
“trophic cascades”
: the idea that changes at the top of the food chain can waterfall down to its very bottom. For example, wolf eats elk eats willow: so, more wolves equals fewer elk equals more and taller willows.
This idea was later popularized far beyond the scientific literature, notably by British rewilding advocate George Monbiot, whose
2013 Ted Talk
was used to voice-over the viral Yellowstone wolves video.
But with a further two decades of data to draw on, scientists have found that this linear chain of causes and effects is an oversimplification of ecology. Wolves eat elk, yes, but so do humans and bears and mountain lions.
Reductions in elk populations, caused by this varied suite of carnivores, did allow some degree of tree recovery in some parts of the national park. But that
recovery has been exaggerated
and falls far short of the landscape-wide reversal (from elk-dominated grasslands to willows and beaver ponds) that is often portrayed in popular accounts.
The park’s lead wolf biologist described the reality as more of a “trophic trickle” than a cascade.
Another reason why wolves did not radically transform Yellowstone is that elk aren’t so scared of wolves after all. This might sound odd—who’s ever heard of prey that’s not scared of its predators? Actually,
it’s feeding that takes priority
in elk behavior: hungry animals will seek good grazing, predators or no predators.
Why we wanted to believe
For all its scientific shortcomings, the story satisfies some of our deepest beliefs and cravings.
First of all, the idea that nature is a balanced machine where the pieces fit precisely and interact like clockwork. Take a single cog away, and the machine falls apart: elk run rampant and the ecosystem collapses. Put the cog back, and in the blink of an eye, things run smoothly as they used to.
But ecosystems aren’t machines: they are dynamic, ever-changing, and often unpredictable.
Second, and more perversely, the story satisfies the common belief that only humans can disrupt nature’s harmony, and that it’s only by leaving nature alone that the balance is restored.
For instance, in the viral video about wolves in Yellowstone, there is not a single image of a human being. The narration describes the wolves as having “turned up” and says, “The number of beavers started to increase.” In fact, the wolves were flown in from Canada, and beavers had been deliberately released into the park’s surroundings. These human interventions are absent from the story the video tells.
In a way, this is a continuation of a much
older view of wilderness
as something untouched and unpeopled. This view of nature inspired the founding of many national parks, Yellowstone included—eventually displacing
millions of people
Third, the Yellowstone story satisfies the craving to conceive of nature as a healing power. It’s the ecological equivalent of
“nature cure”
stories in popular culture, in which damaged people recover by going on an outdoor journey. What the Yellowstone story portrays, if you like, is a nature-nature cure: in this case, it is not a person but a wilderness that is healed by nature.
Wolves can be worth saving regardless of whether they save Yellowstone. Personally, I think ecologists should learn to say, simply, that they love wolves – and that these objects of their love need serve no purpose beyond themselves.
Before turning to the humanities, I was trained as a conservation biologist. Many biologists, like my earlier self, tend to think of emotions as too soft to include in their publications by contrast with data (especially numerical data), which is seen as hard and indisputable.
Now, though, this seems upside down to me. We don’t need a theory of trophic cascades to justify loving wolves. It is love and sorrow that are solid and beyond dispute, not fickle arguments about the balance of nature.

title: Scientists Discover 45-Million-Year-Old Crocodile With a Strange Connection to Egypt’s Great Sphinx
content:
Reconstruction of the extinct Herugavialis cairensis with the Great Sphinx and pyramids depicted in the background. Credit: Karim Zanaty
Fossils of a newly recognized Egyptian crocodile species come from the same rocks as the Great Sphinx, and a missing snout tip helped inspire the animal’s name.
Crocodile fossils recovered in Egypt in the 1920s were initially grouped with a living long-snouted crocodile called the false gharial because of their outward resemblance. A new examination, including CT scans that let researchers look inside a nearly complete skull, has identified the Egyptian fossils as a distinct extinct species,
Herugavialis cairensis
Dr. Paul Burke, a researcher at the Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm, led the international team from the UK, Sweden, Germany, and Egypt. Advances in paleontological analysis allowed the researchers to identify several differences between the Egyptian fossils and the false gharial, challenging their original assignment to the genus
Tomistoma
Long-snouted crocodiles once lived at sea
The fossils came from Egypt’s 45-million-year-old Mokattam Formation. At that time, shallow seas covered much of the region, and
Herugavialis
shared those waters with at least two other species of gavials, a group of crocodiles distinguished by their long, narrow snouts.
Today, gavials live only in freshwater environments on the Indian subcontinent and in Southeast Asia. Just two species survive,
Gavialis gangeticus
Tomistoma schlegelii
, the false gharial. Their fossil record, however, spans more than 100 million years and documents a nearly worldwide distribution, with many species inhabiting shallow marine environments.
The Sphinx inspires a crocodile’s name
The Egyptian skull also has an unusual connection to the Great Sphinx. It comes from the same rocks used to build the monument and, although otherwise relatively well preserved, is missing the tip of its snout.
“Given this coincidence with the famously missing nose of the Great Sphinx, we decided to name the new crocodile after the Egyptian god Heru, who was possibly the inspiration for this iconic monument,” says Professor Philip Mannion of University College London, who co-led the study.
How the Mediterranean lost its crocodiles
The shallow seas inhabited by
Herugavialis
were part of a much longer history of crocodile life across the Mediterranean.
“Throughout much of the last 50 million years, the Mediterranean region hosted a high diversity of crocodiles, including gavials,” says Burke, the study’s lead author.
“However, this diversity fluctuated over time, seemingly corresponding to changes in global temperature and sea level, before the loss of all crocodiles in this region as a result of the drying of the Mediterranean approximately 6 million years ago.”
