title: Something Strange Is Happening Beneath Nicaragua’s Masaya Volcano
content:
Masaya Volcano is a broad volcanic complex located southeast of Managua, Nicaragua, and forms part of the Central American Volcanic Arc. Its activity is driven by the Cocos tectonic plate sinking beneath the Caribbean Plate. Credit: Shutterstock
Satellite measurements of Nicaragua’s Masaya volcano suggest magma is entering one reservoir as another drains, offering clues that could improve monitoring for future hazards.
Visitors come to Nicaragua’s Masaya volcano to look into its lava lake, while roughly 2 million people live within 13 miles (21 kilometers) of the active volcano. The molten rock exposed at the surface offers only a glimpse of a shifting underground system whose connections remain poorly understood, making it difficult to recognize changes that could eventually threaten nearby communities.
Penn State researchers tracked that hidden activity through satellite measurements of the ground above it and found two movements unfolding together. Between 2018 and 2024, the ground within Masaya’s caldera, a large volcanic depression, initially sank and then began rising. Around the active Santiago crater and its lava lake, however, the surface kept sinking throughout the study. Their findings, published in
Geophysical Research Letters
, suggest that different parts of the magma system were changing independently.
Masaya’s ground moves in opposite directions
Passing over Masaya about once every 12 days, the Sentinel-1 satellite collected radar measurements through the clouds that frequently cover tropical volcanoes. Its microwave signals bounced off the surface, and the researchers used interferometry to compare returning radar waves from separate passes. Changes in those waves revealed changes in the distance between the satellite and the ground, a technique called interferometric synthetic aperture radar, or InSAR.
Magma draining from an underground reservoir can cause the ground above it to settle, while incoming magma can make it swell. The researchers interpreted the caldera’s reversal from sinking to rising as evidence that Masaya’s main reservoir was inflating, possibly supplied by a new magma source deeper underground. Those measurements capture movement at the surface, so the explanation for what happened below remains an interpretation.
“At the same time, the area directly around the active Santiago crater deflated over the entire study period independently of the transition to inflation of the main reservoir,” said lead author Lizzie Johnson, who conducted the research for her Schreyer’s Honors College thesis and graduated from Penn State with a bachelor’s degree in geosciences in May. “This indicates that the plumbing system is more complex and could be due to decreasing magma in a second, shallower reservoir.”
Santiago’s continued sinking raises the possibility that magma was leaving a shallow reservoir even as the main reservoir expanded. Tracking these separate movements could help researchers untangle how magma passes between storage areas and the surface, giving them a clearer basis for assessing changes in the volcano’s activity.
Masaya’s hazards extend beyond lava flows
Sulfur dioxide escaping from Masaya already presents a hazard, with persistent emissions often reaching dangerously high concentrations even though the volcano’s last major lava flow occurred in 1772. The researchers did not identify an immediate danger to surrounding communities from the changes examined in this study.
Following the ground’s movements over longer periods, alongside further modeling of the underground system, could help clarify the connections suggested by the satellite observations. Johnson said that work could also improve hazard monitoring at other basaltic volcanoes with lava lakes, where researchers face similar challenges in understanding what lies beneath the exposed molten rock.
Johnson joined the research group after hearing a talk by Christelle Wauthier, a professor of geosciences and computational sciences hub director in Penn State’s Institute for Computational and Data Sciences. With help from graduate students, Johnson learned to analyze the satellite data and conduct academic research. Among those graduate students was coauthor Young Cheol Kim, who recently completed his doctorate in geosciences at Penn State. He explained that continuous monitoring helps researchers establish the volcano’s baseline behavior and recognize changes that might signal increased activity. “And then if there is a need to warn people, we can do that in a timely manner.” For the communities surrounding Masaya and the visitors peering into its lava lake, the aim is to turn shifts in the ground into time to act.
Reference: “Double Trouble: Two Active Magma Reservoirs Identified at Masaya Volcano, Nicaragua, Using Satellite Geodesy” by E. Johnson, Y. C. Kim and C. Wauthier, 23 July 2026,
Geophysical Research Letters
DOI: 10.1029/2026GL123214

, as well as by the computational research infrastructure of the Institute for Computational and Data Sciences at Penn State.

title: A Hidden Molecular Switch Could Change How We Treat Aggressive Prostate Cancer
content:
A newly discovered connection between protein synthesis and cancer cell identity could help scientists identify aggressive prostate tumors and improve future treatment strategies. Credit: Shutterstock
A protein-building molecule helped switch resistant prostate tumors back into a drug-sensitive state in experimental models, offering a potential target for future treatments.
Many treatments for prostate cancer, one of the most common cancers in men, target a protein called the androgen receptor, which fuels tumor growth. Tumors can escape that approach by becoming less dependent on the receptor, shifting into a more aggressive form that responds poorly to therapy.
Researchers at Fred Hutch Cancer Center have found that restoring a single molecule involved in protein production can make treatment-resistant tumors sensitive to those drugs again in experimental models. Their study, published in
, is the first to show that a single transfer RNA, or tRNA, can control prostate cancer cell identity and influence treatment response.
Microscope image of human prostate cancer with a high amount of a distinct tRNA, as shown in dark purple/pink staining. High amounts of a specific tRNA (called tRNA1Arg(UCU)) were associated with the prostate tumor being dependent on the androgen receptor for growth and with sensitivity to therapies that target the androgen receptor. Credit: Hsieh Lab, Fred Hutch Cancer Center
Protein builders can shape cancer identity
During protein production, cells use instructions carried by messenger RNA, or mRNA, to assemble proteins. Transfer RNAs match that information with the appropriate amino acids and deliver them to be joined together.
“The discovery opens an entirely new realm of cancer biology that was previously unrecognized,” said co-corresponding author Andrew Hsieh, MD, a professor and associate director of Fred Hutch’s Human Biology Division. “Historically, tRNAs have been thought to play a bystander role in cell maintenance and disease, but our study shows that tRNAs can actively shape the identity of cancer cells.”
Andrew Hsieh, MD, a professor and associate director of Fred Hutch Cancer Center’s Human Biology Division, and Yeon Soo Kim, PhD, a Fred Hutch postdoctoral researcher, in Hsieh’s lab at Fred Hutch. Hsieh holds the Larry and Virginia Gordon Endowed Chair in Prostate and Bladder Cancer Research at Fred Hutch. Credit: Fred Hutch Cancer Center
First author Yeon Soo Kim, PhD, a Fred Hutch postdoctoral researcher in Hsieh’s lab, investigated how this protein-building process contributes to treatment resistance. “We already knew that genomic mutations or transcriptional factor-dependent genetic expression are altered during the cancer progression and can lead to the development of treatment resistance,” Kim explained. “But we wanted to know more about how mRNA translation — also known as protein synthesis — is involved when the disease becomes more aggressive.”
Restoring sensitivity to prostate cancer drugs
Kim examined prostate cancer cell lines, mouse models, and tumor samples from patients. Across these systems, a particular tRNA called tRNA1Arg(UCU) was abundant in cancer cells that depended on the androgen receptor. Levels were lower in tumors that were less dependent on the receptor and resistant to treatment. In follow-up experiments, supplying this tRNA to resistant tumors restored their sensitivity to therapies targeting the androgen receptor.
“We found that we can shift the cell state between androgen receptor-dependent to an androgen receptor-independent state with a single tRNA,” Kim said. “This is important because changes in cell identity are a major reason prostate cancers become resistant to treatment. We found that this tRNA can influence whether cells remain in a drug-sensitive state or transition to one that is more aggressive.”
Microscope image of human prostate cancer with a low amount of a distinct tRNA, as shown in few areas of pink staining. Low amounts of a specific tRNA (called tRNA1Arg(UCU)) in prostate tumors were associated with the tumor being less androgen receptor dependent and therefore less likely to respond to androgen receptor targeting therapies. Credit: Dr. Yeon Soo Kim, Hsieh Lab, Fred Hutch Cancer Center
tRNA could guide future cancer treatment
Kim and Hsieh are also investigating whether tRNA could serve as a biomarker for aggressive prostate cancer or as a therapeutic target. Those potential uses could help guide more precise treatment choices or lead to new therapies for patients.
“In this study we used prostate cancer as an archetype to study tRNA-dependent state changes, but we think it’s just the beginning,” said Kim, who plans to pursue this research when she establishes her own lab. “We can apply this approach to any type of disease models or other types of cancers that undergo identity switches after treatment, such as lung and breast cancers.”
Reference: “tRNA dosage regulates lineage dependency and resistance in prostate cancer” by Yeon Soo Kim, Sonali Arora, Dave Young, Ava Tsou, Amy Shiuan, Cynthia L. Wladyka, Dmytro Rudoy, Jin Yeong Kim, Jennifer A. Waters, Samantha L. Schuster, Ilsa M. Coleman, Mridu Kapur, Marek Sobczyk, Christopher D. Katanski, Amin M. Bayat Tork, Wen Zhang, Peter S. Nelson, Gavin Ha, Michael C. Haffner, Eva Corey, Colm Morrissey, Yuzhuo Wang, Arvind R. Subramaniam, John K. Lee, Susan L. Ackerman, Tao Pan and Andrew C. Hsieh, 7 October 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11153-8
The study was funded by multiple grants from the National Institutes of Health, including the Pacific Northwest Prostate Cancer SPORE, and the U.S. Department of Defense. Additional funding was from the Prostate Cancer Foundation and the American Cancer Society.

title: Alpha Precision Systems and VON ARDENNE collaborate to provide APS Turnkey Production Lines for Perovskite Photovoltaics
content:
Alpha Precision Systems and VON ARDENNE collaborate to provide APS Turnkey Production Lines for Perovskite Photovoltaics
Alpha Precision Systems Inc. (APS) and VON ARDENNE GmbH are joining forces to include VON ARDENNE’s equipment portfolio to offer integrated turnkey production lines for perovskite photovoltaic manufacturing. The collaboration combines APS’s expertise in solution-based processing, slot-die coating, drying and overall line integration with VON ARDENNE’s extensive experience in vacuum deposition technologies and industrial-scale coating systems.
APS has been developing equipment and integrated manufacturing solutions for perovskite solar cells and modules, with platforms ranging from R&D and pilot-scale systems to larger production lines. Its portfolio covers key manufacturing processes including cleaning, laser processing, slot-die coating, vacuum drying, thermal processing, vacuum deposition, ALD, encapsulation, testing and line automation.
VON ARDENNE brings extensive experience in vacuum coating technologies, including sputtering and evaporation, as well as the engineering and scale-up of vacuum coating systems from R&D to industrial production. Over the past few years, the company has established a strong footprint, especially in European R&D facilities, and is actively supporting perovskite photovoltaic development.
“The collaboration between our two companies strengthens the vacuum deposition portion of APS’s turnkey offering and combines the respective technologies and experience of both companies into an integrated manufacturing platform rather than establishing a new technology base from the ground up.”, says Miguel Friedrich, CEO of APS.
First project in the USA with delivery in 2027
APS’ first project in the United States to include VON ARDENNE’s vacuum deposition systems is a 300 x 300 mm pilot line, with delivery planned for 2027. The line will provide a platform for perovskite process development, device optimization and manufacturing scale-up, integrating solution-based and vacuum-based deposition processes within a coordinated production concept.
The companies expect the collaboration to support future projects at different production scales, aiming to provide perovskite manufacturers and developers with a more integrated path from process development to pilot production and, ultimately, industrial-scale manufacturing.
Depending on the customer’s device architecture, process flow, substrate format and required throughput, APS can configure turnkey solutions combining wet coating, drying and thermal processing with vacuum deposition and other key process technologies.
About Alpha Precision Systems Inc. (APS)
Alpha Precision Systems Inc. develops precision slot-die coating, vacuum drying, thermal-processing and integrated manufacturing solutions for perovskite photovoltaics, semiconductor packaging and other advanced thin-film applications. APS offers perovskite platforms ranging from 300 × 300 mm R&D and pilot systems to larger production-scale turnkey lines, integrating process equipment, automation and process support.

title: Electrode redesign pushes perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells to 32.3% certified efficiency
content:
Electrode redesign pushes perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells to 32.3% certified efficiency
Researchers at Southwest Petroleum University, the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai Normal University, Chongqing University and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences have developed perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells with a champion efficiency of 33.06% and a certified efficiency of 32.28%, by redesigning the front electrode instead of changing the light-absorbing layers.
The front electrode of a tandem cell has two parts: a transparent conductive oxide layer that collects charge and moves it sideways, and a metal grid that carries the current out but also blocks some sunlight. The team replaced the commonly used indium zinc oxide with tungsten-doped indium oxide (IWO). IWO has a lower work function, which improves electron extraction, and it lets more near-infrared light through to the silicon bottom cell. With identical metal grids, this raised the champion efficiency from 31.65% to 32.49%, mainly through a higher fill factor (78.74% to 79.51%).
The team then built a simulation tool to weigh the shading from the grid lines against the resistance losses in the electrode. Narrower lines block less light, while wider or denser lines carry current more easily. In experiments, the best results came from lines about 50 µm wide, spaced 2.5 mm apart. This gave the champion cell, with an open-circuit voltage of 1.973 V, a short-circuit current density of 20.72 mA/cm² and a fill factor of 80.87%.
Unencapsulated cells with the IWO electrode kept 91.3% of their initial efficiency after 500 hours of maximum power point tracking under one-sun illumination, compared with 86.1% for the standard electrode.
The researchers note that industrial methods such as screen printing, electroplating and laser transfer printing can already make metal lines down to about 10 µm wide, so the design rules could apply to manufacturing. The cells were small-area devices, and the team lists large-area, uniform deposition of the transparent oxide within the perovskite’s temperature limits, and cutting indium use, as open challenges.

山西交控新能源发展有限公司于9月20日公示了2026—2027年度光伏组件供应商入库框架协议入围结果，英利能源、晶科能源、晋能清洁能源、华阳集团（阳泉）新能源销售公司及正信光电共5家企业成功入选。本次招标旨在保障山西省高速公路分布式光伏发电项目的建设需求，采用框架协议形式统一遴选合格供应商。项目仅设1个标段，即“高速公路分布式光伏发电项目所需N型单晶硅双面双玻光伏组件”供应商入库，服务内容涵盖组件供应、运输、安装指导、培训、检验检测、验收、保险、税费及售后服务等全流程。入围企业有效期为框架协议签订后1年，供货范围限于山西省境内招标人指定地点。
英利能源连续两年以综合评分第一入围山西交控光伏组件供应商名录，彰显其在“光伏+交通”领域的领跑地位。依托零碳智慧充电站、高速智能光伏示范项目等标杆实践，英利以高适配性产品与多场景解决方案，加速推动基础设施绿色转型。
中国石油青海油田公司乌图美仁凯驰100万千瓦光伏电站，作为中国石油首个百万千瓦级集中式并网发电项目，截至8月17日累计获取绿色电力证书120万张（对应12亿千瓦时绿电），完成绿证交易33万张，创历史新高。该电站于2024年11月底全容量投运，通过提前取得电力业务许可证、构建产销协同体系、自研功率预测模型等举措，有效应对省内新能源竞争与出力波动挑战；依托中长期协议托底、现货交易增效及绿证市场化运作，形成“发电—售电—绿证交易”多元盈利模式。自2025年9月完成首笔内部绿证交易以来，已建立月度申领、数据核验、按需匹配的闭环管理机制，推动绿电环境价值高效转化。（199字）
本文报道了陕西定边一批因大风灾害受损的光伏组件通过线上平台完成公开竞价交易的情况。该批标的共约415块光伏板，由金诺国际拍卖集团于8月7日11时在金拍网启动竞价，采用按单价竞拍模式，起拍价未明确披露，但竞价开始时当前价为115元。整个竞价过程高效迅速，仅用14分钟即于11时14分成交，期间累计获得19次围观。交易以现场实际清点数量为准，体现了受损新能源设备资产处置的规范化与市场化运作趋势。
本文解读国家能源局《关于组织推进非公共电网可再生能源发电项目绿证核发的通知》（国能综通资质〔2026〕60号），指出该文件首次将离网光伏、工商业屋顶自发自用光伏、绿电直连等不接入公共电网的可再生能源项目纳入绿证核发体系。此前因缺乏电网计量数据，此类项目无法获得绿证认证；60号文明确其发电量可申请绿证，其中上网电量对应可交易绿证，自发自用电量对应不可交易绿证，分别用于市场交易和绿色电力消费证明。该政策与同期发布的《可再生能源电力消纳责任权重制度实施办法》（第42号令）形成配套——后者自2026年8月起对重点用能企业实施强制性绿电消费考核，并以绿证为唯一核算依据。文章进一步梳理了绿证申领的八步流程、三类适用主体、两类绿证用途差异及企业实操需关注的九项关键事项。
《非化石能源电力消费核算指南（试行）》由国家发改委、国家能源局等五部门于2026年5月联合印发，自印发日起试行，适用于2026年起的年度核算。该指南旨在支撑“双碳”目标落实，完善碳排放统计核算体系。其核心围绕三大原则：一是统筹衔接，兼顾能源统计、碳排放核算及物理连接、电能量交易、绿证绿电交易等多维度因素，分类明确省、市两级及终端用户的核算规则；二是稳妥有序，推动核算机制逐步从单一电能量交易基础转向电能量与绿证交易并行模式，并计划未来探索缩短核算周期；三是科学合理，优先依据物理连接和市场交易直接认定，对无法直接认定的情形实施合理分摊，确保跨区域核算平衡，杜绝重复计入。（199字）
截至5月18日，中国石油首个百万千瓦集中式并网发电项目——青海油田乌图美仁凯驰光伏电站100万千瓦光伏电站，累计获取绿色电力证书超104万张，其中成交超25万张。这标志着中国石油青海油田公司在绿电价值转化领域取得重大突破。
绿色工厂、碳排放核算指南与央企绿色供应链这三道门槛，正在重塑制造企业的生存规则。无论是屋顶光伏还是更大规模的工商业光伏项目，均能有效支撑央企绿色供应链的减排数据申报。未来，中正能源将持续以"工商业光伏投资+绿色工厂认证服务"双轮驱动，紧扣《碳排放核算指南》规则与央企绿色供应链要求，做企业全周期可信赖的零碳合伙人，让每一家企业都能零门槛跨过碳合规门槛，在双碳时代抢占发展先机。
索比光伏根据广东电力市场2024年度报告、国家能源局最新绿证价格数据，梳理了两条收益路径、三档价格情景，以及五个决定你能拿到哪档价格的关键因素。
近日，《2025年度科创独角兽100强》榜单正式发布，天合富家凭借在分布式光伏领域的技术深耕与创新成果荣耀上榜，成为分布式光伏领域极具代表性的标杆企业，同步上榜的还有杭州六小龙之一DeepSeek等企业。凭借高可靠、高保障、高收益以及好体验的“三高一好”服务优势，天合富家已经为超140万用户提供了原装电站与服务，与200+行业深度合作，成功打造2000+行业标杆项目案例。

title: 同样买 BC，有人多花三成以上：差别藏在招采方式里-索比光伏网
content:
导语：BC比TOPCon贵多少，是市场说了算? 拉完2026年集中式项目的招采样本，我们发现： 价差的大小，很大程度上不取决于行情，
而取决于你把它放在哪个标里招。同样买BC，融合标段比单独招采能把价差压下去21%~37%。
2026年组件价格波动，让不少负责招采的同行直呼"心累"。一个月一个价，月初和月末能差出一大截，窗口踩不准，同样一瓦组件，成本就悄悄多花一截。
但价格只是表面。我们最近拉了一组2026年集中式项目的招采样本，本想看看BC组件到底比TOPCon 2.0贵多少，结果意外发现：价差的大小，很大程度上不取决于市场，而取决于你怎么招。
为了压平月度波动的噪声，我们先算各标段的月度均价，再汇总成季度均值。两类招采方式一摆出来，反差就明显了。单独为BC开标段时，BC相对TOPCon 2.0的价差，26Q1是0.0845元/W，26Q2仍有0.0651元/W;而当BC与TOPCon 3.0放在同一个标段、高效标段同场竞标时，相对Topcon2.0的价差直接滑落到0.0532元/W(Q1)和0.0515元/W(Q2)。算笔账，融合标段把价差压低了21%到37%——同样一块BC板子，在融合标段里的溢价，大约只有单独招采时的六到八成。
更扎眼的是"稳"。单独BC标段的月度价差在0.045~0.114元/W之间来回跳，最高月是最低月的2.5倍还多。融合标段的价差却几乎贴着0.05元/W走。总体更低，而且更稳。
价差为什么会被"压扁"?道理不复杂，主要是三股劲儿拧在了一起。其一，同场博弈：BC和TOPCon 3.0摆在同一份高效标段的标书里竞价，供应商想拿下整包，自然会考虑Topcon3.0高效产品报价的竞争，价格竞争更充分。其二，避免被"锁定技术"：单独BC标段相当于明牌告诉供应商"我就买这一种"，对方没有理由让利，溢价自然守得高。其三，规模换筹码：融合标段整体体量更大，对供应商的吸引力更强，市场供应体量也更大，业主手里的议价牌也更多。
机制说得通，真实项目里的数字也给出了印证。把几个已披露的样本摊开看，BC相对TOPCon 2.0的溢价区间大致在0.04~0.11元/W.
溢价本身难免，但溢价"高到什么程度"，样本之间差得很明显，这恰恰说明招采方式是能撬动这块成本的。
总的来说，招采文件里的一处结构设计，可能直接决定了你为BC多付多少钱。以2GW项目、BC装机占比约一半估算，融合标段相对单独招采，仅BC溢价一项就能省下1500万~3100万元。另外，价格更稳带来的测算可靠性提升，又是一笔没算进去的隐性好处。当然，融合标段不是万能解，它考验的是对组件配比、交付节奏和供应商资源的统筹。但它至少提醒我们，在价格波动的年份，招采策略本身就是一种降本手段。

title: “青字号”光伏产品走俏海外 前8个月出口同比增长1.5倍-索比光伏网
content:
10月12日，来自西宁海关的数据显示，今年前8个月，青海省光伏产品累计出口3.1亿元，同比增长1.5倍。
近年来，全球能源转型持续深化，海外光伏市场需求持续释放。依托得天独厚的清洁能源禀赋，青海光伏制造产业乘势而上，“青字号”光伏产品加速走向国际市场。作为辖区光伏产业链上游骨干企业，青海高景太阳能科技有限公司是本轮出口增长的核心力量。公司负责人张振忠说：“近年来，公司持续深耕光伏硅片产业并不断开拓国际市场，海关的精准服务为我们抢抓海外市场机遇提供了坚实支撑，助力我们的国际订单实现高效交付。”
针对光伏产品批次多、交付时效要求高的特点，西宁海关主动靠前服务，深入辖区重点光伏企业开展调研走访，量身定制“一企一策”帮扶方案。一方面持续跟踪全球主要光伏市场技术性贸易措施动态，精准推送监管标准与合规指引，引导企业规范申报、主动应对贸易壁垒。另一方面，充分发挥属地海关贴近生产一线优势，畅通企业诉求快速响应通道，第一时间解决出口通关环节疑难问题，落实预约通关、优先查验等便利化举措，全力保障光伏产品高效通关。
西宁海关将持续聚焦辖区光伏产业发展需求，加大政策宣讲与精准帮扶力度，提升通关便利化水平，助力青海光伏企业深度融入全球产业链供应链。

title: 福建漳州市：累计获批集中式光伏电站项目47个、总装机规模6423MW-索比光伏网
content:
近年来，漳州市发改委立足区域清洁能源资源禀赋，锚定能源枢纽建设目标，坚持“资源赋能产业、产业支撑发展”，聚焦光伏等优势产业，以资源开发夯实基础、以龙头招商促进集聚、以服务赋能推动升级，加快培育光伏产业集群，推动清洁能源资源优势转化为产业发展优势。
一是统筹资源开发，夯实产业基础。坚持集中式光伏与分布式光伏并举，不断拓展商业建筑、公共机构、村居屋顶等应用场景，全域推进光伏资源规模化开发。全市累计获批集中式光伏电站项目47个、总装机规模6423MW，其中12个项目并网投产、总装机容量879MW，获批规模、投产规模均居全省首位。通过规模化资源开发，为光伏制造项目落地提供资源支撑和市场空间，推动资源开发由单点突破向全域成势转变。
二是聚焦龙头招商，促进链式集聚。以旗滨光伏玻璃项目为牵引，深化龙头招商、以商引商，围绕光伏玻璃、高效组件核心环节精准延链补链，招引光伏逆变器、支架、储能装备等配套企业落地，推动产业链链式集聚。依托临港区位与东南亚市场优势，支持龙头企业协同创新、产能共建，构建上下游紧密配套的光伏先进制造集群，夯实面向国内、辐射东南亚的光伏产业供应链支撑。
三是强化服务赋能，推动提质升级。靠前服务，支持安泰新能源等企业做大做强，打通“光伏资源—光伏制造—市场应用”发展链条，推动产业从资源端向制造端、市场端延伸，提升产业发展层次。
下一步，漳州市发改委将持续抓好光伏产业链补链、延链、强链，做实龙头企业全周期服务，持续开展龙头招商，吸引上下游配套企业集聚，加快培育光伏产业集群，夯实能源枢纽建设的产业基础。

title: 安徽出台行动方案 全链条保护光伏和新型储能产业知识产权-索比光伏网
content:
10月12日，记者获悉，安徽省市场监督管理局联合省工业和信息化厅印发《安徽省加强先进光伏和新型储能产业知识产权保护行动方案(2026-2027年)》，围绕先进光伏、新型储能产业实施知识产权全链条保护，破解行业“内卷式”竞争，以知识产权制度保障赋能全省新能源产业集群建设，服务安徽省“1188”现代化产业体系与“三地一区”建设。
方案明确，到2027年，安徽先进光伏和新型储能产业知识产权治理体系进一步完善，高价值专利培育布局规模持续扩大，龙头企业打造形成具备全球竞争力的专利组合。行政、司法、协同保护效能全面提升，知识产权转化运用渠道更加畅通，企业海外知识产权风险预警处置能力显著增强，产业链知识产权风险得到有效防范。
方案聚焦产业创新源头，将强化知识产权高质量布局。支持龙头企业联合高校科研机构组建产业知识产权创新联合体，面向钙钛矿、太空光伏、固态储能电池、大容量储能电池等前沿赛道，以及关键原辅料、生产设备等配套环节开展核心专利储备。围绕TOPCon、异质结、锂电池储能等量产技术迭代挖掘专利组合，发挥专利导航作用，助力关键核心技术攻关突破。
为提升专利服务质效，方案提出优化专利预审服务。组建产业专利预审专家服务团队，深入企业开展“一对一”布局指导，引导企业在研发初期融入预审思维。优化国家级知识产权保护中心预审流程，压缩审核周期，建立重点企业预审服务档案，落实
“一企一策” 精准服务，产出更多符合预审标准的高质量专利申请。
围绕产业链安全，安徽将健全知识产权风险防控体系。健全知识产权安全与科技、经济安全协同机制，监测产业纠纷、专利流转及舆情动态;搭建光储产业知识产权专题数据库，定期发布风险预警报告，推动企业建立覆盖原材料、核心装备、电池组件、系统集成全链条侵权风险监测机制。
在保护维权方面，方案提出，构建多部门协同保护格局。高效办理专利侵权行政裁决，推动案件信息跨部门共享联动，对故意侵权、重复侵权行为加大规制力度。同时畅通行政、司法、调解、仲裁多元纠纷化解渠道，依托保护中心、行业协会推动纠纷快速调处，强化行业自律自治。
方案提出，打通知识产权价值实现通道，加速创新成果落地转化。推动高校科研机构专利开放许可，共建产业知识产权运营中心，探索产业链专利池建设，推动专利交叉许可;开展专利密集型产品备案认定，在政府采购、首台套认定等工作中给予政策倾斜，促进创新成果转化为现实生产力。
针对产业出海痛点，方案明确，强化海外知识产权风险应对。跟踪涉外知识产权动态，建立48小时应急响应通道，为涉诉企业提供法律援助;落实海外维权补助，鼓励设立维权互助基金，引导企业做好海外专利、商标布局。同步推进商标品牌建设，实施商标保护专项行动，打击商标侵权、恶意抢注行为，培育一批具有国际影响力的安徽光储品牌。
此外，方案提出加大企业知识产权能力培育，开展专题业务培训，培育复合型知识产权人才，夯实企业合规管理基础。

国家能源局四川监管办公室原党组书记、监管专员马军杰因涉嫌严重违纪违法，正接受中央纪委国家监委驻国家发展改革委纪检监察组的纪律审查，以及四川省监察委员会的监察调查。该案件由中央纪委国家监委驻国家发展改革委纪检监察组与四川省纪委监委联合通报，表明其问题线索涉及党的纪律和国家监察双重范畴。马军杰曾长期在能源监管系统担任重要领导职务，其被查反映出能源监管领域反腐败工作的持续深化。目前调查仍在进行中，尚未公布具体违纪违法事实及情节。此次审查调查属于中央纪委国家监委统筹部署下对垂直管理单位领导干部开展的常规监督执纪行动，体现了对公权力运行全过程监督的强化。
贵州能源集团有限公司原党委副书记、副董事长、总经理兰海平因涉嫌严重违纪违法，于2026年6月18日被通报正接受贵州省纪委监委的纪律审查和监察调查。兰海平，1965年12月出生，重庆忠县人，长期在贵州能源系统任职，历任贵州省煤矿设计研究院副院长、省能源局煤炭处处长及副局长、乌江能源集团副总经理、盘江煤电集团董事长等职，2023年3月起担任重组后的贵州能源集团高管职务。该集团系贵州省委、省政府于2023年2月整合盘江煤电与乌江能源组建的省管大型国有能源企业，资产超2000亿元，职工逾6.9万人，是我国长江以南最大煤炭企业和全国24家重点能源企业之一。

title: 光伏“小数点战争”：死磕0.1%的效率，却在后续环节轻易丢掉？-索比光伏网
content:
过去十余年，光伏技术完成了一场波澜壮阔的底层代际跃迁。从多晶到单晶，从PERC走向TOPCon、BC，光伏人习惯了用“转换效率”这个绝对量化的数字来丈量进步，因为它可精确测量、可直观排名、更极易在公众与资本市场中传播。
然而，当底层材料的革命性红利被逐渐吃透，光伏技术的演进不可避免地步入了以
0.1%为单位的“渐进式改进”深水区。在近期的行业角逐中，一线龙头大厂密集发布效率突破的喜报，但若仔细审视这些动辄引爆全网的新世界纪录，会发现巨头们在极限巅峰的身位差，已经被死死地压缩在了0.1%甚至更窄的区间。
光伏行业正陷入一场极度内卷的
“小数点战争”。
当行业为0.1个百分点投入巨大资源时，一个更值得全行业和电站业主正视的问题浮出水面：实验室里死磕出的0.1%效率提升，在真实系统应用和长达25年的电站生命周期中，到底能转化为多少发电量？带来多少真金白银？
真相是：在当前技术基准下，电池端提高
0.1%的绝对效率，难比登天；但在后续电站设计、施工、运维乃至日常风雨中，丢掉这0.1%甚至几十倍于此的真实发电量和收益，却并不罕见。
但价值评价需更完整
要理解当下效率竞争，必须看到光伏行业决策机制的现实。在终端招投标中，效率仍是重要入场券与溢价筹码。央国企组件集采往往将效率作为核心标尺，效率每微升
0.1%或0.2%，就能在评标中获得加分。在分毫必争的当下，这零点几分可能改变上亿元大单走向。
在资本与媒体共振中，效率数字也是极佳的叙事工具。“打破世界纪录、效率再创新高”拥有强视觉冲击，是新闻标题，也是估值故事素材。
这些机制并非没有合理性。效率提升曾经是光伏降本的核心引擎，未来也仍将是技术竞争的重要维度。问题在于，当行业进入微增量阶段，如果仍把单一正面效率作为唯一标尺，就容易掩盖实验室效率与量产效率的鸿沟，也容易忽略真实环境下发电收益的复杂性。
行业需要一场认知升级
不是抛弃效率，而是让效率回归系统价值
如果把评判战场从恒温恒湿、光照一致、一尘不染的实验室，搬到狂风肆虐、昼夜温差剧烈、沙尘弥漫的真实电站，为0.1%效率差算一笔全生命周期账，会发现参数内卷需要重新校准。
加法端，是不断提升的技术投入。在现有电池结构下，转换效率提升
0.1%，往往需要研发团队进入更精细的微观尺度，提升钝化层均匀性，收窄银浆栅线宽度。这0.1%背后，是尖端研发设备折旧、较贵的贵金属耗材，以及更严格的生产环境与良率控制。
减法端，则是容易被忽视的收益折损。设计考虑不足形成
“木桶效应”，施工中组件踩踏，运维不及时造成遮挡，消纳不足带来弃光限电，发电量预测偏差被电网考核……前端投入需要长期积累，后端折损却可能在不经意间发生，终端业主的收益也会受到影响。
真实的户外场景中，组件必须直面暴雪重压与台风撕扯，计算电气与复杂环境带来的真实耗损，也不能忽视绝缘与封装材料带来的长期隐患。组件隐裂、电流失配、功率衰减、杂物遮挡，都可能让发电收益缩水，甚至留下安全隐患。
反过来，如果跳出电池片单一维度，在封装材料、产品设计、系统适配方面综合创新，带来的发电效率提升往往更明显，也更稳健。算清这笔账，结论并非否定电池效率，而是：唯功率论的小数点战争，需要升级为系统价值竞争。终端投资者真正渴求的，不是实验室极限测试报告，而是历经
25年风霜雨雪后仍能稳定输出的真实发电收益。
晶澳“结构效率”给出破局思路
随着光伏产业迈向高质量发展深水区，商业逻辑正在从粗放规模竞赛转向纵深价值比拼。终端市场已经率先寻找更科学、多维的价值评价体系。
在产业界，已经有头部企业发出呼吁，摒弃唯正面效率论，建立以“组件综合效率与综合发电”为核心考量的新型评价指标。这是行业内部对内卷式消耗的深刻反思。
在监管端，工信部最新发布的光伏组件分级新规中，评价维度明显扩展：系统可靠性被赋予
40%权重，发电性能占40%，绿色属性占20%。这并非简单标准修订，而是对“小数点战争”的有力纠偏：优秀组件必须在25年真实自然考验中，证明结构坚韧、发电稳定与环境友好
在这一背景下，晶澳提出的“结构效率”值得关注。它并非否定电池效率，而是跳出单点正面效率博弈，从组件整体结构出发，将有效发电面积、电流损耗、结构稳定性、环境适应性、全生命周期衰减等纳入系统框架，最终指向真实场景下的综合发电能力和客户价值。
DeepBlue 5.0是这一理念的落地：三分片降低电流损耗，提升抗遮挡能力；柔性互联压缩片间距，提升有效发电面积；高绝缘边界密封释放爬电距离限制。反映到客户端，DeepBlue 5.0主流版型达670W、24.8%效率，并在BOS成本优化、投资回报改善和全周期收益提升上体现客户价值。
从单一参数竞争走向系统价值竞争
效率从来不是目的，而是降低度电成本、提升客户价值的手段。中国光伏下一阶段，不是放弃效率，也不是否定行业，而是让效率回归系统价值。过去，行业用效率数字丈量进步；未来，还需要用真实发电、长期可靠和客户回报来定义优秀。
从实验室的0.1%走向真实环境的全面增益，中国光伏需要一套跳出单一参数比拼的新框架。谁能率先完成从参数竞争到系统价值的跨越，谁就更可能在下一个十年掌握主动。全新的系统级效率理念如何落地？怎样改变一座电站的投资回报模型？这将是全行业接下来共同思考的重点。

title: Vopak and Vattenfall partner to support the Dutch renewable energy transition
content:
Vopak and Vattenfall partner to support the Dutch renewable energy transition TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Vopak and Vattenfall partner to support the Dutch renewable energy transition
Infrastructure provider Royal Vopak has signed a milestone tolling agreement
with Vattenfall, marking a key step in the expansion of its energy storage
business.
The agreement follows Vopak's recent investment in battery energy storage
infrastructure. Its 150MW/600MWh project is designed to support the Dutch
energy transition, including the integration of offshore wind power, by
storing surplus electricity and supplying it back to the grid when demand
Under the partnership, Vattenfall will have access to 100MW/400MWh of battery
storage capacity to help balance fluctuations in electricity supply.
"Vopak's purpose is to help the world flow forward. We are known for
the safe storage of vital energy products and are actively shaping a sustainable
future by investing in energy transition infrastructure."
"We are excited to have Vattenfall as a long-term partner," said
Jarno Veldhoven, vice president of business development for battery energy
storage systems at Vopak.
Vopak said the partnership comes at a time when renewable energy is accounting
for an increasing share of the energy mix. The company said the combination
of Vopak's infrastructure expertise and Vattenfall's market presence will
help support the transition to a more sustainable energy system.
The agreement follows Vopak's recent acquisition of a majority stake in
Green Energy Storage (GES) in the Netherlands, further demonstrating its
strategy to expand its energy transition infrastructure portfolio.

title: US government pushes for new review of Revolution Wind permit
content:
The US government has filed a cross-motion for summary judgment in the
legal challenge over Ørsted's
Revolution
Wind offshore wind project.
The filing seeks dismissal of claims against the National Marine Fisheries
Service and the US Army Corps of Engineers.
The US Department of the Interior has also said the court should remand,
or send back, its approval of the project's Construction and Operations
Plan (COP) for further review, stating that it will reassess compliance
with the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act.
They argued that if the COP approval is remanded, the court does not need
to consider the plaintiffs' remaining claims challenging Interior's approval.
The latest filing follows a January 2026 court ruling that granted Revolution
Wind a preliminary injunction against a suspension order issued by the
Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) in December 2025.
TGS | 4C Market Analyst Dan Wiseman said: “This isn’t likely to have
any serious near-term implications for the project itself, but the administration
putting its foot in the door just as Revolution Wind was about to close
it on construction is another headache the project doesn’t need.”
“It shows uncertainty for investors about the safety of their capital,
especially as it gives the administration a potential lever to pull later.
That said, Ørsted has the same judge who previously blocked the government’s
stop-work orders, so we’ll have to see how much weight that carries.”

title: Aventa expands offshore services with ISC acquisition
content:
Aventa has acquired Irish Sea Contractors (ISC), expanding its capabilities
across cable landfalls, marine infrastructure, commercial diving and subsea
cable repair.
The deal combines ISC's 40 years of experience in marine civil engineering,
commercial diving and cable projects with Aventa's expertise in marine
energy and offshore transmission infrastructure. The companies said the
partnership will enable them to offer a broader range of services across
the lifecycle of offshore energy and subsea cable projects.
As part of the acquisition, Aventa's customers will gain access to AERSUB,
ISC's DNV qualified subsea cable repair solution. The companies said the
integration will also strengthen support during the early stages of project
development, helping to improve continuity between project planning, engineering
and offshore execution.
"ISC brings experienced teams, established client relationships and
a strong record of delivering complex marine work. Together, we can support
a wider range of projects and take greater responsibility across their
lifecycle," said Antoine Bosc, CEO and co-founder of Aventa.
Aurélien Zuccarini,
chief growth and talent officer and co-founder of Aventa, said the partnership
would help bridge the gap between project development and offshore operations.
"Clients benefit when knowledge moves smoothly from engineering and
planning into offshore execution," Zuccarini said.

title: Pacifico Energy Vietnam launches first offshore wind survey campaign
content:
Pacifico Energy Vietnam has launched its first offshore technical survey
campaign in partnership with Petrovietnam Technical Services Corporation
(PTSC), marking a key milestone in the development of its offshore wind
portfolio.
The survey forms part of a broader programme supporting the 500 MW Nam
1.3 GW Nam Trung Bo 3 offshore wind projects, following the approval of
sea survey licences by Vietnam's Ministry of Agriculture and Environment
earlier this year.
The campaign will begin with geophysical surveys to assess seabed topography,
geological conditions and overall site characteristics, providing critical
data for project development.
Together, the projects are expected to support Vietnam's renewable energy
ambitions, with the potential to attract more than $6 billion in investment
while strengthening the country's domestic offshore wind supply chain.
In its announcement, Pacifico Energy said it looks forward to working closely
with authorities, local governments and industry partners to successfully
advance the projects.

title: Seaway 7 confirms sale of Seaway Moxie support vessel
content:
Seaway 7 has confirmed the sale of its installation support vessel, Seaway
Moxie, to offshore wind walk-to-work vessel specialist CBED.
The vessel has been in service since 2014 and helped set new industry standards
for safe and efficient personnel transfer and installation support operations.
Seaway Moxie measures 74 metres in length and 17 metres in breadth. The
vessel is equipped with a 3D motion-compensated extendable boom crane,
an offshore access gangway transfer system and an active motion-compensated
gangway.
According to Seaway 7, the sale reflects the company's continued focus
on its core offshore wind installation activities, while providing greater
flexibility to source support vessel capacity according to the requirements
of individual projects.
Despite the transaction, Seaway Moxie will continue supporting Seaway 7's
existing commitments and is expected to remain on contract with the company
until early 2028.

title: OpenAI’s Math Breakthroughs Rattle Cryptography Leaders
content: OpenAI’s release last Tuesday of more than 300 math results it says an internal model solved has sparked concern among some of the world’s leading cryptographers, or experts in encoding information to keep it private and secure. They worry that AI’s continued math advances could find new algorithms that make our current methods of protecting information on encrypted services, from online payments to messaging platforms like WhatsApp, easier to crack. The basis for modern internet security is the assumption that some math operations are easy to do, such as a process of encoding using a number known as the public key. But they are hard to undo, or decode, without knowing a specific number, called the private key. This assumption of difficulty is the foundation of secure communication over the internet, which has helped enable e-commerce, cryptocurrencies and digital accounts. AI models from OpenAI and others, which have been solving problems that have stumped math experts for decades, have raised the prospect that powerful AI systems could find ways to solve those problems without that key. “I am anticipating a vast change in mathematics, cryptanalysis included,” said Whitfield Diffie , who helped invent public key cryptography in 1976 with the Diffie-Hellman key exchange algorithm , in an email to me. “I don’t know the timescale. A year is probably too soon; five may not be,” said Diffie, now a consulting scholar at the Stanford Center for International Security and Cooperation . Martin Hellman , a professor emeritus of electrical engineering at Stanford University who created public key encryption with Diffie, was more optimistic. He said he expected AI-aided attacks to disrupt cybersecurity in the short term. In the long term though, he expected people to better integrate AI as a tool to patch security holes. Such comments were more mild than some that rang out on X last week. “I think we might lose public key cryptography,” Matthew Green , a professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University and founder of encryption startup Zeutro , wrote after OpenAI’s math release. And Justin Drake , a security researcher at the Ethereum Foundation , called upon the blockchain industry to plan for “bunker mode ” due to possible AI advances in cryptocurrency. OpenAI’s Crypto Efforts Possibly increasing the alarm was the fact that OpenAI’s trove of math papers did not include any cryptography results. The absence caused some experts to speculate OpenAI was sitting on results it wasn’t sharing publicly. OpenAI may have chosen to disclose any cryptography discoveries to the U.S. government first because of their security importance, Green told The Information in an interview. There’s a chance the public might never find out about any such discoveries, says Hed Kovetz , CEO of cybersecurity firm Silverfort . OpenAI did not comment on whether it has tried to use internal models to solve cryptographic problems. Green said he believes AI companies have already put substantial resources into solving cryptography problems. Indeed, OpenAI has previously released theoretical results in quantum complexity and lattice cryptography it said were found by its latest model Astra , released in September. OpenAI has also employed prominent cryptography experts including Harvard University professor Boaz Barak , who has made breakthroughs on the limits of secrecy in cryptography and is a member of OpenAI’s technical staff. Green said he could imagine frontier AI in the next two years making a more fundamental break in elliptic curve cryptography, one of a small number of common encryption algorithms. “Things get really bad if that happens because it doesn't have to happen across too many problems, it just has to happen across two [algorithms]” to impact a large share of encryption, Green said. A single elliptic curve encryption algorithm called X25519 “ now secures the majority of Internet connections ,” web infrastructure and security company Cloudflare found in 2025. The loss of elliptic curve cryptography could necessitate a shift to less understood encryption methods that might be even less secure, Green said. Others are more skeptical of the possibility of AI breaking common encryption methods. “These are problems that we designed specifically for them being not breakable,” said Ewin Tang , a professor of computer science at Princeton University . Tang became something of a legend in math at age 18, when she disproved decades of quantum theory by finding classical algorithms that match the speed of quantum algorithms. Tang believes the implementation of the algorithms into code is likely to contain more vulnerabilities than the algorithms themselves. Still, while she expects widely-studied common algorithms to largely be safe, Tang said some less-studied encryption algorithms, including those meant to be unsolvable by quantum computers, could be solved or weakened by AI. Anthropic had already released results this July that largely broke one post-quantum algorithm, which had been proposed to the National Institute of Standards and Technology . Tang said more of the same could follow. Anthropic shared its July research in advance with the U.S. government and industry partners and plans to continue to disclose cryptography work, a spokesperson for Anthropic told The Information. “We will responsibly disclose and act on any significant findings if and when we find anything,” the spokesperson wrote. Here’s what else is going on… OpenAI’s Crime Thriller Moment The news Tuesday that the FBI had arrested a Saudi national working at OpenAI had all the makings of a crime thriller—or at least the pilot of one! The employee, a Saudi national who had previously worked at Meta , had allegedly inserted what OpenAI called a “sophisticated recording device,” wrapped in toilet paper, into the USB port in the back of a TV in a conference room used by its executives, the Justice Department said. But while the news spooked OpenAI employees, some very senior ones had already been girding for such attacks. Well before Dario Amodei left OpenAI to start Anthropic in 2021, he had pushed OpenAI to review research for potential “information hazard” risks that could potentially tip off U.S. adversaries like China, my colleagues reported in September . Amodei worried that China, Russia or other nations could hack into OpenAI and steal its research. In fact, he often wrote memos at home on an air-gapped computer, meaning one isolated from Wi-Fi and external networks, and printed out the memos to share with colleagues, rather than work in Google Docs. Such precautions don’t look so odd anymore! Overheard Microsoft has discussed making significant cost reductions in its Azure cloud unit, The Information reported late Tuesday. Girish Bablani , president of Microsoft’s Azure cloud unit, recently told senior leaders in his group to think about ideas for reducing costs by at least 20%. JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said on Tuesday that the bank is carefully monitoring its AI exposure as the capital expenditure demands of the AI buildout grow. JPMorgan also said it’s blocking external AI agents like Meta’s Muse and Instinct from accessing client accounts. Character.ai , a five-year-old startup that lets users create and interact with AI-powered personas, on Monday said it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy after encountering “significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds.” Court Watch A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the lawsuit Apple filed against the ChatGPT maker in July, alleging that it was stealing trade secrets. Apple will be able to view documents, like interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals and scripts, associated with OpenAI’s interviews with former Apple employees. title: Inside a TPG-Backed Accounting Firm’s Plans for AI and More Acquisitions
content: Smith + Howard, an accounting firm backed by private equity giant TPG that has grown in part by snapping up smaller firms, is gearing up for a new round of acquisitions—including two that could close by the end of the year. As it grows, the firm is exploring how AI could handle basic work where there’s “a lot of lather, rinse, repeat,” CEO Sean Taylor said. The firm is hoping AI will help it expand without having to hire accountants at the same pace it did previously—reflecting a broader bet among private equity firms and AI labs that the technology can help boost profits when consolidating professional services firms. Smith + Howard, which has more than 800 employees across seven states, expects to bring in about $175 million in revenue this year, a number that has grown around 10% to 15% annually for the past decade, excluding acquisitions. It was an active buyer of smaller firms under previous backer Broad Sky Partners, which sold its stake to TPG in August. Now it’s continuing that strategy, aiming to add another 20% to 25% of its 12-month forward revenue through acquisitions. It will likely lift its target size for acquisitions to between $5 million and $50 million in annual revenue versus $2 million to $20 million previously. Smith + Howard is planning more acquisitions in 2027. The Atlanta-based firm is seeking to expand in more U.S. cities and add services it typically refers to outside firms. It expects human work to remain central to its business and client relationships, but it is exploring AI to cut down on manual work and outside software costs when it makes sense. Private equity firms and AI labs have been touting the potential of AI to boost returns on portfolio companies, spurring partnerships including OpenAI’s majority-owned Deployment Co., which launched in May with backing from TPG and others to embed engineers inside businesses. Venture capital firms are getting in on the action too, with Thrive Capital launching Thrive Holdings last year to buy and modernize businesses such as accounting firms, while General Catalyst is pursuing AI-focused rollups . But there’s some debate about whether businesses will pass on the savings from AI to customers, which would wash out the technology’s financial benefits. Brian Goffman, managing director of AI at TPG, said the accounting industry has a track record of holding onto gains, with fees for services like audits continuing to climb after major cost-cutting moves in the sector like offshoring. “In some cases businesses are cutting costs or they’re becoming more efficient, but all the value gets passed on to the customer, which is a nice thing, but it’s sort of a race to the bottom,” he said. “In accounting, that doesn’t seem to be the case.” For Smith + Howard, the view that AI could boost accounting stood out at a time when private equity investors had split into two camps—“those that were very excited about how AI could affect our industry and those who were very scared of how AI could affect our industry,” fearing it would reduce billable hours and therefore revenue, said Taylor. Smith + Howard has rolled out Anthropic’s Claude companywide, allowing employees to experiment with it and suggest uses for it. That effort would likely start with automating some simple work in its core business, such as industry-specific audits, Taylor said, though complex financial statement audits would be much harder to automate. The firm is also evaluating ideas for new products it could sell to clients, and it’s searching for a C-suite executive to lead AI efforts. The accounting firm isn’t a customer of OpenAI’s private equity venture, though Goffman said that could change as the venture hires more technical experts to expand its capacity. TPG has other close relationships with AI firms including Anthropic, Microsoft and Google. Gauging Returns Private equity firms and large publicly traded companies have been consolidating professional services companies for years, pushing valuations up broadly. But AI is giving some investors a fresh reason to pay up for businesses they believe the technology can help grow and make more profitable. “We’ll pay more than the other firm because we know we can create that value” using AI, Goffman said. And firms like Smith + Howard that are growing in part through acquisitions could put AI capabilities to work in each subsequent deal, he said. At the same time, there’s a wide range of prices small accounting firms can fetch—ones with a solid client base but few tech or marketing capabilities are fetching multiples as low as five to six times Ebitda, whereas established firms taking direct private equity backing are approaching multiples of 12 times Ebitda or higher. Smith + Howard is targeting firms that fit somewhere in the middle, Taylor said. Meanwhile, payoffs from AI spending can be difficult to predict, and companies are grappling with how to forecast and manage the expenses of the technology. Smith + Howard, for its part, is tracking returns on investment month to month and accounting for expected costs and growth in five-year cash flow projections to determine when building in-house software makes sense. “We are monitoring it, but we definitely feel like the return is going to be there,” Taylor said. He said the firm is no stranger to internal tech work, with its own development team that’s been automating some processes for years and that previously built sales tax compliance software for in-house and client use. And through TPG, Smith + Howard has brought in outside AI trainers that partner with firms such as Anthropic. In return for a minimum spending commitment, they spend several weeks training employees to use the technology efficiently, Taylor said. AI also poses a challenge for private equity owners used to cost-cutting measures like offshoring, which can deliver savings that show up quickly in financials. AI work, by contrast, requires up-front investment and could take a few years to pay off. “In the short term, you’re actually spending money, and anyone who knows how to build AI products knows that…the pancake comes off the griddle sometimes not perfect,” Goffman said. TPG sees revenue per employee as the primary metric for tracking whether AI is translating into gains and is still trying to figure out what other measures make sense, Goffman said. For an accounting business, for instance, it might make sense to track how many audits a given employee can do.

title: OpenAI’s Bug and Bumble’s AI-Powered Exit
content: When is someone going to make a TV show set at OpenAI? It’s got swarms of rogue AI agents causing havoc across the internet, not to mention periodic corporate drama. And today we learned that an OpenAI engineer allegedly planted a “sophisticated recording device” inside a company conference room. The Justice Department identified the engineer—who has been arrested—as a Saudi national and revealed that the bug was attached to the back of a TV set in a conference room where “discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information” were often held. OpenAI is a gift that keeps on giving…to journalists everywhere. (Check out our scoop today about how OpenAI is trying to fix its safety issues). In other news, brace yourselves: We’re starting to see acquisitions of distressed companies dressed up as AI-driven purchases. At least, that’s how investment firm Ithaca Holdings described its deal, unveiled on Tuesday, to buy dating app Bumble at a $1.3 billion valuation. As Ithaca co-CEO Ravi Gupta, a former Sequoia partner, said in an X post , “Bumble stood out” from “hundreds of companies” Ithaca had reviewed to see which “would become more valuable as AI advances.” Sure, AI could improve Bumble’s service or at least make it more efficient. But Bumble could apply AI to its operations without being acquired. It could just hit up Google or Palantir for help: They send out AI consultants everyone loves to call “forward-deployed engineers” to help businesses adopt the new technology. The real reason Bumble is selling is surely that its business is troubled. Revenue fell 10% last year and another 15% in the first half of this year. The company had $450 million of debt as of June 30 but only $154 million in cash. That’s why it’s a bit hard to take at face value the “congrats” offered by Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky to Bumble’s founder and outgoing CEO, Whitney Wolfe Herd, in an X post Tuesday. Bumble is selling at $6.05 a share, one-seventh of its $43 a share IPO price. It’s not exactly the future Herd painted when the company went public. Then she wrote in Bumble’s IPO prospectus that the offering “marks the start of a very bright future for Bumble Inc, one that we believe will…drive great value for shareholders.” None of that is to say that Gupta and his co-CEO, former Meta Platforms executive John Hegeman, can’t turn Bumble around. Maybe Herd will turn out to be right, as she said in a statement on Tuesday, that “the best is yet to come.” It’s just a pity the public market investors who got burned won’t get a chance to participate in that bright future. Character’s Steady Slide Into Oblivion Another troubled company, early AI startup Character. AI, filed for bankruptcy on Monday in what’s likely to be one of the final steps in the company’s long slide into oblivion. Its investors probably didn’t mind too much, though, as they cashed out with a decent profit in 2024 when Google paid $2.7 billion to license Character.AI’s models. As part of that same deal, Character’s co-founders, former Google engineers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, rejoined Google. (Shazeer later bolted for OpenAI .) The Google licensing deal was one of a number of similar arrangements tech firms struck to get hold of key talent and technology from AI startups in 2024, also including a deal Microsoft did with Inflection AI and Amazon’s Adept one. By structuring them as licensing deals rather than acquisitions, the tech giants hoped to avoid antitrust scrutiny. ( Many of the deals got investigated anyway.) Sometimes what’s left survives: Inflection recently launched Inflection AI Labs , which it said was an effort to shape “the future of personal intelligence.” On the other hand, Adept’s website hasn’t been updated since mid-2024, shortly after its Amazon deal. Then there’s Character, which in mid-2025 hired Karandeep Anand , who had previously worked at Meta, as CEO. A few months later, we reported that Character was considering raising money. Things went in a different direction. Last month, Walt Disney Co. hired Anand as chief technology officer, along with other members of Character.AI’s technical team. Disney also has bid $20 million to license the company’s intellectual property as part of the bankruptcy process, Character said on Tuesday. In Other News • Candle Media, the Blackstone-backed media rollup effort run by former Disney executives Kevin Mayer and Tom Staggs, is selling Reese Witherspoon’s production company, Hello Sunshine, back to Witherspoon, along with French firm Mediawan), Bloomberg reported . Candle had bought the Hello Sunshine at a valuation of $900 million in 2021, considered a steep price at the time. • Apple is launching a tabletlike smart home device as part of a renewed push into the home. The $299 HomeView is a 7-inch screen that sits on kitchen counters or mounts on walls. Apple said it is designed for watching and listening to content as well as smart home management. • JPMorgan said it’s blocking external AI agents like Meta’s Muse and Instinct from accessing client accounts. “We’re not going to allow just any outside agent to come in inside the company because that’s just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan,” said Jamie Dimon, CEO of the bank, on its third-quarter earnings call on Tuesday. title: OpenAI Eyes Acquisition That Could Boost Cybersecurity Business
content: OpenAI, which is trying to develop a substantial cybersecurity business, is in early talks to buy Trail of Bits, a firm that finds and fixes vulnerabilities in open-source software, according to people familiar with the matter. The size of the potential deal couldn’t be learned. OpenAI has sometimes paid in the low hundreds of millions of dollars in the form of stock to acquire small startups, though it sometimes pays less. Discussions are ongoing and the deal could fall apart, said the people. The startup’s staff could aid one of OpenAI’s most promising business opportunities. This year, OpenAI and its archrival Anthropic have tried to one-up each other in developing specialized AI for identifying vulnerabilities in software. Founded in 2012, Trail of Bits provides security research and tools while helping to maintain open-source projects. It has a team of more than 40 employees, mostly security engineers, according to its website. Instead of typical venture funding, it received a grant of around $10,000 from the Department of Defense in 2015 and a $1 million loan in 2020 from the federal paycheck protection program. In June, the startup partnered with OpenAI to work on a software-patching initiative, Patch the Planet. Staff from Trail of Bits work on open-source projects, such as the popular programming language Python, to find, review and fix bugs, with the help of OpenAI Codex tools, including models specialized for cybersecurity. “We had a lot of existing relationships in the open source community and have earned their trust over more than a decade of work,” said Trail of Bits CEO Dan Guido in a promotional video announcing Patch the Planet. “Codex enabled our team to ship things in a day that would have otherwise taken us weeks of time.” Security has been a focus for AI labs as models have advanced. Hackers have already used publicly available AI in a slew of cyberattacks around the world, according to independent security researchers. Last week, Crowdstrike said the perpetrator of a recent hack of South Korean financial institutions used  an open-source Chinese AI agent and Chinese large language models. OpenAI and Anthropic, in coordination with the White House, have allowed other large businesses to use their most advanced models to find and patch security vulnerabilities in their own software. The AI providers have neutered such capabilities for models they have released to the broader public because of the potential for malicious actors to use the models in attacks. Cybersecurity software firms such as Palo Alto Networks also have utilized models from OpenAI and Anthropic to boost the products they sell to businesses. In another sign of its ambitions in cybersecurity, OpenAI recently hired Dali Rajic, a former executive at the Google-owned cloud cybersecurity unit Wiz, as its chief revenue officer.

title: Microsoft Cloud President Asks Leaders to Find 20% Cost Cuts
content: Microsoft has discussed making significant cost reductions in its Azure cloud-server-rental unit, according to a person with direct knowledge of the situation. Girish Bablani, president of Azure, in recent weeks told senior leaders in his group, which has about 11,500 employees, to come up with ideas to reduce costs at least 20%, though it isn’t clear if such a reduction would include layoffs, according to the person. The discussion comes even as Azure’s revenue growth has accelerated, a sign of how heavily Microsoft’s data center spending is weighing on its finances. The company hasn’t finalized any cost-cutting measures and they could change, this person said. Bablani oversees just one unit within Azure; the broader cloud division has around 60,000 employees total. Bablani’s unit develops software for the cloud server business and isn’t part of the Azure data center team. A Microsoft spokesperson said in a statement: “Azure leadership has not directed teams to develop cost-cutting plans. Every responsible company prepares for a range of scenarios and market dynamics, both positive and negative. This is inaccurate and careless reporting.” To lower some costs, Microsoft could part ways with contractors who work for the cloud unit, said the person with knowledge of the discussions. In recent months, some leaders at Azure have privately pointed to another reason for the potential cuts aside from the costly data center spending: the costs of talent retention. As Microsoft’s AI rivals such as Anthropic and Meta have hired or tried to hire the company’s employees, Microsoft has had to counter such competitive offers, said a person with knowledge of the situation. Azure chief Scott Guthrie has also discussed a desire to increase AI spending budgets for existing employees as the company automates more tasks, this person said. Microsoft has been increasing its spending on AI per employee in recent months, and has been encouraging staff to use AI to increase productivity in realms like sales and software development. Microsoft’s total headcount was slightly lower as of June compared to a year earlier, following several waves of job cuts and voluntary buyouts. Microsoft cloud chief Scott Guthrie in 2024. Photo via Getty Other major cloud providers including Oracle and Amazon Web Services have also made cuts, including layoffs, despite boosting revenue growth after their rising capital expenditures for AI data centers have hurt their respective free cash flows. The discussions at Microsoft come as the company reorganizes the cloud unit around senior executive Arun Ulag. He is among a small group of leaders CEO Satya Nadella has been elevating in recent months as numerous longtime senior executives have pared down their roles or retired. Ulag, who previously oversaw Azure’s database products, will now also oversee executives who work on Azure Core, which provides computing power to customers such as OpenAI. The executives include Bablani, Billy Anders, Douglas Phillips and Mark Russinovich, the people said. Guthrie, who announced the changes internally Monday, said Ulag will continue to report to him. Charlie Bell, who previously led Microsoft’s security business before stepping into an advisory role earlier this year, will also now join Ulag’s leadership team while still reporting to CEO Satya Nadella, said the person with direct knowledge of the reorg. That’s another sign of Ulag’s rise at Azure. Azure has long been a key growth engine for the company, but Microsoft only started breaking out the unit’s revenue in dollar terms last month. It said Azure generated $101.9 billion in revenue in the 12 months ending in June, up 40% from the previous year and 43% in the June quarter alone. In comparison, AWS generated nearly $150 billion in revenue in the same full-year period, including 37% growth in the second quarter of this year. While Azure’s 40% revenue growth was impressive, it has been negatively affected by Microsoft’s decision at the start of last year to pause a slew of data center projects, The Information has reported. Still, the unit now represents about 31% of Microsoft’s total revenue. At the same time, spending on AI data centers is taking a toll on its cash generation. The company generated $20 billion in free cash flow in the June quarter, up more than $4 billion from the cash it generated in the first quarter but down 20% compared to its free cash flow in the second quarter of last year.

title: OpenAI Scrambles to Fix Safety Issues Before Shipping Its Next Flagship Model
content: OpenAI is grappling with fallout from its use of a controversial innovation in AI design as it works to get its next unreleased model to a place where leaders believe they can safely release it. The model design, known as loop transformers or recurrent depth, can make it harder to monitor the way the AI “thinks,” or how it reasons and processes its response to a question or task, The Information reported last month . That means the technique could erode a key tool that OpenAI and other companies rely on to catch misbehaving models. OpenAI hasn’t publicly acknowledged the technique, but Microsoft last week accidentally confirmed OpenAI’s use of it in one of the AI company’s most advanced commercially available models, GPT-6.1 Sol, in a blog post it has since edited to remove the disclosure. Internal concerns about the use of loop transformers also appear to be connected to the work of three safety researchers whom OpenAI recently fired and who are now publicly feuding with the company over the circumstances of their dismissal. In a letter sent last week to OpenAI’s board directors and other safety advisors to the company, the three researchers emphasized that they didn’t disclose the use of loop transformers to The Information, but said that the company needs to take steps to ensure that the “thinking” of frontier models remains monitorable. The researchers also said they’d been involved in work with other companies, which OpenAI had sanctioned, to limit the development of “unmonitorable architectures” for AI. OpenAI has said in response to the letter that the firings weren’t related to researchers sharing safety concerns. “Safety and research debates happen every day at OpenAI, often spirited and highly critical,” OpenAI research leaders wrote in a recent memo. “We actively encourage these discussions and consider them essential to making the right decisions.” The company didn’t comment on its usage of loop transformers, but the memo said the research leaders agree “that preserving the monitorability of frontier models requires an industry-wide commitment, including from OpenAI.” Still, the researchers’ dismissal has raised anxiety among some other employees as well as outside AI safety advocates about whether OpenAI is seeking to discourage staffers who flag safety issues with its models. The feud involving researchers has played out as OpenAI has been in an all-hands-on-deck mode to prepare its next major model for commercial release, after publicly announcing its decision to halt the release of a different, less-capable model due to safety concerns. Preparing the new model—which a person familiar with the situation said also uses loop transformers—could take a while. The process involves getting the new model to align its objectives with what OpenAI researchers and customers want, and securing the software being used to test the model’s capabilities, employees say. After leaders get comfortable with the model’s performance on safety evaluations, OpenAI will need to share the model with the U.S. government for testing up to 30 days before it can share the model with trusted partners and then broadly release it, one employee said. OpenAI agreed to such a process following an executive order from President Trump regarding evaluations of advanced AI. Even still, OpenAI is likely to release one or two new models by the end of the year, if not the major upgraded model it is racing to prepare, employees said. Shifting More Compute to Safety Work The increased focus on safety and security at OpenAI comes after a spree of AI-powered breaches caused by the company, including most prominently an incident this summer where a swarm of OpenAI agents broke out of a testing environment and gained access to open-source repository Hugging Face and other businesses. The AI agents did so despite acknowledging in writing that they weren’t supposed to. The agents’ acknowledgement is the kind of legible reasoning that looping architectures threaten to hide. Other AI developers including Anthropic, Google and Meta have experienced similar AI-powered breaches in recent months. Last week, Anthropic said that its AI had used the internet to inadvertently fill out government forms with incomplete information and also submitted a false homicide crime tip to the Philadelphia police department. Model Fallout : A Timeline of Events Since the Hugging Face Incident July 2026 July 2026 July 2026 • OpenAI discloses Hugging Face breach by agents powered by GPT‑5.6 Sol and a more capable, unreleased model. Aug. 2026 Aug. 2026 Aug. 2026 • OpenAI says the agents were trying to cheat on an evaluation by finding solutions online. Sept. 2026 Sept. 2026 Sept. 2026 • The Information reports that OpenAI is using recurrent depth or looped transformers in new models. • OpenAI’s chief scientist says it is prioritizing making AI reasoning legible to humans. • OpenAI says its AI accessed parts of the Department of Education website and improperly interacted with sites run by the SEC. • OpenAI commits to embedding outside safety evaluators in its offices, following similar Anthropic commitment. • OpenAI fires three safety researchers. One, Tomek Korbak, said he was told he was fired over how he communicated with METR, a safety organization OpenAI partnered with to investigate the Hugging Face incident. • FTC says it is investigating OpenAI, Anthropic and others over consumer safety issues. Oct. 2026 Oct. 2026 Oct. 2026 • Microsoft inadvertently confirms GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Sol use looped inference. • The three researchers publish a letter calling for industrywide safety measures. • OpenAI says a thorough investigation found the researchers violated policies on handling sensitive information, which they deny. • OpenAI staff work on safety measures to prepare its next flagship model. • OpenAI says it is “finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors” and will announce details soon. In the wake of the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI shifted about 10% of its total computational resources, or hundreds of megawatts of data center capacity, toward so-called alignment and safety work, a person with knowledge of the figure said late last month. It isn’t clear how many servers were previously dedicated to such work or what the current level is, but renting that amount would cost OpenAI a minimum of billions of dollars on an annual basis at the current market rate. OpenAI also has poured resources into efforts to beef up security around its AI. For instance, a number of engineers and researchers are focused on “hardening” the digital sandboxes that are supposed to keep unreleased models away from the internet and other software during testing, according to an employee. Such sandboxes were a key channel through which OpenAI’s AI agents escaped during the Hugging Face breach. Amid those safety concerns, OpenAI’s use of loop transformers has been a sensitive aspect of its model development. OpenAI uses such looping in both its model training and inference, when its completed models handle tasks for customers. The Microsoft disclosure about OpenAI’s use of the technique came in a technical description of GPT-6.1 Sol. OpenAI launched that model earlier this month, saying it performs nearly as well as its recent flagship GPT-6 Astra at a much lower price. Microsoft, which has access to OpenAI’s intellectual property, said in the now-deleted section of its post that the model relies on looping inference, or a form of reasoning where the model thinks through the same problem in multiple “passes” before generating an answer. GPT-6.1 Sol “uses the same base model weights as GPT-6 Sol with two inference passes instead of three,” according to a copy of the webpage viewed by The Information. That description was an accurate summary of what OpenAI privately shared with Microsoft about the model, according to someone with direct knowledge of the situation. Microsoft later removed the passage after realizing it was meant to be kept secret, this person said. Looping models repeatedly process the same problem in ways humans can’t read. OpenAI has limited its use of loops with Astra so the model still produces legible information about its reasoning, known as chain of thought, and the company’s researchers can still sufficiently monitor it. The company says it’s working hard to preserve that legibility despite new challenges that have made it harder, separate from any changes to its models’ architecture. Plugging Security Holes in Other Software Beyond the work to make models safer, engineers at OpenAI have also been focused on finding security vulnerabilities in various types of software the company uses internally. For example, in recent weeks, engineers found vulnerabilities and wrote patches for FFmpeg, popular open-source software that’s used to process videos, said a person with knowledge of the incident. Engineers also found a number of vulnerabilities in open-source software the company uses to convert data into a widely-used format called JavaScript Object Notation,which AI models often use in giving responses that require a consistent structure, the person said. It’s important for OpenAI to fix these vulnerabilities because they represent potential avenues for AI models to conduct cyberattacks, the person said. However, AI has also helped engineers find these vulnerabilities and patch them much more quickly, they said. The recent focus on safety and security has especially helped to elevate OpenAI’s security team internally, the person said. That team is led by Chief Information Security Officer Dane Stuckey, who previously held the same position at Palantir and who reports to OpenAI Co-founder and President Greg Brockman. Many of the incidents the security team works on are closely guarded, as leaders are concerned that if bad actors within or outside the company were to learn of these vulnerabilities, they would be able to more easily exploit them, the person said. OpenAI is also making changes to its process for starting so-called training runs to develop more-advanced AI. One change requires leaders to write documentation, otherwise known as safety cases, explaining the risks of the training run and why they believe it’s safe to proceed with it. The company in a blog post last month outlined some of these changes, which are either already in place or will be soon, a person with knowledge of the situation said. Those changes include requiring several leaders to sign off on each safety case, each with the power to singlehandedly veto the training run; holding the senior leader responsible for a training run accountable for any incidents as part of their performance reviews; and implementing a system that will either automatically pause a training run or alert an employee if an incident occurs. Outside evaluators who get special access to unreleased models for safety or performance testing have also received instructions from OpenAI in recent months to have stricter cybersecurity protocols, including to use two factor authentication and to have special processes for monitoring models when they’re running, said a person from one of these evaluation organizations.

title: Why Companies Can't Prove Their AI Spending Pays Off
content: The trillion-dollar question of the AI boom is whether businesses’ spending on the technology pays off. But measuring that return is often uncertain, confusing or incomplete. That’s because it takes time for AI to show a return on investment that can be demonstrated in a company’s income statement, as we’ve written . A new study from the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School and GBK Collective, a consultancy, echoes this idea, showing that most companies are still tracking ROI by measuring whether it makes their workers more efficient rather than whether it is driving more revenue. The study, based on online surveys of 1,400 U.S.-based employees from firms that have at least 1,000 staff and generate more than $50 million annually, showed that 40% of managers measured AI’s impact on their business in terms of “hours saved per employee” and 37% tracked how AI reduced their workers’ errors. Only about 27% of managers said they track the revenue they generate from AI features, apps and tools they provide to their customers. Perhaps worryingly, 44% of managers said that over the next one to two years, AI’s primary role will be to improve productivity and just 8% said it would be to drive new revenue or create new products. Of course, improving productivity isn’t something to sneeze at, especially when it means that companies are using AI to replace labor for things like external contractors, customer service or responding to IT support tickets. Still, Jeremy Korst, one of the Wharton study’s authors, said it was “very difficult” to find “actual, materially measurable financial impacts” from AI spending. Today, measuring returns is more about vibes and managers’ “perception” of a return, rather than hard numbers, he said. AI is still in the early rollout phase, he said, so this level of return is “normal” or in line with previous technology adoption cycles. Some 80% of managers in the study reported positive returns from using AI, and many of them work in IT, finance or HR. But the 28% of managers who went a step further to say their organization was showing “strongly positive” returns were also more likely to work at companies that measure AI returns based on “growth outcomes” such as new revenues generated, not just cost savings from worker productivity, Korst said. (In comparison, 35% of The Information subscribers—which tend to be from technology businesses and investment firms— said in a recent survey that they were getting a “multiple” return on their AI spending, though only 52% of respondents said they were getting a positive return overall.) In our own reporting, examples of non-tech firms getting revenue gains from AI seem to be few and far between. Novo Nordisk previously told us it built AI agents to audit and coordinate clinical trials , with expected additional revenue in the tens or hundreds of millions of dollars a year. And Walmart CEO David Guggina said during the Goldman Sachs technology conference in September that customers using its AI assistant Sparky spent 40% more on their orders on average. Most other examples cited in this column over the years showcase labor and time savings. The Wharton study suggests that corporate spending on AI will keep rising quickly only if companies show a strong return on that spending, linking it to growth outcomes such as new revenue from AI and higher output, such as how much equipment a manufacturer produces, rather than cost-cutting. For now, though, spending is rising at a decent clip. About 45% of managers said their companies are set to spend $10 million or more on AI this year, up from 39% in 2025. But substantial increases in AI budgets may not be as plentiful in 2027, the study suggested. Just 10% of managers in the survey said they expect their company’s AI spending to rise “substantially” in the coming 12 months, compared to 19% of managers who said so in 2025. One bright spot: Companies may be getting better at tracking their AI spending. Some 40% of managers in the survey said they were “very” confident in their company’s ability to track such spending, and another 39% said they were “fairly confident.” Just 17% were “somewhat confident.” Workday Joins Salesforce in Providing ‘Headless’ Option Workday on Tuesday revealed new tools that let customers use AI agents made by firms such as Anthropic, Microsoft and OpenAI to automate tasks in their Workday accounts more effectively. The tools are similar to Salesforce’s SIforce, which last month was known as AIforce and, before then, Headless 360. As I reported in detail last week , some employees and investors worry that Workday and Salesforce’s new tools are effectively a capitulation to the new crop of AI providers, and that the software firms will become “dumb” infrastructure, or glorified databases. But Workday and Salesforce leaders say they’ll make plenty of money this way. “I would basically say we‘re giving customers choice,” CEO Aneel Bhusri said in a press briefing ahead of the company’s customer conference in Las Vegas. “We do have a user experience that is direct through Workday, through Sana [Workday’s AI platform] that is absolutely world class. But if a customer wants to choose headless”—meaning, using another company’s AI to access Workday—“that’s fine,” he said. “I'd always prefer if they use our user interface, but headless will be equally good for Workday.” Workday will charge customers based on how often they use AI agents to tap connectors and perform actions in Workday starting in February of 2027, at the end of the company’s “grace period” for customers to use such tools without extra fees. title: The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
content:
The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
Plus: The FBI has arrested an OpenAI engineer accused of snooping.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The US military’s race to make fake blood
In February 2007, a US military helicopter carrying blood to a field hospital was shot down in Iraq, killing all seven crew members. The mission was a reminder of the risks of transporting blood, which has a limited shelf life and is often in short supply.
Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. The idea is to develop dried blood products that can be stored for long periods and deployed quickly on the battlefield.
The project aims to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. But getting it all done will be tough, and researchers still have major questions about the safety and effectiveness of synthetic alternatives.
Discover how the military hopes to make blood last longer.
—Andrew Rosenblum

10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: WeLion New Energy and its semi-solid-state batteries
WeLion New Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.

Explore WeLion’s push to make safer, higher-capacity batteries.
—You Xiaoying

MIT Technology Review Narrated: Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers
Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds. They might also slow the aging process.
Drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their GLP-1 drugs age less quickly, according to molecular “aging clocks” that track changes in DNA or levels of key proteins.
The findings add to speculation that GLP-1 drugs could be acting on basic causes of aging and might be true longevity treatments. But how much can we read into these results?
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads

One more thing
Is the Pentagon allowed to surveil Americans with AI?

Surprisingly, the answer is not straightforward. More than a decade after Edward Snowden exposed the NSA’s collection of bulk metadata from the phones of Americans, the US is still navigating a gap between what ordinary people think and what the law allows.
Today, the legal complexity has a new edge: AI is supercharging surveillance—and our laws haven’t caught up. Here’s how the Pentagon’s use of AI has exposed legal gray areas.
